How NBC News Projects Races

The NBC News Decision Desk provides real-time, accurate election results as soon as they are made available by election officials, and independently analyzes vote tallies to decide when races can be projected. Projecting a winner means that the Decision Desk has determined that the trailing candidates cannot catch the leader and that the leading candidate will win the race. This determination is made through a comprehensive analysis, and the Decision Desk only projects a race when it is certain of the outcome.
How are votes counted?
In the 2026 primaries, vote data will be collected in all 50 states for statewide offices, the House of Representatives, key ballot measures and other races of national interest. The Associated Press provides election results data to NBC News and other major news organizations. Data collection is done through multiple sources on Election Day, with data reporters and interviewers across the country calling in county- and precinct-level results on a timely and rolling basis all day long. Vote data is also collected through state and county websites and feeds.
How does NBC News ensure accuracy?
Vote results are rigorously checked and verified. Part of quality control involves checking that vote data is consistent across sources, and we also compare the vote to past election results to see whether the results look extremely different across multiple past races. All projections are made independently of other outlets.

news.title: Sara Haines splits from ‘The View’ hosts by defending Rep. Haley Stevens’ GOP endorsement
news.text:
“The View” co-host Sara Haines defended Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., during a discussion on Monday about the Democrat’s decision to endorse Michigan Republican US Senate candidate Mike Rogers over Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, pushing back against critics who called the endorsement a betrayal.

Co-hosts Sunny Hostin and Ana Navarro both argued that Stevens endorsed Rogers for the wrong reasons, with Hostin saying, “Shame on her,” if the move was motivated by a bruised ego. Stevens said during an interview on Sunday that it was El-Sayed’s “anger” and “lack of kindness” that led her to endorse Rogers.

“I disagree. And I actually think that, although there’s a lot of Islamophobia here that are muddying the waters, there are deep concerns about his beliefs,” Haines said. “Campaigning with Hasan Piker, you could not put enough room between me and that man. And we went after the Republicans for going around with Nick Fuentes, also problematic.” 

“We have got to know when we denounce someone,” she continued. “And if crossing party lines can be an act of conscience for Liz Cheney, I don’t know why the automatic response was that this was betrayal somehow.” 

Haines, a registered independent, said Stevens’ decision was “brave.”

“Integrity is not just backing your party when you support your party,” the co-host added. “The real test is backing them when it costs you something. I keep hearing, ‘Donald Trump is so dangerous,’ and that is true, but that can’t end every conversation we have about what we’re willing to accept on our own sides.” 

“Honestly, the hateful rhetoric and demeaning language, I don’t have to agree with a candidate on everything at all, and compromise is absolutely necessary, but you cannot loan your loyalty and support out to a party,” Haines continued. “They must earn it every single time. And that’s why this was actually a very brave thing for her to do.”

Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital in a statement, “Haines’s defense is hard to square with the facts. I was one of the early Democrats who said El-Sayed needed to put real distance between himself and Hasan Piker. And he did. He said Piker did not speak for his campaign, stopped campaigning with him, and reportedly even called him directly to say his rhetoric was hurting the campaign and counterproductive. That all happened well before Haley Stevens’s last-minute endorsement.” 

“So Haines is using an issue El-Sayed already addressed to excuse this wild switch-up, while openly acknowledging the Islamophobia on the other side and then instantly brushing past it,” he added.

Shroff argued that Haines was treating hate from one side as disqualifying, but not the other, and said, “That is not principled, balanced, or reasonable. It is just a glaring double standard.”

Co-host Whoopi Goldberg brought up the timing of the endorsement as Haines argued that El-Sayed had also told Stevens he did not want her to campaign with him.

Navarro reiterated that she believed Stevens’ decision was motivated by El-Sayed’s reluctance to have her at the event.

Fellow co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin said that Stevens had raised “real issues” about antisemitism.

Griffin also compared Stevens endorsing Rogers with Liz Cheney endorsing former Vice President Kamala Harris earlier in the segment.

“We shouldn’t just praise independents when Liz Cheney breaks with Republicans, because she thinks that’s the principled position. If this woman feels this is the principled position for her, she has every right to do that,” Griffin said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the El-Sayed and Rogers campaigns for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Shroff argued the Cheney comparison did not hold up, telling Fox News Digital, “Cheney crossed party lines because of Trump’s conduct and her stated concerns about democracy. Stevens, by contrast, says she is crossing party lines because she cannot tolerate hate, yet she is endorsing Mike Rogers in a race where anti-Muslim hate has been Rogers’s central campaign strategy.”

“Moreover, Haley still maintains that Republicans — folks like Mike Rogers — are allowing Trump to act as a ‘dictator.’ It just doesn’t add up any way you try,” he said.
news.summary: Co-host compares Stevens crossing party lines to Liz Cheney's decision to back Kamala Harris

news.title: Democrats likely to gain control of Congress in US midterm elections as Senate lead expands
news.text:
The Democrats have an 82% chance of gaining control of the Senate in the US midterm elections this week, and remain overwhelming favourites to gain control of the House of Representatives in US analyst Nate Silver’s forecast model. In the last week, there has been clear movement to Democrats in the Senate.

We should know by Wednesday afternoon Australian Eastern Daylight Time if the Democrats have wrested control of Congress from the Republicans – but it’s far from clear exactly how things will play out.

Democrats lead Republicans by 9.4 points on the generic ballot, and President Donald Trump’s net approval is -20.4, but it has rebounded from lows below -24. If Republicans do better than expected in the polls, a drop in petrol prices since late September is likely to be responsible. However, the stock market has tanked in the last two trading sessions.

But with Democrats holding only modest leads in the polling in many Senate contests, there’s a wide range of plausible outcomes – from a narrow Republican majority to a big Democratic majority.

Trump’s ratings

In Silver’s aggregate of US national polls, Trump’s net approval is -20.4. Currently, 58.8% of Americans disapprove of his performance and 38.4% approve. Trump’s net approval had fallen to a new low of -24.3 on October 21 before rising. It’s now at its highest since mid-September.

Trump’s net approval was -23.3 in my October 26 article. It’s below any past president since Harry Truman at this point in their term, with Joe Biden the closest at -11.2.

On four issues tracked by Silver, Trump’s net approval is -12.1 on immigration, -27.0 on trade, -28.6 on the economy and -44.2 on inflation. 

Since my October 26 analysis, Trump’s net approval on all issues has improved one to four points, with his net approval on inflation up five points in the last two weeks.

Trump’s ratings are worse if his approval is sorted into strong and weak approval and disapproval. Currently, 48.6% of Americans strongly disapprove of his performance, 20.5% strongly approve, 18.0% weakly approve and 10.2% weakly disapprove. That gives him a net strong approval of -28.2.

People who strongly approve or disapprove of Trump will be more motivated to vote at the midterms.

Silver also has an aggregate of US support for the Iran war. Currently, 56.5% of Americans are opposed to the Iran war, while 35.9% support it, for a net support of -20.6. This compares to -18.9 in my October 26 article.

Midterm elections on Wednesday

All 435 federal House of Representatives seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats will be up for election in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with results coming in Tuesday night on the US east coast (late Wednesday morning AEDT).

In the 2024 elections, Republicans won the House by 220–215 over the Democrats and the Senate by 53–47. Due to Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote, Democrats need at least a net four-seat gain to win control of the Senate.

As I previously wrote, owing to Republican gerrymandering, Democrats need at least a four-point margin in the generic ballot to have a good chance to win the House majority. 

The Senate is more skewed towards the Republicans as every state has two senators. Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win the Senate on a uniform swing.

In Silver’s midterm election forecast model, the generic ballot gives Democrats a 52.8–43.4 lead over Republicans, a 9.4-point margin. (This is slightly lower than the 9.5-point margin in my October 26 analysis). 

Silver’s model gives the Democrats an 82% chance to win the Senate and a 96% chance to win the House (it was respectively 75% and 95% on October 26). This is a new high for Democrats in the Senate this cycle. Democratic chances of winning the Senate had fallen to a low of 50% on September 7, and their chances of winning the House had dropped to 81% on September 3.

While the uniform swing indicates Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win control of the Senate, Silver’s model has Democrats as the favourites to win with a five to six point margin in the generic ballot. In the House, Democrats are favourites if they win by two to three points.

Democrats lead Republicans by one to four points in polls of the key toss-up Senate races in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Alaska and Ohio. Trump won all these states by double-digit margins in 2024. However, Democrats only lead by four to five points in Republican-held Maine and Democratic-held Michigan. Kamala Harris, the Democratic presidential nominee, won Maine by 6.9 points in 2024, while Trump only won Michigan by 1.4 points.

In South Carolina and Nebraska, Republicans only lead in polling for the Senate races by about one point. If the Democrats have a great election night, they will win all the Senate seats where they currently lead, as well as South Carolina. An independent (Dan Osborn) could also expect to win in Nebraska. That would give Democrats a 55–44 Senate majority, plus one for Osborn.

However, Democrats only lead by more than five points in one Republican-held Senate seat (North Carolina). If the polls are systematically overstating Democrats by four points, North Carolina could be the Democrats’ only gain, for a 52–48 Republican Senate majority.

The large majority of elections in the US use the first-past-the-post system. Usually, this has little impact as minor party candidates get under 2% of votes in US elections. But in Montana, Silver’s aggregate has Republican Kurt Alme on 41.2%, independent Seth Bodnar on 32.6% and Democrat Alani Bankhead on 17.0%. Preferential voting could give Bodnar a much better chance at victory.

Poll closing times in key Senate contests

Some states and key moments on Wednesday AEDT will be:

At 10am, the first polls close in the eastern time zones of Indiana and Kentucky. Early counting there will give observers an idea of how much damage Democrats are doing to Republicans in their rural strongholds
At 11am, polls close in South Carolina and Florida’s eastern zone. Counting in Florida will be fast. In South Carolina, Republican incumbent Senator Darline Graham leads Democrat Annie Andrews by 1.3 points in Silver’s aggregate, and in Florida, Republican incumbent Senator Ashley Moody leads Democrat Angie Nixon by 5.9 points
At 11:30am, polls close in Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown leads Republican incumbent Senator Jon Husted by 3.0 points
At noon, polls close in Maine and in Texas’, Kansas’ and Michigan’s eastern zones. In the Texas Senate race, Democrat James Talarico leads Republican Ken Paxton by 3.5 points; in Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton leads Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall by 3.3 points; in Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by 4.7 points; and in Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson leads Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins by 4.0 points
At 1pm, polls close in Iowa, Nebraska and Louisiana. In Iowa’s Senate race, Democrat Josh Turek leads Republican Ashley Hinson by 0.7 points. In Nebraska, Republican incumbent Senator Pete Ricketts leads independent Dan Osborn by 0.8 points (without a Democrat in the race). In Louisiana, Republican Julia Letlow leads Democrat Jamie Davis by 3.9 points
At 4pm, polls close in Alaska’s eastern time zone, with polls closing in the western part of the state an hour later. Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan by 2.6 points.

Poll closing times listed here are from The Green Papers. I’ve included all Senate contests where Silver’s aggregate is within five points. Some states are split across two time zones. In this case, polls in the leading time zone usually close an hour before those in the trailing zone. 

The earliest statewide races can be called is when all polls are closed.

Economic data

Americans head to the polls this week at a difficult time for the economy.

Americans are currently paying an average of US$4.17 a gallon for regular petrol – historically high but down from US$4.29 a gallon in my October 26 analysis and US$4.48 on September 25. Owing to profits and taxes, the retail price of petrol will be higher than the commodity price.

The commodity price of petrol had surged from a low of US$2.99 a gallon on August 27 to US$3.59 on September 23. The price today has crashed 8.1% to US$2.90, the lowest since early August.

I previously reported there had been similar surges in the price of oil, but that surge hasn’t yet carried over to the petrol price, but today’s oil price slump has carried over. On election day, the petrol price will be much cheaper than in late September.

In last night’s session, the benchmark US S&P stock market index dropped a further 0.5%, following a 1.8% slump last Friday, to fall to its lowest level since July 31. It’s down 3.6% from the October 6 peak, but still up 8.6% from the week before the Iran war began in late February and up 14.4% from its worst point in the Iran war in late March. Some of the gloss has come off the AI boom.

In September, personal income increased by 0.2%, but expenditures increased by 0.5%. The personal savings rate was down 0.2% since August to 3.8%, its lowest since October 2022.

In the September quarter, GDP increased 3.4% in annualised terms (0.85% in quarter on quarter terms). GDP growth was up from 2.2% annualised in the June quarter.
news.summary: Trump’s net approval is below what any past president since Harry Truman had at this point in their term.

news.title: The Top Fundraiser for the Midterms Is...
news.text:
Until recently, the top fundraiser for this election was Jon Ossoff, but he has now slipped into the No. 2 position behind James Talarico.

State Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Texas, was the top individual fundraiser of the 2026 midterms, bringing in $146.3 million through mid-October, according to the last reports filed to the Federal Election Commission before the election.Other Democrats: Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff ranked second, with $136.6 million, and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown — attempting a comeback in Ohio this year — ranked third, at $68.4 million.More than half of Talarico’s haul, $75.3 million, came from small-dollar donors — those giving less than $200 total. It’s a crucial demographic, able to give more without hitting contribution limits while also reflecting grassroots enthusiasm.

There's definitely enthusiasm for Talarico. What CNN doesn't mention in this story is that most of it comes from other states.

Of the itemized contributions that went to Talarico and Paxton, about 47% and 73% came from within Texas, respectively. Of their out-of-state contributions, Talarico saw the most come from California and New York while Paxton received the most from Florida and California.

In case that wasn't clear, 53% of Talarico's itemized contributions came from out of state. Itemized contributions (those over $200) represent about half of his total fundraising. It's not clear if the other half, the small dollar contributions, came from Texas or somewhere else. My guess is somewhere else. Talarico is exactly the kind of Texas Senator they'd like to see in New York or California.

All of the top 10 fundraisers this election on the Senate side have been Democrats. On the House side, 8 of the Top 10 were Democrats including AOC in top place.

View this post on Instagram

Of course that isn't the complete picture. Overall, this midterm is expected to be the most expensive in history by quite a lot, even adjusted for inflation.

In 2022 the midterms cost $8.9 billion, or $10.2 in inflation-adjusted dollars. With the 2026 election expected to reach $11.9 billion, it will surpass the total spent on congressional elections in 2024 as well. Outside spending, driven by super PACs, is fueling the increased spending. In 2022, outside spending totaled $2 billion. Our analysis shows it is expected to reach $3.9 billion in 2026, an 85% increase. 

And when it comes to those outside donations, Elon Musk was the biggest funder, followed by several more big donors giving to Republicans.

Tech mogul Elon Musk once again led all political donors, contributing more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside spending organizations ahead of the 2026 midterm election, according to an OpenSecrets analysis of federal campaign finance disclosures.Musk also topped the donor rankings during the 2024 federal election cycle with more than $291 million. He was one of three donors to surpass $100 million this cycle. The others in the top three were shipping supplies company founder Richard Uihlein and his wife, Elizabeth, and trading firm co-founder Jeff Yass. They combined to contribute more than $706 million, all supporting Republican candidates and conservative causes.Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, who ranked fourth overall, was the top donor to Democratic causes and candidates, contributing $83.4 million. The top 10 individual donors contributed $1.1 billion combined.

news.title: Flanagan vs. Tafoya: Early Voting Surges in GOP-Leaning Minnesota Counties
news.text: Minnesota's record-breaking early voter turnout is rising fastest in seven rural counties previously won by President Donald Trump, offering a potentially encouraging sign for Republican Michele Tafoya in the state's closely watched Senate race against Democrat Peggy Flanagan, though some analysts warn the turnout data is not a reliable predictor of which party will benefit once all ballots have been cast. Several key Senate races are unfolding this year that will determine control of Congress. Republicans seek to defend their narrow House and Senate majorities and Democrats look to capitalize on competitive races that could flip control of both chambers in their favor. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win control of the Senate and a net gain of three seats to win control of the House. In Minnesota, Democratic Senator Tina Smith is retiring when her term ends on January 3, which leaves an open Senate seat. While Minnesota has long been considered a Democratic stronghold, Tafoya has gained ground during this election cycle. Corruption has emerged as a key issue for voters, with both candidates using it as a line of attack. Flanagan has centered much of her messaging on allegations of corruption tied to Trump, while Tafoya has sought to link Flanagan to controversies that have occurred during her tenure as lieutenant governor under Governor Tim Walz. Newsweek reached out to both campaigns by email for comment on Monday afternoon. Early Voting Turnout in Minnesota Shatters Midterm Records The closely watched midterm elections have led to a surge in early voting this election cycle, with several states having broken records, including Texas, where early voting began with a record 19 million registered voters eligible to cast ballots, and Georgia, where in-person early voting set a record last week at more than 2.2 million voters. Minnesota has also seen record-breaking turnout as of last week. More than 886,000 Minnesotans have voted early in-person or by absentee ballot as of Sunday, Minnesota's Secretary of State's Office reported. In 2022, the last non-presidential election, there were 687,062 ballots cast during early voting in Minnesota. Minnesota's record-breaking early turnout is not confined to Democratic strongholds. Although large numbers of ballots have been cast in Minneapolis and other blue areas, seven rural counties previously won by Trump have seen some of the state's fastest growth in early voting since 2022, a trend that could be encouraging for Republicans in the competitive Senate race. The seven counties are Swift, Clearwater, Chisago, Renville, Rice, Wadena, and Winona, according to an Axios report on Monday. "The Republicans have their best shot in 20 years at winning the state," Hamline University professor of political science and legal studies David Schultz recently told Newsweek, crediting the state's issues with corruption and "Democratic Party fatigue" as reasons why Republicans might secure a win. He added that he would not be surprised if Tafoya won the election. Meanwhile, the high voter turnout comes as both candidates have urged voters to get to the polls to cast their ballots. "Elections here are won by the people who show up. This race is going to be close, and every single ballot will make a difference," Tafoya posted on X on Monday. "Bring your family, your neighbors, and anyone who’s ready for a change. Tomorrow, we can restore accountability in Washington." "Minnesota, if you’re ready to: Hold Donald Trump accountable for his corruption. End the war. Pass Medicare for All. Ban prior authorization. Rip ICE apart. Raise the wage. Block the bombs. Save Social Security. Make your plan to vote by 8 PM tomorrow," Flanagan posted on X on Monday. Flanagan vs. Tafoya: What Latest Polls Show Flanagan is leading Tafoya in all recent polls. What Prediction Markets Show In prediction markets as of Monday evening, Flanagan is strongly favored among traders. Kalshi traders give Flanagan 91.6 percent odds of winning, compared to Tafoya at 8.4 percent. On Polymarket, Flanagan's odds are even greater at 94 percent, compared to Tafoya's 7 percent. Is Minnesota a Blue State? Minnesota last voted for a Republican at the presidential level in 1972, but it has still been close in recent contests, giving Democrats only narrow victories. Former Vice President Kamala Harris carried the state by only about four points in 2024, a narrower win than former President Joe Biden’s seven-point victory in 2020. In 2016, Minnesota backed former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by less than two percentage points. Former President Barack Obama did better in the state, carrying it by nearly eight points in 2012 and more than 10 points in 2008. Minnesota last elected a Republican senator in 2002, backing Norm Coleman. In 2008, he lost reelection to Democrat Al Franken. What Happens Next Early voting ended in Minnesota on Monday. Polls will open again on Tuesday morning for Election Day. They will close at 8 p.m. local time in Minnesota. As long as voters are in line by the time polls close, they will be allowed to vote. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anthony Murray and Anna Skinner.
news.summary: While Minnesota has long been considered a Democratic stronghold, Tafoya has gained ground during this election cycle.

news.title: Letitia James Leans Hard on Trump at Brooklyn Rally With Rep. Jasmine Crockett
news.text:
New York Attorney General Letitia James appeared alongside outgoing Texas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett at Brooklyn Borough Hall on Sunday, during one of her last days of midterms campaigning. James is running in the November 3 election to keep New Yorkers safe from crime and malfeasance, but her remarks leaned heavily on her record of fighting the Trump administration rather than local policy specifics.

James Touts Lawsuits, Vows to Keep Fighting

James told the crowd that Congress had been neutered and was not positioned to rein in the administration's excesses, arguing that Democratic attorneys general had instead stepped up to do that work, according to the New York Post. She touted the number of times she had sued the Trump administration and vowed to continue challenging what she called Trump's illegal and unconstitutional activity, saying she would use the law to defend democracy and the rule of law. James also pointed to her office's record of removing more than 10,000 illegal guns from the streets.

James's office previously detailed some of that legal fight in an April 2025 statement marking the first 100 days of the Trump administration, saying it had filed or joined 15 lawsuits and 22 amicus briefs alongside Democratic state attorneys general since January 20, efforts the office said had successfully blocked some administration actions, according to the New York State Attorney General's office.

Crockett Urges Black Voters to See Election as Personal

Crockett, who is leaving Congress on January 3 after losing her reelection primary to fellow Democrat James Talarico, used the Brooklyn stage to make an explicit appeal to Black voters to oppose the Trump administration. She said she appears in Congress unapologetically Black every day and asked the crowd whether they were ready to fight for their liberation, per the Post's account. Crockett added that neighbors had been attacked because of their skin color or accent, telling attendees that voting must be personal. The speeches by James and Crockett were paired with performances of Sam Cooke's “A Change Is Gonna Come” and “Lift Every Voice and Sing.”

Governor Hochul Also Makes Closing Push in Harlem

James's Brooklyn appearance came as New York Governor Kathy Hochul made her own final push, campaigning at Harlem subway stations on Monday before appearing later on the Upper West Side, according to ABC7 New York. Hochul has characterized her opponent, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, as a Trump supporter throughout the campaign. Blakeman, for his part, launched a statewide tour from a diner in Bethpage on Monday with planned stops in Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse and Binghamton, and said his own campaign's polling showed the governor's race was neck and neck.

Hochul was scheduled to close out her campaign at a “New York Fights Back” Election Eve rally in Williamsburg alongside House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, James, lieutenant governor nominee Adrienne Adams and Comptroller Tom DiNapoli. Statewide, more than 1.7 million New Yorkers had already cast ballots during the early voting period, including more than 690,000 in New York City, the same ABC7 report noted.

Polling Shows Wide Leads for Both Democrats

Independent polling released before the rallies suggested comfortable positions for both Democratic candidates. A Siena poll of likely New York voters conducted October 19-22 found James leading Republican nominee Saritha Komatireddy, 54% to 39%, according to the Siena Research Institute. That edge was slightly larger than the 52% to 39% lead James held in September. James also posted a 51% favorable, 39% unfavorable rating, with support from 87% of Democrats and a 50% to 40% edge among independents. The poll surveyed 807 likely New York voters.

The same Siena survey found Hochul leading Blakeman 54% to 40%, up from a 50% to 41% advantage in September. Komatireddy, James's Republican challenger, is a former federal prosecutor, as noted by FOX 5 New York, which also detailed James's gun buyback record dating back to 2019. No Republican has won statewide office in New York since former Governor George Pataki in 2002.

Democrats Eye Ground Lost With Minority Voters in 2024

The Brooklyn rally's focus on Black voters comes as Democrats nationally look to regain ground with minority voters after setbacks in the 2024 presidential election, when Kamala Harris's total-vote advantage over Trump was 22% smaller than Joe Biden's advantage over Trump in 2020, with Latino voters cited as part of that falloff. A Pew Research Center analysis found that while 83% of Black voters backed Harris in 2024, Trump's support among that group rose to 15%, up from 8% in 2020. Among Hispanic voters, the share backing the Democratic candidate fell from 61% in 2020 to 51% in 2024, while Trump's support rose from 36% to 48% over the same period.
news.summary: Letitia James and Rep. Jasmine Crockett held a Trump-focused rally at Brooklyn Borough Hall as polls show James leading New York's AG race.
news.author: Damon Caldwell

news.title: Explained | What you need to know about the 2026 US midterm elections
news.text: p>Washington: Early voting has been underway for weeks ahead of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, when US voters will elect members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country.Held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president. But for anyone who thinks they lack drama or importance this year, consider these two statistics:More than 57 million people had already cast their ballots as of Monday, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, well above the 46 million who voted early in the 2022 midterm elections.This election is on track to be the most expensive in US history. The nonpartisan watchdog OpenSecrets estimates a total of $11.9 billion will be spent by candidates and outside political groups..Explained | How US news organisations will make midterm race calls.Elon Musk alone had spent about $366 million to support Republicans as of three weeks ago, according to campaign finance records.Still, midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races. More than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election, for example.Control of Congress at stake Plenty is at stake in this midterm election as Democrats try to win majority control of the US Congress.Currently, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, where there are two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to win control.Democrats also are fighting to win the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. They must net four additional seats to get control. Twelve races, including those in conservative-leaning states like Kansas and Texas, could decide the outcome.Can midterms affect the presidency?Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress. For 2026 that means that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.Midterm election results also can give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.What are polls showing?Approval of Trump's performance is at a near record low of 32%, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to have an impact on the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.At the same time, there is evidence that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans and more of them have already cast their ballots, according to the University of Florida Election Lab.There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics..Elon Musk tests what nearly half a billion dollars can buy in US midterms.However, a landslide for the Democrats is far from assured. Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism towards Democrats, a Republican spending advantage on campaigns, and fears from moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.Recent midterm history Recent history tells the story of the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.In the 2010 midterms, during the Democratic presidency of Barack Obama, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation. Democrats lost their majority. In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time. He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House. They gained a net total of 40 House seats, but lost a net two Senate seats.This year's elections also have races for governors in 36 of the 50 states and voting in nearly every state for seats in state-level legislative bodies.Currently, Republicans control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.Who will be Speaker?If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York. He is currently the House Democratic leader..Can Democrats curb Trump? Five scenarios that could shape the US midterms.Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to launch investigations into a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates. Jeffries repeatedly has said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House. He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job. Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."Marquee racesAmong the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign and an open seat in a Nebraska swing district where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran.Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted, falsely, that there is widespread cheating in US elections. State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.</p

news.title: Voters Get Rare Say Over Who Sets Their Electric Rates
news.text:
Power bills will be on the ballot Tuesday in states where voters directly choose the officials who approve their electric rates.

Nine states, from Georgia and Alabama to Montana and the Dakotas, have utility commission seats up for election, Stateline reported Monday.

In Georgia, Democrats would control the Public Service Commission, holding three of its five seats, if both of their candidates win, according to election tracker Ballotpedia.

Democratic Commissioner Peter Hubbard faces Republican Fitz Johnson, the commissioner he unseated in 2025, the site noted.

Democrat Shelia Edwards and Republican Josh Tolbert are running for the seat Republican Commissioner Tricia Pridemore gave up to mount an unsuccessful bid for the U.S. House, the elections site added.

Hubbard wrote in a May 13 post on X that Georgians “who pay a power bill deserve Public Service Commissioners who are engaged, ask tough questions, don’t take money from companies they regulate.”

He said in a Sept. 14 campaign statement that data centers “should not be allowed here in Georgia, unless they agree to” conditions including renewable power, union labor and no nondisclosure agreements.

Lead Locally, a group that backs what it calls “local climate champions,” named Hubbard and Edwards in an Oct. 20 slate of candidates it said “can regulate, restrict and stop data centers.”

Former Vice President Kamala Harris raised money Oct. 27 for Democratic commission hopefuls in Arizona and Georgia, warning “the stakes are high” because “people cannot afford the basics,” Politico reported.

Johnson warned in an Aug. 3 post on his campaign’s X account that the state “cannot turn over the keys to Georgia’s grid to out-of-state climate activists who give no concern to your job, your monthly power bill, energy supply, or national security concerns.”

Georgia Power cut rates statewide by $285 million under a commission-approved settlement over storm-repair and fuel costs that closed the case in June, a spokesman for the Georgia Public Service Commission said in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation.

“Georgia Power estimated the average household would see their bills drop by about $50 a year,” the spokesman added.

He noted in the same statement that he “cannot comment on the election or on party politics.” (RELATED: Google Agrees To Help Pay For Georgia Nuclear Upgrades In Deal Utility Says Would Protect Other Customers)

A Democratic majority on Georgia’s commission could slow power deals for big corporate projects, John Boyd Jr., a principal at The Boyd Co., which advises companies on where to build, told Bisnow in an Oct. 28 report.

“Public service commissions are critical gatekeepers in this environment,” Boyd said.

“A new board could delay power contract approvals and spike industrial electricity rates by shifting grid costs onto corporations,” he added.

“People need to understand that blue states have stopped pipelines and shut down dependable power while increasing costs to consumers,” Stuart Turley, president and CEO of the Sandstone Group, said in a statement to the DCNF.

Through August, residential electricity cost about 52 percent more per kilowatt-hour in the 19 states Harris won in 2024 than in the 31 states President Donald Trump carried, Turley said, citing his analysis of Energy Information Administration numbers.

Jordan Nader, a resident senior fellow for energy and environment at the R Street Institute, said in a statement to the DCNF that “Campaign promises to reduce power bills can run into the limits of a commissioner’s authority.”

“Prior rate decisions cannot be undone, but a commissioner can shape future rates by evaluating whether the plants and power lines are needed before cost recovery is evaluated and allocated across customer classes,” Nader added.

All five members of Arizona’s Corporation Commission are Republicans.

Republican Commissioner Kevin Thompson and Republican state Rep. Ralph Heap face Democrats Jonathon Hill and Clara Pratte and Green Party candidate Mike Cease for two seats, according to Ballotpedia. Heap beat Republican Commissioner Nick Myers in the July primary.

The Arizona Corporation Commission did not immediately respond to the DCNF’s request for comment.

About $2 million in spending on Arizona’s race, against billions at stake in one data center project near Tucson, makes the commission “the cheapest veto in American politics,” Alexander Muse, a John Milton Freedom Foundation fellow, wrote in a Nov. 1 op-ed.

Alabama Republicans already turned out both commissioners who sought new terms in 2026, according to Ballotpedia. Matt Gentry beat Commissioner Jeremy Oden in the May primary, and Jim Zeigler edged Commissioner Chris Beeker III in a June runoff.

Most of the country does not vote on these posts. Ten states elect their utility regulators directly, while governors or legislatures appoint them elsewhere, Canary Media reported in May.

Jamie Van Nostrand, who once led Massachusetts’ utility regulator and is now with the University of Pennsylvania’s Kleinman Center for Energy Policy, spoke to Reuters for an Oct. 31 report.

“The governors are using this crisis on energy affordability as an opportunity to take a deeper dive into the utility regulatory model and see if it makes any sense,” Van Nostrand said.

“We’re in a moment where utility profits are soaring, customers are struggling and the asymmetry there is something that affects everyone in this country,” Karlee Weinmann, a researcher at the Energy and Policy Institute, a self-described utility industry watchdog, told Straight Arrow News.

“Regulators are sitting right in the middle of it,” she added.

Ted Thomas, a Republican former chairman of Arkansas’ utility commission who advises PowerLines, a consumer advocacy group, told Stateline that power prices as a campaign issue “began to emerge in 2024 as part of the overall concern on inflation.”

In some regulator races, power bills were a central issue well before 2024. (RELATED: Democrats Campaign On Power Bills After Blocking GOP Data Center Plan)

In Louisiana, newcomer Davante Lewis unseated Lambert Boissiere III, a member of the state’s utility commission for almost 18 years, in a December 2022 runoff, the Associated Press reported. Both men are Democrats.

Entergy customers had seen their bills jump months after Hurricane Ida, when the commission approved storm-repair charges the utility said it needed, Grist reported.

Lewis campaigned against such fees and had the backing of a super PAC funded largely by the Environmental Defense Fund’s advocacy arm, the outlet noted.

Lewis won 59.5 percent of the vote, according to Ballotpedia.

In Georgia, Republican Commissioner Lauren “Bubba” McDonald narrowly held his seat in a January 2021 runoff against Democrat Daniel Blackman, keeping every seat on the commission Republican, E&E News reported. This happened at the same time both then-incumbent Georgia Senators, Republicans David Perdue and Kelly Loeffler, lost reelection to their Democratic challengers Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, respectively.

Who should pay for Georgia Power’s over-budget expansion of its Vogtle nuclear plant was a central issue in that race, Georgia Public Broadcasting reported.

Georgia Power customers saw a monthly line item on their electric bills covering Vogtle costs, the outlet noted at the time.

Blackman wanted to move some of the Vogtle costs back onto Georgia Power, while McDonald backed the project, the AP reported.

In Arizona, utility giant Arizona Public Service gave $10.7 million to dark-money groups in 2014, the Phoenix New Times reported in 2019, citing company documents.

Millions of those dollars backed groups that poured money into electing Republicans Doug Little and Tom Forese to the commission, the outlet noted.

Four years later, Democrat Sandra Kennedy won back a commission seat, according to Ballotpedia.

She had called recent rate increases the commission approved for the utility “unjustified,” Cronkite News reported less than two weeks before the vote.
news.summary: ‘Who pay a power bill’
news.author: Simon August

news.title: Trump promised 'no more wars'. His foreign policy tells another story
news.text:
When Donald Trump returned to the White House, he promised an “America First” foreign policy, pledging to keep the United States out of foreign wars and prioritise domestic interests.

But two years into his second term, his administration has been deeply involved in conflicts and diplomatic disputes around the world. Here is a look back at some of the defining moments of his foreign policy since returning to office.

Ukraine: A promise to end the war remains unfulfilled

One of Trump's most prominent campaign promises was to end Russia's war in Ukraine, which he vowed to resolve on his first day back in office.

But the conflict is now in its fifth year, and Trump's approach has been marked by dramatic shifts in Washington's relationship with Kyiv. Tensions reached a low point in February 2025, when Trump and Vice-President JD Vance publicly berated Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a heated Oval Office meeting, accusing him of failing to show sufficient appreciation for American support.

The confrontation was followed by a temporary US suspension of military assistance and intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Washington's position on weapons deliveries has also fluctuated. Ukraine has repeatedly sought additional Patriot air defence systems to protect its cities and infrastructure, but deliveries have been limited amid depleted US stockpiles.

Trump subsequently welcomed Russian President Vladimir Putin back onto the international stage at a summit in Alaska, where the two leaders discussed the war. No agreement was reached, with Trump acknowledging that negotiations had yet to produce a breakthrough.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have since faced further strain, including over Trump's announcement of a diesel export deal with Russia, which Zelensky criticised as a "weak decision".

More recently, Putin proposed a trilateral summit involving Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss Ukraine, despite Kyiv itself not being invited to the table. Despite Trump's repeated promises to bring the conflict to an end, the war continues.

Greenland and Canada: Trump's territorial ambitions strain relations with allies

Trump's foreign policy has also raised questions about Washington's relationships with some of its closest allies, particularly after he repeatedly expressed interest in acquiring territory belonging to NATO partners.

Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, became a particular focus.Trump argued that the United States needed Greenland for national security reasons. In January 2026, he refused to rule out using military force to take control of the territory, despite repeated assurances from both Greenland and Denmark that it was "not for sale."

The comments prompted a strong response from European allies. Several NATO countries rallied behind Greenland, with some deploying military personnel to the territory.Trump responded by threatening higher tariffs against countries that opposed his plans.

In September, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new defence agreement expanding America's military presence on the island, without transferring sovereignty.

Canada has also been a target of Trump's territorial rhetoric. He repeatedly referred to the country as America's "51st state", mocking former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau by calling him "Governor Trudeau". Trump also falsely claimed that Canadians wanted to join the United States, suggesting they would benefit from lower taxes and better healthcare.

Canada's new prime minister, Mark Carney, has firmly rejected the idea of the country becoming part of the United States. But Trump has continued to suggest that he has not ruled out the possibility, and ties between the neighbours remain strained as Ottawa seeks to align itself closer to Europe.

The 'Donroe Doctrine': US intervention in Venezuela

Trump's approach to Latin America has been dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine", a play on his name and the 1823 Monroe Doctrine, which warned European powers against further colonial intervention in the Americas.

Successive US presidents have invoked the original doctrine to justify American influence across the region, at times through military intervention.Trump explicitly embraced the comparison in January 2026, following a US military operation in Venezuela that resulted in the capture of President Nicolas Maduro, who was taken to the United States to face criminal charges.

The operation marked a significant escalation in Washington's involvement in the region.Trump described the move as a revival of the Monroe Doctrine, joking that it should instead be called the "Donroe Doctrine".

Following Maduro's capture, Trump said American oil companies would help rebuild Venezuela's oil industry. Washington has since secured control over Venezuelan oil reserves and gained influence over how the proceeds are spent.

However, the promised return to democracy remains uncertain. Meanwhile, the US military has carried out a series of strikes against vessels in the Caribbean, off Venezuela's coast, killing hundreds of people.

The Trump administration has described the targets as "narco-terrorist" boats involved in drug trafficking and says the operations are intended to prevent narcotics from reaching the United States. But officials have not provided evidence that the vessels targeted in the strikes were carrying drugs, raising questions about the legal basis and justification for the operations.

Middle East: From Gaza's 'Riviera' to the Iran war

Trump began his second term as a staunch supporter of Israel, maintaining Washington's backing for the country's military campaign in Gaza.But his relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also faced moments of tension.

In February 2025, Trump sparked widespread international criticism when he proposed a US takeover of the Gaza Strip and the resettlement of its Palestinian population. He shared an AI-generated video depicting Gaza transformed into a luxury seaside resort, dubbed the "Riviera of the Middle East".

He later presented a 20-point Gaza peace plan alongside Netanyahu in September 2025, describing it as a major achievement of his foreign policy. A ceasefire took effect the following month, securing the release of all remaining hostages and increasing humanitarian access to the territory. However, a year later, the wider plan remains largely stalled. Israeli strikes have continued in Gaza, Hamas remains armed and there has been no full Israeli withdrawal or comprehensive reconstruction.

Disarmament remains a major sticking point. Washington has pushed for Hamas to surrender its weapons alongside a phased Israeli withdrawal, while Netanyahu has insisted that disarmament must come first.

And then there is Iran.

In February 2026, Trump joined Israel in launching a war against Iran, marking one of the most consequential foreign policy decisions of his presidency; particularly striking given his previous criticism of Kamala Harris during the 2024 election campaign, when he accused her of risking a war in the Middle East.

The US-Israeli military campaign resulted in the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several other senior officials. Iran subsequently asserted control over the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial shipping route for global energy supplies, sparking major disruption to international shipping and energy markets.

Despite initially fighting alongside Israel, Trump and Netanyahu have since disagreed over how to bring the conflict to an end. Trump has explored the possibility of a deal with Tehran, while Netanyahu has continued to advocate military action to protect Israel's security interests.

Nevertheless, Trump has continued to publicly support Netanyahu, endorsing him ahead of Israel's latest elections.

With the war in Iran still underway and fighting continuing in Gaza despite a nominal ceasefire, Trump's "peacemaker" pledge to avoid foreign conflicts appears increasingly distant from the reality of his second-term foreign policy.
news.summary: Donald Trump promised an “America First” foreign policy and pledged to keep the US out of foreign wars. But since returning to the White House, his administration has been deeply involved in conflicts around the world. From the war in Ukraine and threats to Greenland and Canada, to the US intervention in Venezuela, Trump's shifting approach to the Middle East and war with Iran, Vedika Bahl examines his foreign policy record since returning to office.
news.author: Vedika BAHL

news.title: 'Totally out of context': CBS insiders bust GOP candidate editing '60 Minutes' clip
news.text:
Insiders at CBS have reportedly accused Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers’ campaign of cutting context from a viral 60 Minutes clip of his Democratic opponent.

“CBS sources have reiterated to me it was the Mike Rogers campaign that clipped this exchange to strip away the context, not the network,” Zeteo media columnist Justin Baragona wrote on X Monday. Rogers’ campaign has not publicly responded to the claim.

Rogers posted the clip Sunday night, the night 60 Minutes aired interviews with him and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Tuesday’s election.

Rogers’ post quoted El-Sayed saying something the clip does not show him saying.

“[Abdul El-Sayed] says it’s ok for MEN to be in girl’s locker rooms,” Rogers wrote, then put this line in quotation marks as El-Sayed’s explanation. “Well because they are going to find out about it on the internet anyway.”

El-Sayed never says that sentence in the 70-second video Rogers shared. The nearest line in the video is his remark about having to “make do with the fact that, like, the Internet is a real thing.”

“This is all over my timeline, and it’s totally out of context,” Vanity Fair Washington correspondent Aidan McLaughlin wrote on X Monday. 

“No one mentions locker rooms,” he pointed out.

“I’m not running to govern sports,” El-Sayed said later in the same answer, according to the extended interview 60 Minutes posted online.

“To me, I think it’s really important for us to fight at the state level to protect access to bathrooms, to locker rooms, to sports teams of choice for young people,” El-Sayed told Pride Source during his 2018 run for governor.

By Monday, Rogers’ post had drawn 9.6 million views on X, while McLaughlin’s post flagging the missing context had about 83,000, according to the platform’s counts. The clipped version drew more than 100 times as many views as the post disputing it, a day before Michigan votes.

The clip came from extended interviews 60 Minutes posted Sunday alongside a fact-check that said both candidates made claims “that were false, misleading or unsupported by our reporting.” Among them was Rogers’ charge that El-Sayed “wrote a letter in support for the Muslim Brotherhood.”

The network reported that El-Sayed signed a letter to Egypt’s then-president, a Brotherhood leader, and that El-Sayed denies any ties to the group. Rogers drew his clip from the same release in which the network had taken issue with his own claims about El-Sayed.

During the 2024 race, CBS News called it “false” when President Donald Trump, then a candidate, accused 60 Minutes of deceitfully editing its interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris, Fox News reported.

This time, CBS sources say, the editing came from Rogers’ campaign, which CBS noted has Trump’s backing.

Rogers’ clip left out the part of the question about Islam, in a race where Trump had cast El-Sayed as a “jihadist” and Rogers had questioned his loyalty.

Before he reached sports, 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat asked El-Sayed about “tension between Islam and Muslim voters and what I’m calling cultural liberalism,” including “what is taught in school,” according to the extended interview. Rogers’ clip starts after that.

On Oct. 25, a week before the interview aired, Trump told a Port Huron rally he had come “to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” the Associated Press reported, describing his remarks as anti-Muslim rhetoric.

“Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers asked El-Sayed at their final debate, the AP reported.

According to the AP, there is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed, who would be the nation’s first Muslim senator, said the question was shameful, the news service reported.

news.title: Final Poll Shows Democrat Defeating America's Most Popular GOP Governor
news.text: Being the most popular governor in the United States may not be enough to save Vermont’s Phil Scott from an historic upset, according to a new poll. A new University of New Hampshire (UNH) Green Mountain State Poll, released Sunday, found Democrat Amanda Janoo leading the Republican incumbent 51 percent to 43 percent among likely voters, including those leaning toward a candidate. Independent Brian Judd had 4 percent. “Republican Governor Phil Scott has comfortably won re-election in recent years, but he trails Democrat Amanda Janoo in the final days of the 2026 campaign,” the poll’s press release said. UNH is the only pollster that has shown Janoo ahead in the general election, and the most recent competing survey, from State Navigate, had Scott up 3 points last week (49 percent to 46 percent). “We started this campaign with a goal of building a movement of Vermonters who love this state,” Janoo said in a statement to Newsweek reacting to the poll. “Vermonters who may not share the same backgrounds or lived experiences, but who believe we can do more for each other and for our state than sit on the sidelines when things get hard.” Newsweek reached out to Scott's campaign for comment. America's Most Popular Governor In Morning Consult's most recent state rankings, based on surveys of registered voters from April 1 through June 30, Scott had a net approval rating of +52, the highest of any governor. North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong followed at +50 and Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon at +49. A Morning Consult ranking released in February put his approval at 74 percent, with 19 percent disapproving, and listed him as the most popular governor for the 14th consecutive quarter. Vermont Public found his approval at 45 percent this fall, down 15 points from 2022. UNH had him at 47 percent approving and 47 percent disapproving in September. State Navigate's poll showed that Scott had 58 percent approval. Scott has said this is his toughest race since he first won in 2016, and he has pinned much of that on Democratic enthusiasm. Scott vs. Janoo, How the Race Has Shifted Scott’s number has barely changed in UNH’s polling this year. He had 42 percent in June, 44 percent in July and 43 percent in both September and October. Janoo, however, has climbed over the same period, going from 27 percent to 33 percent, then 49 percent and now 51 percent, the first UNH figure to count leaners. The partisan breakdown shows why. Janoo wins 78 percent of Democrats, up from 73 percent in September, while 20 percent stick with Scott. Scott holds 85 percent of Republicans, with 10 percent going to Judd, and carries independents 51 percent to 39 percent. He wins 25 percent of former Vice President Kamala Harris voters, while 38 percent of Janoo's supporters say they voted for Scott in 2024. The poll also found that Janoo, a 39-year-old economist who has never held office, was viewed favorably by 54 percent of likely voters and unfavorably by 29 percent. Scott’s numbers were 42 percent and 40 percent. Sean McKinley, the UNH Survey Center’s project director, told Newsweek in September that Scott had “a bit of a hill to climb.” Democratic leaders had originally hoped for a more established candidate. The party tried to recruit Attorney General Charity Clark, Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas and Treasurer Mike Pieciak to take on Scott, but all three decided to seek reelection to their current offices. What Vermont Voters Are Worried About Money tops the list. Asked to name their most important issue, likely voters in the UNH poll most often cited affordability or inflation, at 17 percent, followed by economic health or financial security and the tax burden or public spending, at 10 percent each. The candidates have split sharply on how to deal with them. Janoo has proposed higher taxes on top earners and universal primary care, a plan Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent, backed at a Winooski event last month. Scott argues the state has too few wealthy residents to carry that load. "One person makes a billion dollars, and when that's gone, that's gone," he said at an October 21 debate. Education is another dividing line, with Janoo opposing the forced school mergers she says Scott's overhaul would bring. AI data centers have also surfaced as Scott vetoed a bill regulating them in May, while Janoo supports a moratorium. Scott vs. Janoo, What Other Polls Say The State Navigate survey of 1,752 likely voters, conducted October 23-25, had Scott ahead 49 percent to 46 percent, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.3 percentage points. Its early October poll showed him up 46 percent to 43 percent. State Navigate also found Scott keeping 66 percent of his 2024 voters while 30 percent moved to Janoo. He won 25 percent of Democrats, a bigger share than UNH found, and his job approval stood at 58 percent, with 40 percent disapproving. A Vermont Public poll conducted September 10-21 gave Scott his widest lead, 44 percent to 34 percent among likely voters, with 16 percent undecided. Scott's campaign has fought the UNH numbers since September, when campaign manager Dustin Degree called that month's poll "statistical malpractice" and pointed to a sample with far more Democrats than Republicans. The center's final 2024 poll had Scott winning 65 percent to 26 percent. He won 73.4 percent to 21.8 percent. Andrew Smith, the center's director, defended its methods at the time while acknowledging it had underestimated Scott's margin. UNH says its data were weighted in part to 2024 election results, and its October sample was 60 percent Democrats, 29 percent Republicans and 11 percent independents. The Cook Political Report moved the race from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican" last month. Sabato's Crystal Ball and Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin have it at "Lean Republican." Polymarket and Kalshi both gave Scott about a 68 percent chance of winning on Monday. National Environment Republicans face a difficult final week nationally ahead of the midterms. A Reuters/Ipsos poll of likely voters had Democrats leading the generic congressional ballot 53 percent to 44 percent, while an NPR/PBS News/Marist poll had them up 52 percent to 44 percent, with Trump's approval at 40 percent and his disapproval at 59 percent. Trump is far weaker in Vermont, where UNH put him at 20 percent approval and 77 percent disapproval. Democrats there are also more engaged, with 69 percent saying they are extremely interested in the election, compared with 59 percent of Republicans. Scott has opposed the White House on tariffs and National Guard deployments, among other issues. Nearly 140,000 Vermonters had turned in ballots by Friday morning, according to the Vermont Secretary of State's Office. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anthony Murray and Jason Lemon.
news.summary: Phil Scott, America’s most popular governor, trails Democrat Amanda Janoo in the final UNH poll of deep-blue Vermont.

news.title: Election ‘Nostradamus’ Reveals Final Midterm Prediction
news.text:
Presidential guru Allan Lichtman has revealed his final prediction on the upcoming midterm election. 

With President Donald Trump and the GOP’s approval rating at historic lows, Lichtman, who correctly predicted all but one presidential election since 1984, has given his verdict. 

“When the approval rating for a president is as low as Trump’s, on average the White House party loses 40 House and six Senate seats,” he told The Times of London. “It’s not a prediction; that’s just showing how heavily the winds are blowing against Republicans.

“The other thing I look at is not just the horse-race polls, but the generic congressional poll, and that’s very heavily favouring Democrats, by seven to 11 points. That’s pretty predictive, more so than the individual race polls,” he explained.

He explained that Democratic “enthusiasm” is much higher than Republicans’ this cycle, which can only help the party. He also noted that Democrats have been voting early at higher rates than Republican voters, meaning to him that “So far, it looks pretty good for Democrats.”

“I have predicted a 67 per cent chance that the Democrats would take back the Senate,” Lichtman told the outlet. “I think the most likely but not necessarily definitive outcome is 51-49. This is not based on a model, understand; it’s just based on my knowledge of history and current politics.”

Of the states that could be potential pick-ups for Democrats in the Senate, Lichtman explained that he had a good feeling about Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas, but said he was unsure about Michigan in the race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers. 

Lichtman is best known for developing what he calls the “13 Keys,” which he says are 13 points that can show who will become the next president. But Lichtman explained that his tool can also predict midterm elections. 

“We are in a strange time but when you look at situations where there’s an unpopular war and the president’s approval rating is low, 1966 is a great example,” he said. “Lyndon Johnson [a Democratic president] had just won one of the biggest landslide victories in 1964. But then things were going bad for the country, the [Vietnam] war was going sour. Urban riots were sweeping the country and Democrats took a huge pasting in 1966.”

Still, his assessment of the state of play comes just after he incorrectly predicted that former Vice President Kamala Harris would win the 2024 presidential election. His prediction that Al Gore would win the 2000 election has also come under question.

news.title: You can become US president and see how your decisions could change America with online simulator
news.text:
Ever wanted to test your luck at running the country? While it may not be possible to just walk into the White House, there's an online simulator that provides the next best thing.

While sports fans have had the opportunity to manage their favourite soccer team in Madden, or play as their baseball hero in the MLB video games, those interested in politics have had no such joy.

Well, that was until Fantasy President Career was launched, an online simulator that allows you to step into the shoes of Donald Trump, Joe Biden and many other past presidents and see if you can do a better job.

The premium version of the game, which costs $8 a month allows players to start a political career between 1990 and 2025 as jobs including governor, state legislator, US representative, senator or POTUS.

Like any other career mode simulator, the world advances month by month and a player's popularity can change based on actions you make.

You can enter political races at your desire, including a presidential election in a bid to run the entire country.

There's also the option to start in the White House right from the start of the game should you wish.

"Would you be a good president? Everyone thinks they would. Fantasy President puts you in the Oval Office on day one, with the real Congress, real crises and a country that answers back," the Fantasy President Career's X account explains.

There's also a free, demo version of the political simulator available to play, which allows players to jump into the shoes of Trump, Biden or Barack Obama.

Fancy taking over the country in January 2025 as Trump returns to the White House after beating Kamala Harris? Well, now's you chance.

You can also enter the White House in January 2021 as Biden at the height of the Covid pandemic and just a matter of weeks after the Capitol Building riots.

Or if you decide you want to become president in January 2013 as Obama started his second term, there's that option too.

And of course, as Fantasy President Career is a simulation game, you can make decisions different to that of what was made in real life.

But be aware, every bit of legislation passed could make you awfully unpopular.
news.summary: Think you'd made a good president? Well, now you have a chance to prove it

news.title: Georgia Dem gubernatorial nominee blasted for disturbing 'full embrace of radicals' who bashed Trump supporters as 'roaches' and heaped praise on notorious anti-Semite Louis Farrakhan
news.text:
The Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Georgia has come under fire for embracing a controversial pastor – with a history of bashing MAGA voters as 'roaches' and heaping praise on notorious anti-Semite Louis Farrakhan, the Daily Mail can reveal.

Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta and who served as a senior adviser in the Biden administration, has been joined by New Birth Missionary Baptist Church’s senior pastor Jamal Bryant at several campaign rallies in the lead-up to Election Day.

But as Bryant has busied himself firing up the crowds at the events – including one where former President Barack Obama was the keynote speaker – critics have warned that the activist pastor's past rhetoric could actually be a liability for Bottoms in Tuesday's election for the governor's seat. 

‘You are the company you keep, and Bottoms’ full embrace of these radicals shows Georgians she won’t stand with them,’ Anna Marian Block, the Republican Governors Association's deputy communications director, told the Daily Mail. 

Bryant, who went viral last year for organizing a 40-day boycott against Target after the retailer scaled back Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) initiatives, has ignited fierce backlash for comparing the Trump administration and Republicans to cockroaches.

‘Roaches only start running when you turn the lights on. As long as the lights are out, they're going to be comfortable,’ Bryant declared during an Easter sermon just last year, noting that it was 'dark in America.'

‘I came to give a warning, Elon Musk, the light is getting ready to come on! Donald Trump, the light is getting ready to come on! JD Vance, the light is getting ready to come on! MAGA, the light is getting ready to come on!’ 

And Bryant's past support of Farrakhan, the notorious antisemitic Nation of Islam leader whose record includes calling Jews ‘wicked’ and comparing them to termites, has also sparked outrage. 

Bryant has been a vocal supporter of Farrakhan over the years and described the anti-Semite as ‘one of the greatest leaders of our people’ when he interviewed him back in 2015. 

‘We welcome to the Word Network and the entire world, the honorable Minister Louis Farrakhan! We’re honored to have you, sir,’ Bryant said at the beginning of the interview. 

‘I’m so appreciative to be able to mark in history that I lived in the same chasm of time as one of the greatest leaders of our people.’

The pastor also said he was ‘humbled’ to be in Farrakhan’s presence, in a since-deleted 2019 social media post. It was among dozens of other pro-Farrakhan posts that have now been deleted, along with his old X account. 

Bryant’s past remarks resurfaced after he was spotted at several of Bottoms' campaign fundraisers and rallies in her fight to become governor. 

The pastor, who donated $5,000 to Bottoms' leadership PAC in late October, joined controversial civil rights attorney Ben Crump at a campaign fundraiser just last week where Bryant lavished praise on Bottoms. 

Days later, Bryant also joined a rally for Bottoms and Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, which featured Obama, where he called for Georgia Democrats to get out to vote and to ‘dress up as change makers’ on Halloween. 

In a Facebook post recapping the event, he was ‘honored to be one of the keynote speakers.’ 

Bottoms, for her part, appeared earlier this year on Bryant's Let's Be Clear podcast and said: ‘I am honored to be here…I love you. I love your family and I watch your podcast, so I am just honored to be counted in the number.’ 

And Bryant used another episode of the podcast to tell his audience that ‘we gotta support Keisha Lance Bottoms, not just because she’s black, but because she is the best.’ 

The Republican Governors Association have come out swinging over the gushing public support – and Bottoms's apparent embrace of it. 

‘Jamal Bryant praises anti-Semites and calls Republicans “roaches,” Ben Crump profits off racial division, and Keisha Lance Bottoms calls them allies,' Block said. 

‘Not a smart move days before the election,’ a Democratic consultant told the Daily Mail. 

Meanwhile, Bryant’s past remarks also include criticizing gay people, which he framed as a ‘sin’ during a 2012 sermon at the Baltimore Empowerment Temple, encouraging believers to make sinners feel ‘uncomfortable in [their] sin.’

He further expressed frustration over the Obama-Biden stance on same-sex marriage, asserting that black pastors were betrayed by the lack of advance notice of the administration's support for gay marriage and that Obama was ‘black and wrong.’

Bottoms, who has been a longtime supporter of gay rights and has called for ‘protecting the dignity and freedom of all who call Atlanta home,’ appointed the city’s first LGBTQ affairs coordinator and formed an LGBTQ advisory board during her tenure as mayor.

She isn’t the first Democratic politician that Bryant has campaigned with.

He hosted failed Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 at his church and previously campaigned with twice-failed Georgia gubernatorial nominee Stacey Abrams, a Democrat.

Bryant previously called Harris an ‘American hero’ and a ‘voice of the future’ in 2024. Harris returned the praise by saying she was honored to be in attendance at his church to ‘celebrate’ what he has ‘accomplished.’

The Daily Mail reached out to Bryant and the Bottoms campaign.

news.title: Pro-Life Group Exposes Shady Dark Money Mail Campaigns Tricking Republican Voters With False Pro-Abortion Claims
news.text:
A pro-life political advocacy group shed light on an allegedly pro-America First and anti-globalist dark money group targeting conservative voters through an alleged organized campaign of misleading mailers.

Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America (“SBA Pro-Life America”) pushed back by releasing an ad Friday exposing the American Forge Coalition — a tax-exempt nonprofit with undisclosed donors created in May — for trying to trick voters into voting against pro-life Republicans in several races. The pro-life group said the nonprofit did this by sending crafty mailers that distort candidates’ records on abortion and provide faulty information on their policy stances.

SBA Pro-Life America President Marjorie Dannenfelser slammed the mailers in a statement shared with the Daily caller News Foundation.

“Don’t fall for the disgraceful dark money attacks on stalwart pro-life candidates across the country. American Forge Coalition did not immediately respond to the DCNF’s request for comment.

SBA Pro-Life America’s partner super PAC Women Speak Out released an ad Friday exposing an American Forge Coalition mailer specifically targeting House candidate Laurie Buckhout, the Republican nominee for North Carolina’s First District.

“Laurie Buckhout would permit states to allow abortions up till birth,” the mailer said, as shown in the ad. 

SBA Pro-Life America was quick to come to Buckhout’s defense.“This is a complete lie,” the ad’s voiceover said. “Laurie Buckhout is the only pro-life candidate.”

Buckhout stated in 2024 that she is “personally pro-life” but believes abortion should be a state issue, WITN reported at the time. The candidate’s 2026 campaign website does not appear to include a position on abortion. She is running against Democratic North Carolina Rep. Don Davis in a race the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates as a “toss up.”

The American Forge Coalition attempted to sway voters away from Republican candidates in battleground House races across the country by misrepresenting them and promoting third-party candidates in their place, the News & Observer reported. “ADD YOUR NAME: AMERICANS FIRST, FOREIGNERS LAST,” states the sign up-form on the group’s website, dubbed “FORM 1776.”

There is no record where the anonymous group behind them gets its funding from as the website lists no address and shows nothing filed with the Federal Election Commission (FEC). 

The group’s national operation has hit Republicans in many states across different regions of the country. 

Besides Buckhout, several other candidates that found themselves to be victims of the mailers are endorsed by SBA Pro-Life America including: Republican South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham; Aaron Flint, Republican nominee for Montana’s First District; Republican Wisconsin Rep. Derrick Van Orden and Republican Virginia Rep. Rob Wittman. 

“With Senate and House majorities and countless babies’ lives on the line, wherever the mailers originate, the deception plays right into the hands of Democrats who vow to impose taxpayer-funded abortion up to birth within their first 100 hours of taking power,” Dannenfelser added in her statement. “We’re fighting back with truth and couldn’t be prouder to stand with champions like Sen. Darline Graham, Laurie Buckhout, Aaron Flint, and all our allies to stop Democrats’ pro-abortion extremism.”

Republican New York Rep. Mike Lawler, who the group allegedly targeted through both fake mailers and fake texts, called on his constituents to report them to the FBI on Saturday. Lawler, one of just a small handful of Republicans to represent seats Kamala Harris won in 2024, is currently locked in a tight race with Democrat Cait Conley, which Cook rates as a “toss up.”

“The Justice Department has confirmed to my campaign that it referred the group to the FBI, and the Post reports the feds are investigating it as a voter suppression effort,” a Saturday public service announcement from Lawler’s campaign titled “Who the Heck is the American Forge Coalition?” read.
