news.title: Let the race to succeed Trump begin
news.text: Even those who merely skim through the current state of politics in the United States are unanimous that the Republican Party, which President Donald Trump has recreated in his image, will lose one or both chambers of the US Congress in the mid-term polls on November 3 (November 4 in India).Yet, throughout his adult life, Trump has bounced back from adversities like the proverbial cat of nine lives. He has changed the US, perhaps forever, and the world in our time. Like the personification of many legends, he is erratic and unconventional, resulting in the unpredictable.The outcome of the mid-term congressional elections, therefore, can be reduced to one word: turnout. Democrats will turn out to vote on November 3 with missionary zeal. Many Republicans have soured on Trump, yet they cannot bring themselves to vote for the other party. They are very likely to sit at home on election day. So will many right-leaning independents and undecided voters who tend to cast their ballots for right-of-centre nominees at the last minute.Candidate George W Bush had Karl Rove—nicknamed ‘the Architect’—to ensure massive turnouts of voters who made up the Republican base. Rove was to Bush Jr what Amit Shah is to Narendra Modi. Similarly, candidate Barack Obama had David Plouffe, David Axelrod and Valerie Jarrett to ensure the turnout.Trump is severely handicapped in this regard. His earliest campaign managers like Corey Lewandowski and Steve Bannon are either about to go to jail for their corruption in his current administration or have done a jail term for wrongdoings in his previous presidency. Trump, as he approaches sunset at the pinnacle of his public life, is happier now in the company of his executive assistant—the 35-year-old Natalie Harp—than among hard core political operatives.On the critical need for mobilisation, there is an example by which Indians can relate to the relevance of turnout in US elections. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Eshwer Prasad Teki, who is Union Minister Hardeep Singh Puri’s chief aide in charge of development of his adopted district of Sonbhadra in Uttar Pradesh, went there to check on the vaccination drive. To his horror, Teki discovered that the vaccination centres were deserted. No one from the district’s villages was getting vaccinated. They did not have the means or the money for transport to the vaccination centres.Teki also found that 30 ambulances were idly stationed at one location in the district headquarters. His request to the health authorities to ferry villagers on these ambulances to be vaccinated was turned down on the ground that the ambulances were kept for emergencies. “All 30 ambulances?” Teki exploded. “What huge emergency would be requiring 30 ambulances at the same time?” The district health authorities were unmoved.Luckily, the young district collector was open-minded and Teki convinced the collector to use these ambulances to transport villagers for vaccination. Their turnout became impressive. Sonbhadra was soon at the top of the vaccination records in UP. This and other similar initiatives in people mobilisation catapulted Sonbhadra to one of the top five slots among the Aspirational Districts Programme of NITI Aayog for six consecutive years..Pundits have so far focused on how much of a lame duck Trump will become if Democrats reclaim the House of Representatives with a workable majority. They have also been discussing the chances that the President will be impeached if Democrats retake the Senate as well. Trump himself has expressed such fears while motivating the Republican base to turn out to vote.There is much more to the mid-term results than these. For example, the results will be a pointer to who will succeed Trump as his party’s candidate in 2028. Trump is in his second presidential term. The American Constitution prohibits a President from serving more than two terms.As of now, Vice President J D Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are at the top of the list of probables. Their Senate seats, which both men resigned to join the Trump administration, are in play. Vance, as an elected politician, is allowed to campaign in this by-election from his home state of Ohio. By convention, the secretary of State, an appointed official, does not campaign in any elections. His old Senate seat is in Florida.If these two men cannot convincingly demonstrate their continuing hold on their home states, their probability as Republican presidential hopefuls in 2028 will recede. According to the latest opinion polls, Rubio’s former seat is leaning towards Republicans. Ohio’s seat is most likely to flip to Democrats. At stake is also Ohio’s governorship, where Indian-American Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is trailing at present.On the Democratic side, an undercurrent in the fight for the next US Congress has been the slow but steady emergence on the national scene of New York City’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani, an Indian American. Several of Mamdani’s associates and progressive sympathisers are in the fray from Pennsylvania to California, including Mamdani’s base of New York state.The first New York mayor was appointed in 1665, when it was a British colonial province. For the better part of almost four centuries, mayors of the city have been larger-than-life figures. Recent examples were Rudi Giuliani and Michael Bloomberg. Both men sought America’s presidency, but came up short in the gruelling primaries. Mamdani can never seek the White House, because he was born outside the US, in Uganda. His ambition, therefore, is to shape the Democratic Party’s national agenda in the coming decades as a socialist. It is a gamble worth watching.In addition, the mid-term outcomes will decide the political future of Kamala Harris, whom Trump defeated two years ago for his historic comeback. Harris has said she may throw her hat in the presidential ring next year for 2028. If Democrats win big in Georgia, Michigan, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, those victories will strengthen her potential candidature. Harris has campaigned in all these states last month in the final stretch of the current campaign. If she can turn out African-American voters in some of these states with significant black populations, other presidential aspirants from her party may find in her a powerful challenger, rising from the ashes once again.K P Nayar | Strategic analyst(Views are personal)(kpnayar@gmail.com).Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Vance's midterm rally blitz draws attention from GOP insiders weighing 2028 predictions
news.text: SWANTON, Ohio — As Republicans rally ahead of a midterm election that will determine whether the GOP maintains control of both chambers of Congress, Vice President JD Vance is taking to the campaign trail once again to speak with voters in New York and Ohio on Monday. Vance’s role in the midterm blitz has been eyed by many top GOP strategists and insiders who say his actions on the trail could offer insight into what a 2028 run might look like for the 42-year-old vice president. "Vice President Vance is constantly on the road," House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., told Fox News Digital. "I believe he's been in just shy of 50 battleground districts and or states this cycle. He's been a workhorse. I mean you look at Donald J. Trump, who's out there constantly. He just doesn't stop. And of course, people don't maybe notice than the vice president is keeping a schedule himself that is frankly incredibly impressive." EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE VANCE'S INTIMATE CAPITOL HILL HUDDLE AS REPUBLICANS CONFRONT TOUGH MIDTERM TERRAIN Vance has held 19 rallies since the GOP midterm convention in early September and dozens of events across the country prior to the convention in Dallas. His role in the midterm has fueled further speculation about his potential run for president in 2028. Former White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer explained that his midterm campaign efforts add to his resume, but that his fundraising abilities and his role as finance chair of the Republican National Committee will also be an important advantage that Vance would have in a run for president. SECOND LADY USHA VANCE KEEPS 'OPEN MIND' AMID JD VANCE 2028 SPECULATION "I think which makes this vice president unique, though, is that it's a combination of the policy chops that you just mentioned, but the political chops," Spicer told Fox News Digital I've noted this over and over again that, like, he is the first vice president to ever be the finance chair of the RNC." "His network of donors is going to be a massive advantage if he runs in '28," he added. TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028 Vance has repeatedly told reporters that he is focused on his current portfolio of work and has shied away from questions concerning a potential run for the Oval Office. He is, however, the favorite in several prediction markets. President Donald Trump told reporters in late October that he is focused on the midterms before looking at which Republican may run in 2028, saying: "It’s early. We are very early right now. We have to get through the midterms. We’ll see how it goes." As for the work Vance is doing off the campaign trail, former White House Chief of Staff and former RNC Chairman Reince Priebus compared the responsibilities of former Vice President Kamala Harris to Vance, saying that Vance has had to take charge of more key issues — from leading the anti-fraud task force to negotiating a peace deal in the Middle East. "If you compare it to the portfolio of Kamala Harris, whose first job was to secure the border, it ended up being a complete and total disaster," Priebus told Fox News Digital. "He's a trusted administrator of huge problems facing our country. So that is very clear. He's a little bit of a whiz kid too." POLL FLASHES WARNING SIGNS FOR REPUBLICANS IN 7 BATTLEGROUND SENATE RACES Pollsters predict that Democrats have an edge in the House as the midterms approach, while the Senate remains "on a knife edge," according to Priebus. The former RNC chairman noted that traditional red and blue waves are far rarer now that in previous midterm elections, noting a smaller number House seats shift between parties every cycle. THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND "There are so few districts in our entire country that are up for grabs," Priebus said. "At 435 house seats, how many are really in play? Maybe 30? And in those 30, there's probably only about 5,000 votes in each of those 30 that could go either way. So, that's why you have ripples, I think, nowadays and not waves. The Senate races are all on a knife edge." While President Trump is known for hosting a staggering number of rallies, Vance’s increased presence in the midterm blitz has led to his name emerging alongside President Donald Trump as the face of the party, according to former White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows. "I think a lot of people have seen him in the shadows of Donald Trump, not as an individual campaigner," Meadows told Fox News Digital. "But as someone who would continue the Trump legacy." THE ONE LINE FROM JD VANCE’S GOP KEYNOTE THAT REVEALS HIS VISION FOR AMERICA "I think for the first time, a broader spectrum of people are seeing JD Vance as the campaigner, and not as a campaigner for him personally," Meadows said. "And, you know, I point out that most of his dynamic interactions have not been in Iowa or New Hampshire or South Carolina." GOP members of Congress have also noted the increased presence of the vice president as they fight to maintain the majority in the House. Rep. Brandon Gill, R-TX, told Fox News Digital he traveled with Vance to Texas and noted the impact that the vice president had in the state. "Kamala Harris couldn't go out and campaign for people because nobody would want to see her," Gill said. "The American people love Vice President Vance. I mean, at all the rallies I've been out with them, they were packed, people were fired up." The vice president held two rallies ahead of the midterm on Monday, one in Rome, New York and the other in Swanton, Ohio – advocating for GOP congressional candidates and pushing for the Republicans to maintain the majority. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Take your friends, take your neighbors, take your grandparents. Get out there and let them know that we are going to send a message that America belongs to those who love it, not those who hate it," Vance told voters in New York on Monday.
news.summary: Vice President JD Vance has held 19 rallies since September as GOP strategists say his midterm election blitz offers a preview of a potential 2028 run.

If Haley Stevens thought she would receive the media’s “Liz Cheney Country Over Party” award, she was sadly mistaken.

On Saturday, before Stevens’ announcement, el Sayed said he did not want Stevens to attend a big party unity event on Sunday. “I don’t want any distractions,” el Sayed said. Let’s just say that el Sayed did not get his wish.

At the same time, el Sayed had to be pleased with the results of the final New York Times/Siena poll of the race. The survey put el Sayed ahead by 11 points, 53% to Rogers’s 42%, by far his largest lead of the campaign.

The poll immediately seemed like an outlier. Seven recent polls listed in the RealClearPolitics average showed el Sayed with a lead from 1 to 7 points. The New York Times had it at 11, which felt like it was in line with the unreliable polling that has bedeviled this race and others.

In the Democratic primary, el Sayed went into election day with a 10.2-percentage-point lead over Stevens, according to the RealClearPolitics average. In the actual election results, el Sayed won by exactly 1 point.

Even before primary election day, when el Sayed was contending not only with Stevens but with Michigan state legislator Mallory McMorrow, unreliable polling played a part in the race. In late June, a poll appeared seemingly out of nowhere from an outfit called “Wedgewood Polls” showing el Sayed at 46% and Stevens at 39%, while McMorrow’s support, which had been in the mid-teens and 20s, fell to 9%. Calls arose for McMorrow to quit the race, which she did, leaving it to el Sayed and Stevens.

Later, Wedgewood Polls published a statement on X revealing that the organization was fake and the poll was fake. It was all an “experiment.” In a post on its now-deleted account, the group wrote, “We wanted to test a simple hypothesis: How easy is it for an entirely fabricated polling firm to gain traction, to be taken seriously, and expose how little scrutinization exists in media and public commentary? The short answer: Far too easy.”

Who was behind Wedgewood Polls? It’s still not clear; it might have been some Democratic dirty trick designed to boost el Sayed or Stevens. In any event, the immediate victim was McMorrow. “Here’s the impact of this ‘experiment,'” she wrote on X. “Donations dried up. Volunteers were devastated and pleading for guidance on what to do. Reporters hounded me with calls to drop out.”

So McMorrow left the race to el Sayed and Stevens. Now, there’s another poll, this time from a real polling outfit — Siena Research, working with the New York Times — showing el Sayed with another big lead. New York Times journalists seemed clearly nervous about it. Almost immediately after releasing the Michigan poll, along with polls from other states that showed Democrats with smaller leads, the paper published an article by its poll expert, Nate Cohn, with the headline: “The Final Polls Show a Blue Surge. Can We Trust Them?”

It was an extraordinary thing for a news organization to say about a big poll it had just released. In this case, the New York Times was worried about something known in the polling business as “partisan nonresponse bias,” a phenomenon in which supporters of one political party are less likely to respond to pollsters than those from the other party. For the last several years, the nonresponse has come from the Republican side — GOP supporters are less likely, sometimes far less likely, to cooperate with pollsters than Democratic supporters.

“This cycle, Democrats are once again responding to Times/Siena polls at a much higher rate than Republicans,” Cohn wrote. “Across these final battleground polls, registered white Democrats were about 30 percent likelier to take the poll than registered white Republicans. That’s actually a bit higher than in the final polls in 2020 … The persistence of this kind of nonresponse bias introduced the risk of systematic polling error like those in 2016 or 2020.”

To correct the nonresponse problem, pollsters use a technique called “weighting,” in which they estimate what each candidate’s support would be if voters from both parties responded in numbers that accurately represented their percentage of the electorate. They’ve been doing that for a while in an effort to correct the mistakes from 2016 and 2020 to which Cohn referred. And now, they’re weighting more than ever.

Cohn even revealed what the result of the new Michigan poll would have been if the weighting formula from earlier elections had been applied to the latest results. With the old formula, el Sayed’s lead would have been 16 points. Using the new formula, the New York Times pegs el Sayed’s lead at 11 points. They’re hoping that is right this time. But they don’t really know, which is why they publish all sorts of cautionary notes.

BYRON YORK: HAS NO TAX ON TIPS/OVERTIME/SOCIAL SECURITY HELPED THE GOP?

There are plenty of nonresponse problems in other key Senate states as well — Alaska, Kansas, and others. But Republican voter reticence might be particularly pronounced in Michigan because el Sayed has so often accused his critics of Islamophobia. He makes it seem that an inordinate number of the people who criticize him are doing so out of bigotry. So say you’re a Republican voter, you’re going to vote against el Sayed, and some polling company calls you up to ask your opinion on the race. Why talk to some stranger about it?

Of course, we’ll know the result soon. In the primary, el Sayed’s lead turned out to be one-tenth the size the polls suggested it was, but he still won. After Tuesday’s election, he’ll either be the next senator from Michigan or a new case study in partisan nonresponse bias.

news.title: How Trump's Popularity Compares to Biden, Obama Days Before Midterms
news.text: President Donald Trump is tied with former President Joe Biden in positive public perception but trails former President Barack Obama, according to a national poll released two days before the midterm elections. AtlasIntel's November 1 survey found that 40 percent of Americans have a positive image of Trump and Biden, compared with 54 percent for Obama. However, Trump's negative rating is higher than either predecessor's, at 58 percent compared with Biden's 54 percent and Obama's 44 percent. The findings provide a snapshot of Americans' views as voting concludes on November 3 in elections that will decide control of Congress for the last two years of Trump's second term. They measure current perceptions of the three men, rather than comparing their approval ratings at corresponding points in their presidencies. How Trump Compares With Biden and Obama Overall Subtracting negative from positive responses gives Trump a net rating of minus 18 percentage points, Biden minus 14 and Obama plus 10. The survey interviewed 3,566 U.S. adults between October 28 and November 1 using AtlasIntel's Random Digital Recruitment method. The poll's reported margin of error is plus or minus 2 percentage points. The distinction between positive and net ratings matters. Two politicians can attract the same proportion of positive responses while differing in how many people view them negatively or answer "don't know." These figures also should not be read as a hypothetical election result. Respondents were assessing their impressions of individual politicians. Trump vs Other Political Figures' Positive Ratings Former first lady Michelle Obama received a 52 percent positive rating and a 44 percent negative rating in the AtlasIntel survey, putting her positive score 12 percentage points ahead of Trump's. Meanwhile, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg—all Democrats—each scored 47 percent, seven points above Trump. Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis matched Trump's 40 percent positive rating. Republican Vice President JD Vance and Democratic former Vice President Kamala Harris each received 38 percent, followed by Democratic former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton at 36 percent and California Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom at 33 percent. Small differences between politicians warrant caution: a numerical lead in a poll does not automatically establish a statistically meaningful difference. Recognition, "don't know" responses and the wording of a question can also affect comparisons. What Other Polls Show A CNN survey conducted earlier this year by SSRS also found Obama substantially more popular than either of his successors. Released on June 18, it put the Democratic former commander-in-chief's favorable rating at 57 percent, compared with 34 percent for Trump and 30 percent for Biden—a 23-point advantage over Trump and a 27-point advantage over Biden. Obama's standing among political independents was more than twice that of either man. He also retained near-universal support among Democrats. Other former presidents occupied the middle ground. Republican George W. Bush received a 42 percent favorable rating and a 33 percent unfavorable rating, while opinions of Bill Clinton, a Democrat, were evenly divided. In a separate, open-ended question asking which president respondents most admired, Obama led with 30 percent, followed by Trump at 19 percent. Abraham Lincoln and Ronald Reagan each received 9 percent. The CNN survey interviewed 2,480 adults from May 7 through May 31, using online and telephone interviews. Its overall margin of sampling error was plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. What Recent Polling Says About the Midterms Separate October surveys offer additional context about Trump's performance in office and the electoral environment. One Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted between October 22 and 26 found that 32 percent of Americans approved of Trump's job performance. Approval was lower on economic issues: 25 percent approved of his handling of the economy and 20 percent approved of his handling of the cost of living. Among likely voters, 53 percent supported or leaned toward the Democratic congressional candidate in their district, compared with 44 percent for the Republican candidate. That survey used Ipsos' probability-based KnowledgePanel and interviewed 1,679 adults. The margin of error for the full adult sample was plus or minus 2.4 percentage points. Meanwhile, a separate CNN/SSRS survey conducted between October 15 and 18 found Democrats holding a 10-point advantage in congressional preference among registered voters. More than three-quarters of voters regarded the election as an opportunity to change things in Washington. That poll interviewed 1,701 adults, including 1,206 registered voters, with margins of error of plus or minus 2.9 points and 3.3 points, respectively. What Happens Next All 435 voting seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are being contested in the elections on November 3. The results will determine control of the next Congress, whose term begins on January 3, 2027. For Trump, the immediate test is whether public dissatisfaction translates into votes against Republican candidates and whether those votes change the balance of power on Capitol Hill. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Robert Greenall and Matthew Robinson

news.title: What the final polls are forecasting for the 2026 midterm elections
news.text:
Midterm week is here, and the polls show a clear trend. But what does that mean for the actual elections? 

With voters casting early ballots at record rates — North Carolina, Texas, Georgia and South Carolina saw midterm early vote numbers never previously reached, and states like Maine, Kansas and Michigan had turnout up over 30% from 2022 — final polls are telling a deeper story about possible results.

Most polls show the Democrats holding an advantage in both the House and Senate races, with forecasters debating whether it will be a blue ripple, a blue wave or a blue tsunami, or if Republicans will outperform the polls. 

Republicans currently hold the House majority with a 218-214 advantage. With all 435 seats in play, including seats that were redrawn through mid-decade redistricting that was originally expected to favor the GOP, Decision Desk HQ gives the Democrats a more than 80% chance to win control of the House, with the Cook Political Report projecting they take between 227 and 240 seats.

In the Senate, Republicans currently hold a 53-47 advantage, but with 35 seats up for grabs Tuesday, a major shift could occur.

A New York Times/Siena poll released Sunday showed leads for Democrats in key Senate races, including leads of more than 5 points in Ohio, Kansas, Maine and Texas, and an 11-point lead for Abdul El-Sayed over Mike Rogers in Michigan. The Michigan race became even more newsworthy over the weekend when Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Rogers. That decision earned condemnation from high-profile Democrats and praise from President Trump.

The poll also showed Democratic candidate Josh Turek with a 1-point lead over Republican Ashley Hinson in Iowa and Mary Peltola leading Alaska's incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by 2 points despite the ongoing controversy surrounding the third-party candidate, also named Dan Sullivan. Both leads are within the margin of error.

Both Georgia and North Carolina, states Trump won in 2024, show the Democratic candidates — Jon Ossoff and Roy Cooper — holding leads outside the margins of error.

For reference, these are the percentage points by which Trump beat Kamala Harris in the following states in 2024 (Harris won Maine by 6.9 points):

Michigan: 1.4 pointsGeorgia: 2.2 pointsNorth Carolina: 3.2 pointsOhio: 11.2 pointsAlaska: 13.1 pointsIowa: 13.2 pointsTexas: 13.7 pointsKansas: 16.2 points

Even in Louisiana, a state Trump won by 22 points in 2024, a Lincoln Park Strategies poll found the Senate race between Democrat Jamie Davis and Republican US Rep. Julia Letlow to be tied.

Polls may not tell the full story, however. In the Trump era, polls have had their own issues. In 2016, forecasters famously gave Hillary Clinton a higher chance to win the presidency than Trump, and polls have underestimated Republican support in several recent cycles. Speaker Mike Johnson has said he believes that polls are "even further off this time because more and more Republicans are unwilling to participate in these surveys."

Analysts point to Trump's approval rating as a factor in the strong Democratic polling. It has slipped to 37%, according to a recent Emerson College poll, down from 39% as recently as September. According to Civiqs' state-by-state tracker, he has positive approval ratings in only eight states: Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming.
news.author: Eric Orvieto

news.title: The Blue Wave Has Arrived: How High Will It Crest?
news.text:
You can’t really blame left-wingers, Democrats, progressives, or libs of all description for looking at wave after wave of positive polling results and responding mostly with anxious, fingernail-chewing trepidation. They have been conditioned into this by painful polling errors and misses in the accuracy of polling Democratic vs. Republican support in recent years, especially in 2020 (where Joe Biden’s victory was narrow instead of the wide one that was generally predicted) and 2024, where predictions of a Kamala Harris victory were less loud, but still present, and pollsters again failed to adapt to the Trump factor even after multiple tries. Lost among the pessimism and anxiety, though, is the point that pollsters have all been trying to make this entire cycle: A midterm election is not a presidential election, and recent midterm polling from nonpartisan pollsters has actually been quite accurate. In both 2018 and 2022, in fact, the ultimate net national polling miss was less than one point, making for two of the most accurate years for polling in modern election history.

Tomorrow, Americans take the polls–if they haven’t already voted early, and record numbers have–to deliver what all logic and data is telling us is almost certainly going to be a blue wave election. There’s no reason to skirt around it at this point; the momentum of Democrats in numerous races is quite palpable and backed up by the data. This combination of data and vibes is showing up everywhere, including in the crystal ball that is betting/prediction markets, where Democrats are now seen as having a nearly 75% chance to walk away with control of the U.S. Senate, something that would have been unthinkable to say six months ago.

The reasons why are not some kind of mystery. An unpopular President results in midterm bloodbaths; this has always been the case. It all flows downward from the historic unpopularity of an 80-year-old Donald Trump, whose party is finally being stung by the stigma of being inextricably attached at the hip to him, something he has tirelessly worked to achieve for a decade. A few days ago, Trump’s approval rating busted through yet another floor in Nate Silver’s polling aggregator, achieving a new all-time low of 36.3%, with more than 60% of Americans saying they disapproved. Republicans running in the midterms, even in states Trump won by double digits only two years ago, have responded by running as far away as they can from the President, with less than 1% of all GOP ads even mentioning Trump’s name in recent weeks.

WELKER: Is a vote for a Republican candidate a vote for the Trump agenda? 
TIM SCOTT: There’s no doubt — President Trump has said himself that the midterm election is about him

— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar.com) 9:46 AM · Nov 1, 2026

But it doesn’t matter if you don’t say “Trump” when your constituents and voters are completely unable to untangle their daily lives from the disastrous economic effects of the last year in particular of Trump’s capricious whims. The Iran War will likely go down in history as the thing that finally eroded the last functional levels of Trump’s power, as its nested effects upon global shipping, gasoline and inflation were finally able to move public opinion on his effectiveness as an economic leader in a way that none of his other scandals could touch. The civic-minded among us will always probably have a difficult time accepting that the “median” American cares far more about how much it costs to fill their gas tank than whether red hat-wearing rioters are storming the Capitol, but the data completely bears this out. For as hopelessly partisan and polarized as our culture has become, simple economics still reign supreme when it comes to motivating (and pissing off) voters. And the many economic factors voters are facing, from the constellation of Iran effects, to Trump’s insistence on making it all worse with trade wars against the likes of Canada, have only guaranteed that voters have plenty of reasons for rage.

This has made messaging for the many Democratic hopefuls of this cycle, running in places that haven’t elected blue congressmen or senators in decades, relatively simple: Acknowledge the painful cost of living, and the clownishness and chaos of the administration, and claim that you can do better. Someone like Josh Turek was not supposed to have a legitimate opportunity to flip a state like Iowa blue, and he still very well may not–that race between Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson is particularly close, and even the betting markets see it as a pure toss-up. But the way he talks about the race is the way that so many other Democrats have also successfully approached it while running in places that have been red bastions for decades. As Turek recently put it: “I’ve gone out there and said to Republicans, ‘Look, I understand why you voted for Trump, because he accurately identified the status quo was not working for the average person. Now they’re ready for a true common-sense prairie populist that’s actually going to make their lives better.”

In a lot of those other “red” states, meanwhile, GOP intransigence has morphed into outright panic. You’ve got Ken Paxton’s attorney general office in Texas suing the county containing Houston because it’s angry that too many minority voters are taking advantage of early voting. The final New York Times/Siena poll of the swing states? It as of yesterday put Paxton’s challenger for the Senate seat, James Talarico, a shockingly 7 points ahead in the race, which is Talarico’s best single poll of this entire cycle. Prediction markets likewise give Talarico a 3-in-4 chance of outright winning the Senate seat tomorrow, which would make him the first Democratic Senator elected by Texas in almost 40 years. These numbers are reaching the point where even an average polling error would still most likely result in Democrats recapturing the Senate.

So tonight’s NYT poll has El-Sayed up by 11 points.
Gift link below

— Bill Grueskin (@bgrueskin.bsky.social) 8:13 PM · Nov 1, 2026

That same Times/Siena poll is full of eye-popping figures, none more garishly optimistic for Democrats than that it places Democratic senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed 11 points ahead of Mike Rogers in Michigan, the kind of chasm that not even the insanely petty, last-minute endorsement flip-flop of defeated primary challenger Haley Stevens would be likely to affect. Everywhere you look in said final poll, the numbers are unabashedly calling for a blue wave. Troy Jackson, up by 6 points in Maine. Sherrod Brown, up by 5 points in Ohio. Adam Hamilton, up an astounding 5 points over Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator SINCE 1932!

When a state is in play for the first time in 94 years, then it’s safe to say something truly notable is happening here. The pure sweatiness on the right side of the aisle is impossible to hide. Look no farther than Marshall, who just reportedly went rogue to release his own campaign ad against the wishes of his campaign strategists, which includes such phrases as “I never had anyone arrested, not once.” Seems like the sort of thing a person probably says in an ad right before they win an election, right?

I am not an election prognosticator, or a data analyst who can look at early voting patterns and turnout indicators and spit out a best guess or conclusion. The guys I trust to do that, however? They’re pretty unified in the assessment: The blue wave is about to swamp Republicans, in spite of the years of efforts of Donald Trump and his cronies to thwart the will of voters and stack the system wherever possible. Here’s hoping it is every bit the tsunami that now looks not just possible, but likely.

news.title: Midterms poll tracker: The 8 Senate races you need to know about as Trump faces losing prized majority
news.text:
Democrats face a steep task in November's midterm elections if they want to take the US Senate from Republican hands.

They need to win at least four seats to make a net gain. Voter discontent with President Donald Trump, the Iran war and rising prices has put races in once-solidly Republican states into play. Thirty-five Senate seats are up for reelection this year.

Republicans are defending 22, while Democrats hold 13. The GOP currently controls the chamber with a 53-47 majority. Because Republican Vice President JD Vance can break tie votes, Democrats need 51 seats to win control. At the start of the year, a Democratic takeover looked unlikely.

Since then, Democrats have become competitive in states Trump won handily in 2024, even as Republicans pursue Democratic-held seats. The political winds are swirling against Trump and Republicans, as they historically do in midterm elections for the party in power.

Voters are dissatisfied with Trump's job performance as the war in Iran continues and gas prices are soaring. Senate Republicans went into the election feeling optimistic, largely thanks to the map.

Here is what that uphill path to power looks like for Democrats.

The most straightforward route to the majority involves Democrats holding all of their seats, including the battlegrounds of Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire. On top of that, they will need to pick up four more seats, and their best opportunities are in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.

Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia is heading into his reelection campaign as a rare bright spot for Democrats. The Democratic senator was first swept into office after the 2021 Georgia U.S. Senate runoff, alongside Sen. Raphael Warnock. That double victory handed Democrats control of the Senate. 

His slickly produced campaign videos have now gone viral. They have driven buzz that he may be seeking the presidency in 2028. 

He has used Trump's baseless complaints of election fraud in Georgia as a foil, calling the president the “world’s most famous sore loser.” His campaign is also benefiting from a weakened GOP nominee.

A New Hampshire political dynasty stands between Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and the Senate seat vacated by Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. Former Sen. John Sununu wants to return to the seat he once held, and he is the brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu and the son of former Gov. John H. Sununu. Sununu beat Shaheen in the 2002 U.S. Senate election. 

Six years later, Shaheen won the rematch. Pappas brings his own New Hampshire pedigree to the contest, through a family business that is a state institution in its own right. He and his family own the Puritan Backroom, a Manchester restaurant that has been around since 1917. The restaurant claims to have invented the chicken tender. 

Polls have shown the race is tight, and Republicans believe the Sununu name can help them flip the seat. The GOP has not won a Senate seat in the state since 2010. The last two governors in the Granite State, however, have been Republican.

Maine Democrats turned to Troy Jackson, a former state Senate president, at an emergency nominating convention after their original candidate withdrew amid an accusation of sexual assault. Polling shows Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins in a neck-and-neck race. 

Collins is the lone Republican representing a state that has never voted for Trump. As in her last election six years ago, Democrats are her top target. Ousting her, however, is proving to be anything but straightforward. 

The party initially nominated Graham Platner, an oyster farmer who ran an energetic grassroots campaign. His bid forced Gov. Janet Mills, Senate Democrats' preferred pick, to suspend her campaign before voters cast ballots. He then withdrew his candidacy after he was accused of sexual assault. 

Jackson finished third in the first round of the gubernatorial primary. He was endorsed in that contest by progressive stalwart Sen. Bernie Sanders.

Democrats have not won a federal race in North Carolina since former President Barack Obama carried the state in 2008. The party believes former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper can end that run, and his decision to run for Senate has given Democrats arguably their best recruit of this year. 

Cooper was first elected governor in 2016 and reelected in 2020, winning his race while Trump won at the top of the ballot. His opponent will be Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman and chairman of the North Carolina Republican Party. Whatley is a staunch Trump ally, with no daylight between him and the Trump administration's policy positions. 

He is making his first bid for public office. Throughout the campaign, Whatley has trailed Cooper in fundraising and polls. Republicans have had the edge in ad spending, but that advantage has tapered as the party has shifted resources to other races. 

Democrats have had success in statewide races in North Carolina, while Republicans have held the edge in federal contests. In 2024, Democrats won the governor, lieutenant governor and attorney general races, all while Trump carried the state.

Mary Peltola's decision to run for Senate has handed a win to Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and his fellow Democrats as they target a Republican-held seat in Alaska. The former House member is taking on GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, a low-key conservative who rarely strays from the party line. 

Peltola first came to Congress through a U.S. House special election in 2022, winning the seat left vacant by the death of Rep. Don Young. She went on to win a full term later that year, defeating former vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin. A former tribal judge, Peltola made history as the first Alaska Native to represent the state in Congress. She would achieve the same first if elected to the U.S. Senate. 

Her House career ended when she lost reelection in 2024 to GOP Rep. Nick Begich. Polls suggest the Senate contest is a very close race, and Peltola has worked to position herself as an independent voice. She has distanced herself from national Democratic political figures.

Iowa will elect a new senator for the first time since 2014, after Sen. Joni Ernst decided to retire from the seat she won for the Republicans that year. Her departure has created an opening that Democrats believe they can exploit in a state Barack Obama once carried in presidential elections. 

The party's nominee is state Rep. Josh Turek, who has spent two terms representing a competitive state House district. He also brings a sporting pedigree to the race, with two Paralympic gold medals. Democrats are hoping Turek can drive their supporters to the polls and appeal to some of the 572,000 Iowa voters registered as nonpartisan. 

Their calculation rests on a political environment that has been difficult for Republicans, with Trump tariffs and rising gas prices affecting Iowans. The contest will not be easy for Turek, however. Trump has won Iowa in each of the last three presidential elections, and Republicans have controlled the governor's office and both chambers of the state legislature since 2017.

Texas has not sent a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, but the party sees a rare opening in this year's Senate race. The last Democratic presidential candidate to carry the state was Jimmy Carter, in 1976. Democrats have not won a Senate race in Texas since 1988. 

The party came close in 2018, when former Rep. Beto O'Rourke fell to Sen. Ted Cruz by roughly 3 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris went on to lose Texas by nearly 14 percentage points. The contest is now firmly in play, largely because of an expensive and bruising primary on the Republican side. Attorney General Ken Paxton defeated incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in that primary, with ad spending surpassing $128 million. 

Paxton, a Trump ally, has been plagued with scandal during his tenure as the state's attorney general, and was impeached by the Texas House in 2023 and nearly removed from office, but the state Senate narrowly voted to acquit him.

Ohio’s Senate race this November pits a familiar Democratic name against a Republican incumbent appointed only this year. Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his seat to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno two years ago, is running for the state’s other Senate seat. His opponent is Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed in 2025 to the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance. Data centers sit at the center of both campaigns. 

Brown has often called his opponent the “face of data centers” in Ohio. Husted has been trying to separate himself from that image. One of his clearest counters to that label, a bill related to energy costs of data centers, failed to pass the Senate last week. His hopes of returning to Washington rest on whether his name and past record still resonate in a state that has grown more Republican. 

Ohio has not elected a Democrat to statewide executive office since 2008, and Trump has carried the state in the last three presidential elections. Despite that shift towards Republicans over the past decade, Brown has continuously outperformed Democratic presidential candidates in Ohio since first winning his old Senate seat in 2006. Democrats are hoping he will do it again.
news.summary: Democrats need to win at least four seats to make a net gain
news.author: Paul Farrell

news.title: On Abortion Rights, Nevada Offers a Perfect Snapshot of the Midterms
news.text:
Decked out in a sparkly plaid shirt and a dangly necklace urging “VOTE,” US Rep. Susie Lee was rallying a roomful of canvassers to knock on doors around Las Vegas in support of Nevada’s abortion ballot measure, Question 6. The four-term Democratic congresswoman talked about her background—homeless advocate, nonprofit educator, mom of two adult children via IVF—as well as her history of miscarriages and the abortion care she needed to treat them. 

Nevada has statutory protections for abortion, but it also has a Republican governor who has described himself as “pro-life.” Question 6 would enshrine those rights in the state’s constitution. “I don’t want to have to worry about it,” Lee told the audience. “I don’t want to have to worry about it for my daughter, for my grandkids, for families all across the state.” 

But abortion isn’t the main topic on voters’ minds this fall—not in Lee’s sprawling Clark County district, not as her MAGA-y opponent Marty O’Donnell describes abortion rights as “satanic,” and not even in this roomful of purple “My Body. My Ballot.” T-shirts. So Lee devoted much of her time to talking about tariffs, the Iran war, $80-a-tank gas, Medicaid cuts, skyrocketing healthcare premiums, predatory housing costs, and student debt. She also drew a direct connection between affordability and reproductive autonomy. “It’s an economic issue for women and families as well.” 

When it comes to how reproductive rights are paying out on the ballot this fall, that scene is 2026 in a nutshell.

Two years ago, fury over the end of Roe v. Wade put abortion at the center of the national political conversation. This year, in an election dominated by Donald Trump’s economy, war, and corruption, abortion’s importance as a political issue has seemingly receded. Yet polls show voters care about reproductive rights as much as ever—and strategists say the issue could be a key factor in determining the size of the predicted Democratic wave. 

In the closing days of the midterms campaign, more and more pro-choice candidates—in Nevada and around the country—are leaning into the economic arguments. “The most consequential economic decision a family is going to make is whether to have a child,” says Mini Timmaraju, president of Reproductive Freedom for All, which has been working to support ballot initiatives and Democratic candidates in key battlegrounds. “The ability to decide if and how to have a family is critical to your economic future. Voters understand that nuance.”

At the same time, abortion-rights groups are doubling down on their main theme of the past two years: the need for Democratic firewalls in Congress and the states as the Trump administration and its far-right allies threaten access.

At the Las Vegas event, Timmaraju pointed out that Trump officials have been ratcheting up their attacks on medication abortion, federal family planning, contraception and IVF, while telling their supporters that the gloves will really come off after the midterms. “Why after the midterms?” she asked. “Because they know how deeply politically unpopular these attacks are.” 

The event’s special guest, Stacey Abrams, focused on the health impacts of abortion bans, including maternal deaths in her home state of Georgia. If Nevada doesn’t enshrine constitutional protections, she warned, it “runs the risk of being in the number of states where no one knows what they’re entitled to, and therefore no one knows what the future holds.” 

That kind of messaging resonates powerfully with voters, says Molly Murphy, president of the Democratic polling firm Impact Research. “In every poll I’ve done this cycle, [abortion] is a top negative against Republicans in focus groups,” she said at a press briefing last week. “Voters will say, this is a deal breaker. ‘They don’t support freedom and access to reproductive health care? I can’t support them. It’s over for me.’” 

Abortion groups are counting on those sentiments to help Democrats not just retake the House (and, if the latest polls are correct, the Senate) but also win new state trifectas by flipping key legislative seats and governorships—like Nevada’s—that Republicans now hold.

Meanwhile, four states have abortion-related measures on the ballot that could determine access for millions of women. 

Here’s a look at some of the biggest reproductive rights battles of the midterms. 

The Fight for Congress

For a while, it seemed as if helping pro-choice Democrats like Lee win their elections and regain the House majority was the most that reproductive rights groups could reasonably hope for. Lee, first elected in the 2018 blue wave, was seen as vulnerable after Trump won her Third Congressional District in 2024 while she narrowly held onto her seat. But Lee has been helped by Trump’s plummeting popularity and by the extremism (and unseriousness) of her opponent. O’Donnell—a millionaire video-games composer endorsed by Trump—has a rabid online following (“The Marty Army,” recently busted for neo-Nazi and white nationalist comments) and far-right views about abortion and LGBTQ rights. Cook Political Report now rates the race as “Likely D.” 

With the House seemingly locked up for Democrats, reproductive rights groups have intensified their focus on the Senate, whose role in picking Supreme Court justices and federal judges makes it an especially important prize. According to one policy brief, anti-abortion messaging moved support toward Democrats by as much as five points and “significantly increased” motivation among independents. But Republican candidates have been playing down (or actively scrubbing) their anti-abortion records, and pro-choice groups weren’t getting through to voters. The repro-rights side has “a believability gap to overcome,” the polling firm Impact Research warned in a July report. “Most battleground voters are not hearing about the issue of abortion, so while many express concerns about Republican policies that restrict access to abortion, they also believe these policies are unlikely to happen.” 

For repro groups, the final weeks of the cycle have been all about filling that information hole. Reproductive Freedom for All has poured $23.5 million into its midterm campaign, which includes support for key Senate races in Michigan, Iowa, and Maine. Planned Parenthood Votes, a PAC affiliated with Planned Parenthood, announced a $47 million investment with targets including Maine’s Susan Collins and Michigan’s Mike Rogers. Timmaraju argues that repro rights has become a compelling closing argument: “[It’s] the tipping-point issue, the thing that really helps make it plain that Republicans are too extreme to represent average voters.”

The Fight for State Trifectas

In 2024, the trifecta that Democrats fantasized about winning was in Congress and the White House. This year, they have their eyes set on the states.

Gaining complete control of state governments has proven to be one of the best defenses against Trump and the GOP, says Sarah Curmi, executive director of States Win, which supports Democrats running for state legislatures. “Trifectas are critical to protecting abortion rights and reproductive rights generally.” 

Democrats could gain full control over state governments in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Minnesota, and Wisconsin by flipping a net total of just 22 legislative seats, Curmi says. Winning gubernatorial races would lead to trifectas in Nevada and Vermont.

“Being under Democratic control … would have a huge impact for those of us living in those states,” says Curmi, who hails from Michigan. “Not just for abortion access… but also voting rights, redistricting, environmental protections, LGBTQ+ equality—we could be here all day listing all the different ways that state legislatures impact our lives.” 

In Pennsylvania, Democrats are hoping that popular Gov. Josh Shapiro wins reelection by a big enough margin to help them take the state Senate, which Republicans have controlled since 1994. If they gained just two seats, Democrats could raise the minimum wage, increase funding for mass transit, repeal decades-old anti-abortion laws, and codify abortion and LGBTQ protections. While Democrats have a narrow majority in the state House, “the Senate is where our bills have gone to die,” says Signe Espinoza, executive director at Planned Parenthood Pennsylvania Advocates. “If we can change things in the General Assembly, we won’t just be playing defense, but really thinking about the needs of Pennsylvania women and families and moving forward legislation that can really support us.”

In Nevada, it’s popular incumbent Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, running for a second term, who is standing in the way of a Democratic trifecta. Lombardo has a reputation as a moderate who, while personally opposed to abortion, has pledged not to impose his views on the state. Although he has signed some pro-choice legislation passed by the Democratic-controlled legislature, he has vetoed bills on IVF and paid family leave and told the Reno Gazette Journal last month that he would vote against Question 6, saying the current statutory protections are “sufficient.” He had been favored to beat his Democratic rival, Attorney General Aaron Ford, but heading into the final stretch, polls shows the race is tied, while early voting has trended strongly toward Dems.

The Fights Over Ballot Measures

Two years ago, 10 states had measures aimed at enshrining reproductive rights. This November, Nevada is one of only three states that do—and a fourth measure, in Missouri, is trying to repeal abortion protections. 

The vibe around ballot initiatives is also different. Two years ago, Democrats and abortion rights groups hoped the measures would drive angry women—including Republicans—to the polls and sweep Vice President Kamala Harris into the White House. This time around, the goals are more state-specific and expectations more muted. A new analysis by economists in Virginia and Texas helps explain why: Despite more than $250 million in spending in 2024, abortion measures may actually have helped Republicans by giving moderate GOP women a way to blow off steam on reproductive rights without abandoning their party or its anti-abortion candidates.

Nevada is a perfect example of how this played out. Question 6—which guarantees abortion rights until fetal viability or to protect the health or life of the mother—must be approved by voters in two consecutive elections. It was on the ballot for the first time in 2024, winning 64 percent of the vote. But Trump took the state. Something similar happened in Arizona, Missouri, and Montana—all passed abortion measures while reelecting Trump by margins ranging from comfortable to landslide. Trump’s handling of the abortion issue in his campaign—insisting that the Dobbs decision left regulation up to the states and minimizing the possibility of a national ban if he were elected—“was almost like a permission structure for Republicans to go vote for a ballot measure and then vote for him,” Timmaraju says.

Another hard-earned lesson of 2024: “It’s not enough to win ballot measures,” Timmaraju says. “If you don’t have the constitutional officers and you don’t have the legislature, you’re stuck.” 

Missouri is a cautionary tale. Two years ago, it became the first state to overturn a near-total abortion ban, passing its Right to Reproductive Freedom Initiative with almost 52 percent of the vote. But as my colleague Sophie Hurwitz has reported, instead of working to implement the amendment, anti-abortion lawmakers pushed back at every opportunity, including putting their own measure on this year’s ballot that aims to overturn the 2024 measure by demonizing transgender kids. “The results of the 2024 election cycle taught us that we cannot fight for abortion access in a silo,” says Brittany Fonteno, president and CEO of the National Abortion Federation. 

That realization is one reason progressive groups are putting so much effort into state trifectas. Michigan and Arizona have both enshrined abortion rights into their constitutions, but without Democratic control of those legislatures, “we haven’t been able to finish the job,” Timmaraju says. Virginia offers a powerful counter-example: It it the only state in the South that hasn’t enacted some sort of abortion ban since Dobbs, thanks to Democratic lawmakers who were able to thwart then-Gov. Glenn Youngkin, an anti-abortion Republican. Now, after winning the governorship and a trifecta in 2025, Virginia Democrats have a trio of progressive constitutional amendments on this year’s ballot: one guaranteeing reproductive freedom and abortion rights through the second trimester of pregnancy, one repealing a 20-year-old ban on same-sex marriage, and one bolstering voting rights for people with felony convictions.

“We are just trying to remind people that we could be like North Carolina, South Carolina, other states across the South,” says Jamie Lockhart, executive director of Planned Parenthood Advocates of Virginia. Enshrining abortion and other protections means “we don’t have to worry about turning into a state that backslides.” All three measures are expected to pass. 

Because of the on-the-ground realities, repro advocates are keeping their expectations in check in deep-red Idaho, where abortion supporters are trying to pass Proposition 1, which would create a right to reproductive freedom and privacy under state law. Today, Idaho has some of the most draconian abortion laws in the country. While a win would send a potent signal to the state’s overwhelmingly anti-abortion lawmakers, because the measure wouldn’t amend the state constitution, those same Republicans could vote to reinstate the ban. A new poll shows the measure is losing.

In Nevada, meanwhile, Question 6 is expected to easily win, but to a lot of voters, it feels like a throwback. At the Las Vegas event, Denise Lopez, director of Nevada campaigns for Reproductive Freedom for All, addressed the problem head on. “Some voters are asking, didn’t we already pass this?” And the answer is yes,” she said. “We have to do it a second time to ensure that these rights are permanent in our constitution.”

The four-term Democratic congresswoman talked about her background—homeless advocate, nonprofit educator, mom of two adult children […]

news.title: Nolte: NY Times, Washington Post Fret over Republicans Ignoring Pollsters
news.text:
New York Times polling gives all seven U.S. Senate swing states to Democrats, including Kansas and Iowa. The Washington Post released a poll last week showing Democrats winning a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas — Kansas! — by ten points.

There is just one thing…

Both of those far-left outlets are stressing over their own results because Republicans are refusing to cooperate with their pollsters at higher rates than ever.

Per the New York Times, here is what’s expected to happen tomorrow night across seven U.S. Senate races:

Michigan: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins by 11 points, 53 to 42 percent.
Texas: Democrat Talarico wins by seven, 40 to 43 percent
Maine: Democrat Troy Jackson wins by six, 51 to 45 percent
Ohio: Democrat Sherrod Brown wins by five, 49 to 44 percent
Kansas: Democrat Adam Hamilton wins by five points, 49 to 44 percent
Alaska: Democrat Mary Peltola wins by two points, 48 to 46 percent
Iowa: Democrat Josh Turek wins by one point, 48 to 47 percent

Clean sweep, right?

If the Washington Post is correct and Democrats win Kansas — Kansas! — by ten points, that is something even beyond a blue tsunami. That is more like a realignment, a country where even in Kansas voters want kids queered and mutilated to appease their trans godz.

If you read between the lines, though, both of these propaganda outlets are admitting to publishing polls they themselves are unsure of.

“This cycle, Democrats are once again responding to Times/Siena polls at a much higher rate than Republicans,” admits the New York Times. “Across these final battleground polls, registered white Democrats were about 30 percent likelier to take the poll than registered white Republicans. That’s actually a bit higher than in the final polls in 2020.”

The Washington Post reports an even bigger problem…

“After more than 85,000 phone calls and nearly 50,000 text messages [in Kansas], a potential problem emerged,” admits the Post. “Registered Democrats were more than twice as likely as registered Republicans to complete the survey after answering an interviewer’s call — 32 percent versus 12 percent — with a similar partisan gap when texting voters to complete the survey online.”

Registered Independents/Libertarians were even less cooperative.

So, the Post then tried to weight its Kansas poll, admitting “it’s possible those efforts fell short.”

RELATED: Trump’s Message Down the Home Stretch to Midterms: “Our Country’s Doing Great”

“After aligning the sample with Kansas voters’ partisanship and demographics, respondents recalled supporting Donald Trump over Kamala Harris by seven percentage points in 2024, which is smaller than Trump’s 16-point winning margin in the state,” explains the Post.

My reason for writing this story up has nothing to do with what I expect to happen tomorrow night. Honestly, I have no idea. Polls suck. There’s no reason to trust them. Most of them are politically motivated by leftist news outlets to suppress the vote and give Democrats victorious news cycles. However, when I see President Trump using his limited campaign time to stump in Kansas, that does worry me.

Overall, though, it does not surprise me that media outlets — especially outlets like the Times and Post that are so openly hostile to Trump supporters — are dealing with a high degree of uncooperation. The reason, I believe, is fairly obvious: These outlets hate us, so why should we do anything to contribute to their efforts? One way to “get back’ at these hateful outlets is to hang up on or outright ignore their pollsters.

The few times pollsters have reached me, they either got ignored or were told I was a black, female, college graduate with four kids.

The corporate media deserve nothing but our contempt, and it’s good to know that’s what they are getting. The more we can deceive them and eat up their resources, the better that is for America.

news.title: Most Americans Don't Trust Polls But Results Still Influence Whether They Vote, Survey Shows
news.text: Americans are approaching the midterm elections with deep skepticism about the surveys measuring the race, according to a new POLITICO poll.The findings show that only 25% believe political polls correctly estimate votes, wxposing a credibility problem for an industry whose numbers shape campaign strategy, fundraising and public expectations. Yet distrust does not necessarily mean indifference, as many respondents said an unfavorable poll would make them more determined to vote.Conducted by PF Global, the online survey of 2,083 U.S. adults ran October 24-27 and has an overall margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points. About one-quarter of respondents said polls suggesting a Democratic wave in November were wrong and expected Republicans to win key races.Meanwhile, 41% said surveys tend to underestimate either Democrats or Republicans, revealing doubts that cross party lines. Republicans who supported President Donald Trump in 2024 were particularly skeptical. Roughly two in five said political polls underestimate their party.That suspicion was stronger among Trump voters who identified as "MAGA Republicans." Three in five said polls indicating Democrats would win key races were incorrect, compared with about one-third of Trump voters outside that group.Republican leaders have reinforced those doubts as closely watched contests tighten. House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Fox News that polls were "grossly underestimating Republican enthusiasm around the country," according to POLITICO.Trump has labeled polls "fake" and "rigged," while Vice President JD Vance has argued that unfavorable surveys can discourage Republican voters. However, the skepticism also reaches Democrats. Just under one-third of respondents who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris said polls tend to underestimate Democratic support.Polling mistakes and fabricated surveys have added to the industry's credibility challenges. POLITICO cited incorrect expectations in Democratic primaries, including surveys that overstated Abdul El-Sayed's eventual winning margin in Michigan's Senate primary.Separately, Wedgewood Polls admitted using fake data in several Democratic primary surveys after scrutiny from FiftyPlusOne, according to the report. Another organization published bogus polling about the Los Angeles mayoral race to test how unverified numbers would spread.Another complication is that respondents can change their minds. One in five Americans surveyed said they had given a polling answer about their voting intentions that differed from how they ultimately voted.Polls measure sentiment during a particular period, but election forecasts use polling and sometimes other information to estimate outcomes. Public confidence in those forecasts was also limited. Only 18% said they trusted poll-based forecasts more than prediction markets, compared with 12% who favored the betting markets. One-third trusted neither.Nevertheless, polling can still motivate participation. Roughly 55% said they would "definitely" vote if surveys showed their preferred candidate far behind. Among Republican midterm voters who believed polls underestimate their party, roughly 75% gave that answer.
news.summary: About one-quarter of respondents said polls suggesting a Democratic wave in November were wrong and expected Republicans to win key races.
