news.title: Midterms poll tracker: 10 House races you need to know about as betting markets tip Dems to obliterate Trump's majority
news.text:
Democrats need a net gain of four seats to seize control of the U.S. House of Representatives in November's midterm elections.

Republicans will go into the 2026 midterms with 219 members caucusing with them in the chamber. That is a single seat more than the minimum required for a majority when all seats are filled. The House has 214 Democrats, along with two vacancies.

History suggests Democrats will pick up seats. Holding such a slim majority could be tough for Republicans in a midterm year, when voters tend to vote against the party in the White House. Republicans have also kick-started a national redistricting battle that could make Democrats' path to a majority slightly more difficult.

Nine states have undergone redistricting ahead of the 2026 general election. Voters in all 435 congressional districts choose their representatives in the U.S. House every two years. Each party's path to a House majority starts with the low-hanging fruit: seats that consistently favor one side so heavily that it isn't worth the opposition trying to compete.

Democrats' path to dismantling the GOP majority depends on flipping the districts where they believe Republicans are most vulnerable. Republicans' path depends on defending the seats they already represent and ousting Democrats running in Republican-leaning territory.

The backdrop to the vote is that President Donald Trump is deeply unpopular, and the combination of tariffs and the war in Iran has elevated cost-of-living concerns. Trump's policies have driven up diesel and fertilizer prices, as voters have said affordability is their top issue this cycle.

Here's how to look at the places that are most likely to determine who gets to 218.

A high-stakes brawl for a razor-thin Colorado congressional seat is getting bloody, with millions in outside cash pouring in and attacks flying over college-era vegan stunts and red-meat politics.

Democratic challenger Manny Rutinel has emerged as a fundraising juggernaut, out-raising freshman Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado’s battleground 8th Congressional District — a heavily Hispanic corridor Donald Trump carried by a razor-thin 1.8 percentage points in 2024. 

Evans is fighting back with scorched-earth attacks, painting Rutinel — a progressive former state lawmaker who took down a moderate in his party's primary — as a radical socialist who's out of touch with everyday voters. In a bid to frame the showdown as "common sense" versus "crazy," Evans recently took to social media to blast a vintage photo of Rutinel demonstrating against the meat industry during his college days. 

The attack has ignited a bizarre proxy war over livestock and ranching in a district known as Colorado's agricultural heartland, prompting Rutinel to hit back with local taco-truck stops to prove his carnivorous credentials. 

Sensing a prime opportunity to flip the seat, Democratic heavy hitters are going all in. Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and members of Colorado’s Democratic congressional delegation stormed the trail alongside Rutinel last week to drum up turnout.

The airwaves have become a nonstop slugfest: Outside groups tied to Democrats have dumped $14 million into the district, narrowly outgunning $13 million spent by Republican outfits looking to save Evans' seat on the eve of voting.

 A brazen Republican scheme to slice and dice Florida’s congressional map is crashing into a wall of Democratic resistance, turning what was supposed to be an easy four-seat GOP power grab into a $40 million slugfest.

Tallahassee Republicans went for the jugular when they carved up districts held by Democratic Reps. Darren Soto, Kathy Castor, Lois Frankel and Debbie Wasserman Schultz. The aggressive redraw paid off immediately in Soto’s territory, which Donald Trump carried by nearly 18 points — a margin that could prove lethal to the incumbent’s reelection hopes.

Yet GOP mapmakers may have bitten off more than they can chew. Democrats have refused to roll over in districts Trump won by 9 to 10 points, triggering a high-stakes dogfight in South Florida's newly configured battleground, where Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz is fighting tooth and nail to fend off former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer. 

Tensions exploded into the open last week during a candidate forum where Singer repeatedly slammed Moskowitz as a coward for refusing to face him in a televised debate.

Moskowitz isn’t backing down, leaning on a staggering $2.5 million personal fundraising advantage to blanket the airwaves and blunt the GOP's territorial push. Deep-pocketed outside groups on both sides of the aisle have matched each other dollar for dollar, dumping an eye-watering $20 million each into the district — transforming a supposed Republican victory lap into an all-out trench war on the eve of the midterms.

Skyrocketing fuel and fertilizer prices have turned a familiar Iowa grudge match into a perilous high-stakes brawl for Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks on the eve of midterm voting.

Democratic challenger Christina Bohannan, a former state lawmaker who came up short against Miller-Meeks in 2022 and 2024, is betting the third time will be the charm as economic misery ravages the state’s agricultural heartland. 

The battlefield shifted dramatically after President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and military strikes on Iran triggered an inflation crisis at the pump and in the field. With national diesel prices spiking to about $6.33 a gallon and regular unleaded hitting $4.23, according to AAA, everyday affordability has replaced partisan loyalty as voters’ top midterm anxiety.

Miller-Meeks scrambled to shore up her rural firewall last week, parading officials from the U.S. Department of Agriculture across a district where farms make up nearly a third of the constituency.

The political optics handed Bohannan an immediate opening: The challenger seized on the federal visits to frame the race as “Iowa vs. Washington,” hammering the incumbent as a creature of the beltway while farmers struggle to stay in the black.

Democrats sense blood in the water. Leaning into a massive air-game edge, Democratic groups have dumped $11 million into the rural battleground to drown out $7 million from Republicans — pushing Miller-Meeks to the brink in one of the Midwest's most volatile House showdowns.

A fight for Maine’s sprawling 2nd Congressional District has turned into a bare-knuckle clash between political royalty and a scrappy state auditor, with $20 million in outside cash flooding the airwaves on the eve of the midterms.

The exit of centrist Democratic Rep. Jared Golden blew the doors wide open for the GOP in a rural district Donald Trump carried by 9 points in 2024. Now, combative former two-term Gov. Paul LePage is mounting a fiery comeback bid against progressive Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap to flip the seat red.

The race has quickly descended into a nasty war over attendance sheets and pocketbooks. Dunlap has relentlessly pounded LePage as a ghost candidate, warning voters the former governor won't show up for them in Washington after blowing off local forums. Dunlap boasts he has held town halls across every county in the district, while claiming LePage hasn't held a single one.

LePage has brushed off the carpet-bombing and gone straight for the jugular on the cost of living. At a testy debate, the conservative populist laid down a blunt ultimatum: a vote for Dunlap means paying more for everything, while backing him means paying less.

Outside spending groups are treating the open battleground like ground zero, dumping roughly $10 million on each side to blanket the state with attack ads. While nonpartisan forecasters still rate the race as "lean Republican," both parties are bracing for a wire-to-wire finish as Maine's notoriously independent voters head to the polls.

A parachute-landing wildfire fighter is giving national Republicans serious heartburn in western Montana, threatening what looked like an open-and-shut hold in the heart of conservative country.

With former Rep. Ryan Zinke stepping aside in a territory Donald Trump locked down by nearly a dozen points two years ago, the GOP tapped combat veteran Aaron Flint to defend the perimeter. But Democrat Sam Forstag, a union organizer who literally leaps out of airplanes into forest infernos as an elite smokejumper, is setting the campaign trail ablaze.

Sensing an upset in the making, the White House rolled out the heavy artillery. Vice President JD Vance barnstormed the state last week alongside Flint and Senate hopeful Kurt Alme, while Trump flooded social feeds with an emphatic two-minute video endorsement.

Forstag countered by going right after the tech industry, branding his opponent "AI Aaron" in biting spots that claim Flint is in the pocket of Silicon Valley data centers.

The strategy—and the candidate's action-hero resume—is moving the needle. Forstag has built a commanding $1.5 million campaign cash edge, forcing GOP operatives to scramble $11 million into local airtime to head off $7 million from Democratic groups.

With two late-October surveys showing the airborne firefighter holding a razor-thin advantage, Big Sky country is suddenly bracing for a shocker.

Republican mapmakers drew the lines to kill off Rep. Don Davis’ political career, but an unforced betting blunder and an eye-popping $39 million campaign blitz have turned eastern North Carolina into an uphill defensive trench.

GOP state legislators redrew Davis’ 1st Congressional District from a territory Donald Trump edged by just 3 points into a double-digit Republican fortress. Rather than packing his bags, the freshman Democrat dug his heels in.

Enter retired Army Col. Laurie Buckhout, a former Trump administration Pentagon official who should have sailed through the newly crimson district. Instead, she handed Democrats free ammunition after getting suspended and slapped with a fine by prediction-market platform Kalshi for wagering about $1,000 on her own victory — an episode she publicly chalked up to "a dumb mistake".

Buckhout has scrambled to shift the spotlight, sounding alarms that "radical leftists like Elizabeth Warren" are pulling strings to keep Davis in the Capitol.

Davis, meanwhile, is avoiding the ideological mud entirely. Taking to social media after chatting up early voters, the incumbent focused squarely on kitchen-table pain points: soaring household bills and the quiet crisis of rural healthcare centers shuttering.

National Democrats, refusing to surrender the seat without a vicious brawl, have poured in $22 million to fortify Davis against a $17 million Republican counter-offensive.

GOP leaders are circling the wagons in suburban New York, desperate to protect Rep. Mike Lawler in the most perilous defensive assignment on the entire congressional map.

Lawler sits in exceedingly hostile territory as one of only three House Republicans stranded in districts Kamala Harris carried two years ago. With Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick favored to survive in Pennsylvania and a similar Nebraska seat open, the Hudson Valley incumbent is widely tagged as the most vulnerable Republican on the ballot.

Democratic challenger Cait Conley, a former combat veteran and national security specialist, has gone straight for the jugular, framing Lawler as a lockstep foot soldier for Donald Trump, tech titan Elon Musk, and controversial corporate data centers.

GOP brass isn't taking any chances. House Speaker Mike Johnson jetted in to flank Lawler at a fiery press event, turning the spotlight onto Conley’s Virginia property records and accusing her of carpetbagging in a district where she pays no local real estate taxes.

The party establishment is putting massive financial muscle behind the rescue mission, unleashing $13 million in outside firepower to shield Lawler, while Democrats have funneled $7 million into flipping the prized suburban corridor.

A bitter family meltdown and explosive domestic abuse allegations have blown a deep-red Ohio congressional district wide open, dragging freshman Republican Rep. Max Miller into a brutal fight for his political life. 

Miller coasted to a 15-point victory two years ago in a sprawling district that outpaced Donald Trump’s own margin. But the incumbent’s reelection bid cratered into personal chaos after his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and a former girlfriend went public with allegations of domestic violence and child abuse. 

The fallout triggered an astonishing intraparty revolt: Moreno’s father, Republican U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno, publicly denounced his former son-in-law, demanding Miller resign from office immediately and scrap his campaign.

Miller has pushed back fiercely, insisting in an ad campaign that every claim levied against him has been completely debunked. Taking to social media to share the spot, Miller struck a defiant personal note, saying "father" is his favorite title and "congressman" is a distant second. 

That defense has drawn scathing pushback from his Democratic challenger, union ironworker and Brook Park City Councilman Brian Poindexter. Brandishing Miller as fundamentally unfit to serve, Poindexter has framed the incumbent as an entitled heir surviving solely on deep pockets, quipping that Miller has blown through more campaign cash than a tradesman could earn in a lifetime. 

Poindexter’s blue-collar pitch is packing an unexpected financial wallop. The challenger has amassed a roughly $400,000 direct fundraising lead over Miller, while national Democratic outfits have overwhelmed the local airwaves, unloading $12 million against $6 million in GOP defense cash to push an erstwhile lock firmly into toss-up territory.

A high-risk Republican redistricting blitz designed to carve out five new congressional seats in Texas is unraveling along the southern border, where an audacious play to wipe out Democrats has detonated into an expensive multiseat headache.

Rather than coasting to easy pickups, the GOP is suddenly scrambling to defend three separate battlegrounds across South Texas. Longtime Democratic Reps. Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar have stubbornly held their ground in seats Donald Trump carried by double digits, while an open clash between Republican Carlos De La Cruz and Democrat Johnny Garcia in the redrawn 35th District has unexpectedly tightened.

The fiercest drama, however, centers on Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, who faces genuine jeopardy against Tejano music icon Bobby Pulido in a Rio Grande Valley territory Trump dominated by 18 points. 

Despite holding the incumbency, De La Cruz has leaned into an underdog posture, blasting Pulido as "a rich celebrity from a corrupt political dynasty" and attempting to tar him over past ties to a former bandmate who was later convicted of a sex offense. Pulido immediately separated himself from the ex-accordionist, stating he was unaware of the man's criminal history.

The contest took an unusual cultural twist after De La Cruz sneered that voters were picking a lawmaker, not someone to "perform at your niece's quinceañera". Pulido pounced on the snub, turning it into a cornerstone of his retail strategy by regularly serenading families at birthday celebrations along the trail. He followed up with an endorsement blitz highlighted by former President Bill Clinton. 

The numbers reflect a full-blown crisis for House Republicans: Democratic groups have poured $12 million into knocking off the incumbent, narrowly eclipsing $11 million in GOP defense cash, as late polling shows the Latin Grammy winner sitting on an improbable 7-point lead.

Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez made a name for herself in Washington by infuriating leaders of her own party, and now that renegade streak faces its ultimate endurance test in a $22 million Pacific Northwest collision.

The blue-collar auto repair shop owner has spent her tenure systematically bucking Democratic orthodoxy: authoring a resolution reprimanding one of her own colleagues and frequently crossing the aisle on signature procedural roll calls to push conservative measures forward.

That hard-nosed, independent posture was carefully calculated to appeal to southwest Washington’s 3rd Congressional District, a timber-rich, working-class landscape Donald Trump carried by a slim margin two years ago.

The strategy hit a turbulent patch during the state's open August primary, where Gluesenkamp Perez placed second behind state Senate Republican Leader John Braun.

Braun, a wealthy manufacturing executive, has gone on the offensive, ridiculing the incumbent as an ineffective showboat who talks tough on cable news but has failed to deliver tangible wins for local timber and maritime communities.

Gluesenkamp Perez has struck back by attacking Braun’s fortune, casting the challenger as an out-of-touch multimillionaire bankrolled by special-interest super PACs trying to purchase a congressional seat.

National Republicans are treating the seat as a prime flip prize, pouring $14 million into outside airtime to overpower the $8 million Democratic groups have marshaled.
news.summary: History suggests Democrats will pick up seats. Holding such a slim majority could be tough for Republicans in a midterm year, when voters tend to vote against the party in the White House

news.title: 13 Dirty Tricks and Messes That Shook Election Eve
news.text:
With Michigan Democrats dealing with a stunning political fallout and Alaska’s Senate race caught up in a bizarre name-related controversy, the final stretch before the Nov. 3 midterms is delivering plenty of drama. But American politics has a long history of last-minute scandals, racial manipulation, secret deals and campaign tactics that leave consequences far beyond Election Day. And Black Americans have often paid a particularly high price. Don’t believe us? Just keep scrolling.

Joe Biden Drops Out 

Bet you remember exactly where you were when this news dropped. Former President Joe Biden abandoned his reelection campaign in July 2024 after a concerning debate performance, mounting questions about his age and growing pressure from Democrats. The decision came just months before Election Day, throwing the Democratic Party into an unprecedented scramble. Former Vice President Kamala Harris inherited the campaign, the fundraising machine and the enormous burden of keeping Donald Trump out of the White House in a historic 100-day campaign race.

Yemi Mobolade and the Fake KKK Threat

In the weeks before Colorado Springs’ 2023 mayoral runoff, a burning cross was staged in front of candidate Yemi Mobolade’s campaign sign, which was also defaced with a racial slur, according to KKTV. The shocking incident appeared to suggest a racist attack against the Black candidate. But prosecutors later revealed it was an elaborate hoax designed to influence the election. Two people were convicted in 2025. 

RELATED: These Black Celebs Push Voter Engagement Ahead of the Midterms

Herschel Walker’s Abortion Controversy

In 2022, former NFL star and Republican Senate candidate Herschel Walker found himself defending against allegations that he paid for a former girlfriend’s abortion in 2009. The controversy was extra explosive considering that Walker had campaigned as an outspoken opponent of abortion rights. As we previously told you, he denied the allegations. Still, the accusations put his political credibility and personal history under an unforgiving spotlight as he challenged Georgia’s Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock.

Michigan’s Last-Minute Democratic Party Fallout

Michigan Democrats entered the final stretch of the 2026 midterms with a political headache nobody needed. After losing the Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, Rep. Haley Stevens stunned the party by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers just two days before Election Day. The fallout included furious Democrats, a departing chief of staff and a party scrambling to contain the damage in a crucial Senate race.

On the other hand, El-Sayed told reporters that he won’t let Stevens’ defection slow down his race. He added, “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.”

Presidential Campaigning During COVID

The 2020 presidential race between Biden and Trump unfolded during a deadly pandemic, forcing candidates to confront an uncomfortable question: How do you campaign when gathering crowds could put people’s lives at risk? Trump continued holding large rallies while Biden leaned heavily into virtual events and socially distanced campaigning. The fight over public health, personal responsibility and presidential leadership became another defining battleground.

Jesse Helms, Harvey Gantt and 2 Elections

North Carolina Republican Jesse Helms made racial politics central to his Senate campaigns against Black Democratic challenger Harvey Gantt in 1990 and 1996. Gantt was leading the polls until Helms’ notorious 1990 campaign ad featured a white man’s hands crumpling a job rejection letter while warning about racial preferences. In both races, Helms walked away victorious.

The message tapped into white resentment and demonstrated how racial anxiety could become a powerful weapon at the ballot box. Ultimately, 

The Willie Horton Political Ad of 1988

George H.W. Bush’s allies found a powerful political weapon in Willie Horton, a Black man who committed violent crimes after escaping a prison furlough. Their infamous 1988 ad used his mugshot to portray Democratic opponent Michael Dukakis as soft on crime. Black activists and other critics sounded the alarm against what they described as a racist advertisement. 

In the end, the commercial helped weaponize racial stereotypes about Black men and crime, leaving a lasting blueprint for fear-based political campaigning.

Alaska’s Dan Sullivans Situation

Alaska’s 2026 Senate race has delivered one of the strangest political controversies in recent memory: two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the same ballot. 

Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Mary Peltola, while a second Republican, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., faces accusations of being a spoiler candidate. According to the Associated Press, Peltola denies involvement, but the Justice Department’s intervention has intensified the election dispute.

Donald Trump’s Access Hollywood Tape

Just one month before the 2016 presidential election, a leaked 2005 recording caught Donald Trump bragging about sexually assaulting women and making vulgar comments about his celebrity status. The fallout was immediate, with Republicans distancing themselves and Democrats demanding accountability. Yet Trump survived the controversy and won the presidency, raising uncomfortable questions about what American voters are willing to overlook.

P.B.S. Pinchback Never Allowed His Seat

Before P.B.S. Pinchback’s 1873 election to the Senate, Louisiana was engulfed in allegations of voter fraud, intimidation of Black voters and competing claims to the governor’s office. Pinchback, a Black Republican and the nation’s first Black governor, was elected to the Senate amid the chaos. According to the Zinn Education Project, his credentials became entangled in the political battle, however, and the Senate ultimately refused to seat him in 1876.

Philadelphia Mayor John Street Discovers Listening Device

In October 2003, Philadelphia Mayor John Street was preparing for reelection when a routine security sweep uncovered a hidden listening device in his City Hall office, CNN reported. The FBI acknowledged the device was connected to a federal corruption investigation, not election spying. Still, its discovery created a political firestorm, particularly in a racially divided city where Street was fighting to retain the mayor’s office.

The Iranian Hostage Crisis and the Alleged Secret Deal

In 1980, President Jimmy Carter was struggling to secure the release of Americans held hostage in Iran while also running for reelection. They were finally released on January 20, 1981, moments after Ronald Reagan’s inauguration. Allegations later emerged that Reagan campaign associates secretly negotiated with Iranian officials to delay their release until after Election Day, even though Carter. The so-called October Surprise remains a controversial chapter in presidential history.

Gary Hart and the Monkey Business Yacht

In 1987, Democratic presidential frontrunner Gary Hart challenged reporters to follow him around if they doubted his character. They did. Soon, reports surfaced about his relationship with Donna Rice, including photographs of her aboard his yacht, Monkey Business. The scandal destroyed his presidential ambitions and became a defining moment in America’s obsession with candidates’ private lives.

news.title: CBS SLAMS Stevens’s ‘Shocking’ ‘Betrayal,’ Rips ‘Islamophobic’ Trump, Touts ‘Moderate’ Talarico
news.text:
Anytime CBS Mornings or NBC’s Today is more liberal and elitist than ABC’s Good Morning America, it’s big news as Monday’s CBS Mornings went all-out to defend Michigan Democrat senatorial candidate Abdul el-Sayed, fretting he’s endured “Islamophobic” rhetoric and must now overcome Democrat Congresswoman Haley Stevens’s “shocking about-face” and “betrayal” of the Democratic Party by backing Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

CBS also heralded el-Sayed’s massive fundraising haul on Sunday, suggested the Stevens endorsement could be much ado about nothing, and even trumpeted Texas Senate Democrat candidate James Talarico as a “moderate” and “seminarian.”

Co-host and former Democrat donor Gayle King kicked off the midterm coverage by wondering if Stevens’s “last-minute endorsement” that “surprised” and “shocked the political world” that “spark[ed] a firestorm within her party” could actually matter.

Chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes said Stevens’s “shocking announcement” came after a “rift between Stevens and El-Sayed appeared to grow last week over an online political ad from an outside group, which appeared to link U.S. military support for Israel to rising grocery prices in the U.S.”

Cordes left out the part where the ad came from prominent far-left commentator Cenk Uygur, whose nephew is former el-Sayed surrogate Hasan Piker.

“On Friday, Stevens urged El-Sayed to condemn the ad. Saturday, he told reporters he has already made clear that the ad was not made by me and I don’t agree with the contents. He also asked Stevens not to attend his campaign event Sunday or future campaign events,” Cordes added.

Cordes made her feelings clear when she attacked Stevens for having “struggled to explain her change of mind” in a Sunday night CNN interview. Notice in the video above how Cordes used a series of screen wipes to make Stevens seem incoherent.

Before resurfacing back live, Cordes boiled down the months-long feud with el-Sayed to the congresswoman “publicly disagree[ing] with his stance on Israel’s actions in Gaza” that he’s “called...a genocide.”

Back live, co-host Norah O’Donnell put her own feelings on the table: “Wow, this is a shocking about-face, betrayal of the Democratic Party and all of the members of Congress she told the night before she wasn’t going to endorse the Republican. Nancy, what happened, and is this about their disagreement over Israel?”

Cordes made it seem like a sophomoric beef, arguing “it may just be” as “simple” as Stevens feeling hurt that el-Sayed’s “campaign saying she was not wanted at an event on Sunday” because “she spent several days publicly criticizing him.”

Back in October 2024, Cordes and O’Donnell fawned over “lifetime Republican” Liz Cheney’s Kamala Harris endorsement as “a big moment.”

Cordes also said in 2024 that the “conservative” Cheney gave the Harris campaign “a major moment” to help “win over even a sliver of Republican voters.”

Returning to 2026, King gave credence to el-Sayed’s claim “say[ing] none of this matters,” since “[c]lose to two million people in Michigan have already voted.”

White House and campaign correspondent Ed O’Keefe did concede that “there are potentially thousands, tens of thousands of Haley Stevens voters out there” who feel the same way, given she did better than el-Sayed among Jewish and black Democrats in the primary.

But O’Keefe then dispatched with those concerns by promoting el-Sayed’s Sunday fundraising haul:

What is telling, though, is the guy managed to raise $1.2 million yesterday afternoon. For anyone, that’s a good afternoon, but it is a signal at least the Democratic Party writ large across the country is ticked off at Haley Stevens for what she did, and that might inspire enough Michigan Democrats to show up and say, ‘no, no, we don’t do that in the closing days when we are facing the administration we are facing.’

After co-host Nate Burleson touted the self-centered behavior of now-former Stevens staffers who quit in protest (even though no one elected them to office, or should care what they think), Cordes boasted Stevens was “almost being excommunicated from the party,” proof of “a real backlash.”

This went into the part when Cordes rallied to el-Sayed’s defense with the cries of Islamophobia and “hateful comments on both sides” (click “expand”):

O’DONNELL: Haley — Haley Stevens, once again, last night accused El-Sayed of making comments and having actions that were certainly anti-Semitic, in — in her words. Does it represent a larger rift within the Democratic Party?CORDES: There’s no question that this is an argument that has been playing out in public among Democrats for some time, specifically over Israel. He has argued he has no quarrel with Jews or Jewish voters; his quarrel is with Israel’s actions. On the other side, you’ve got Mike Rogers, who has been campaigning with President Trump, who has said a number of Islamophobic things about El-Sayed, claiming he is a jihadist, saying you need a metal detector if he makes it into the Senate, so that he can be escorted safely onto the Senate floor. So, there are a lot of hateful comments on both sides.O’DONNELL: On both sides!

The second half-hour yielded even more absurdity as, during a man-on-the-street report from Tarrant County, Texas, Saturday co-host Adriana Diaz promoted Talarico as “a seminarian and former teacher elected to the state house at 29” and “identifies as a moderate fighting corruption.”

In contrast, Diaz tagged Talarico opponent and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton as having “survived an impeachment trial three years ago over bribery and other charges.”

Diaz also boosted Talarico by saying “many” Latinos “are dismayed by the economy and the President’s immigration enforcement,” and could be prevented from voting because the county “eliminated 92 polling places in September as a cost-saving measure, but critics say they were mainly in Black and Latino neighborhoods.”

In the second hour, O’Donnell set the table by dismissing Stevens as the “primary loser” ahead of bringing in CBS News contributors Joel Payne from Obamaworld and former Rubio presidential campaign manager Terry Sullivan.

Payne argued the Stevens endorsement won’t end up mattering, while Sullivan said it helps the GOP turn away from negative economic news (click “expand”):

PAYNE: The way that this has happened, I actually think mitigates the risk for Abdul El-Sayed, because it was so, frankly, odd and so strange and so unexpected. Haley Stevens had previously endorsed Abdul El-Sayed. In fact, she made a pretty strong case against Mike Rogers previously, and something happened in the last week or two that has intervened. I don’t want to speculate, and I think it would be unfair to speculate about her agency in the decision, but regardless, what this is experienced as, as voters feeling, I think, a bit misled by her, and I actually think it could — it could help Abdul el-Sayed. I mean, if you look at national Democrat, they’re uniting behind Abdul El-Sayed, other Michigan Democrats uniting behind him, so it could have a boomerang effect that is beyond what Haley Stevens actually anticipated.O’DONNELL: Terry, this is a bonus to Mike Rogers.SULLIVAN: I’d say Joel and I are not unified on this. This is not going to help El-Sayed. The reality is this not only hurts him, but this helps Republicans nationwide because we are talking about this right now. You know, this has not been a great information flow for Republicans this election cycle, especially recently, and suddenly this helps a bunch. I kind of feel like Jim Carrey in Dumb and Dumber here. You know, “you’re saying there’s a chance?”BURLESON: So, you are saying we are talking about this as in it’s a distraction for Republicans?SULLIVAN: Well, I wouldn’t say it is a distraction. Instead, it changes — instead of talking about higher gas prices, we are talking about this race, and that’s better[.]

King also defended el-Sayed by noting the million-dollar-plus day for el-Sayed, but Sullivan quickly dismissed it by saying the Democrat has “never had a problem raising a bunch of money from activists who are extreme online,” when the real story should be “fighting for...voters in Oakland County, in Macomb County that are swing voters.”

O’Donnell closed with more bias, hitting Trump for “record-low approval ratings” and spending Saturday “holding a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago with his quote-unquote rich friends when the main issue is affordability.”

news.title: In DC on election night? Here’s where to watch results roll in
news.text:
Some races may be too close to call, but one thing will be certain Tuesday no matter what — bar specials.

Residents of D.C. observe election night like some other cities observe major sporting events. And after the Nationals failed to advance to the postseason this year and with the first playoff game for the Washington Spirit still a few days away, the midterms will be the main ticket in town. 

“It’s usually standing room only every time. I don’t think it matters whether it’s presidential or midterms,” said Matt Weiss, who owns Capitol Hill’s Union Pub.

The Halloween vibes aren’t over yet at Union Pub, thanks to a special “Midterm Massacre” menu. Inspired by competitive Senate races, it features $9 cocktails and shooters like the Haunted Horsefeather (Kansas), Maineiac Martini (Maine) and the Devil’s Duck Fart (Alaska).

While the pub will also be showing the Washington Capitals play the Dallas Stars at 7 p.m., Weiss said the sound will be on for election results rather than hockey. He expects around 50 percent more business than a regular Tuesday, which is already a busy night with weekly trivia. 

Weiss said he can’t remember a time when his bar, which originally opened as Red River Grill in 1995, wasn’t showing election returns coming in. 

“It’s just like being open for the Super Bowl or being open for the Washington Spirit being in the finals; we do benefit from having these types of events,” said Jesse Rauch, a partner at metrobar.

Rauch’s bar in Northeast D.C., known for its decommissioned railcar, isn’t usually open on Tuesdays, but election night is different. 

With some races taking longer to call than others, Rauch said he’ll stay open as long as he can. 

“We’re gonna play it by ear,” he said. “I do need to send my team home at some point to make sure that they’re well rested and all that. But we’ll stay open for as long as the energy is good.” 

Given the District’s political leanings, most of the election night fans will be cheering on Democrats up and down the ballot. Kamala Harris carried more than 90 percent of the vote in D.C. in 2024, while President Donald Trump had 6 percent. 

Rauch did point to one thing that might affect his sales, but he said he doesn’t mind. 

“A lot of people in D.C. are in Maryland and in Virginia and in Pennsylvania door knocking, and they’ll be door knocking until the very end. Because of that, some people just aren’t in town, which I’m really proud of my neighbors who are able to do that,” he said. 

If you’re looking for a place to be on election night, here are a few airing the results: 

Teddy and the Bully Bar 1200 19th St. NW“We’ve got $8 oyster shooters, $8 NYC Mules, $4 New York style hot dogs, a $9.99 Angus beef smashburger, $5 soft pretzels with house-made beer cheese, $8 funnel cake with raspberry coulis and powdered sugar, and much, much more.”

Union Pub201 Massachusetts Ave. NE“Midterm Massacre Menu featuring $9 cocktails and shooters inspired by some of the country’s most competitive Senate races.”

Shaw’s Tavern520 Florida Ave. NW“Grab your crew, order a round of margaritas, and settle in as the results roll in … Taco and margarita specials all night.”

Barrel613 Pennsylvania Ave. SE“We’ll have the midterm election results on C-SPAN all night long, and we’re letting the cocktails have their own race: Blue Passion Fruit Margarita, Red Strawberry Daiquiri. Every drink counts as a vote.”

metrobar640 Rhode Island Ave. NE“Slices & Sips Happy Hour till 7pm … $10 pies from El Jefe and our rotating happy hour menu of craft cocktails, local beer, and wine.”

Boundary Stone116 Rhode Island Ave. NW“All parties, independents, political junkies, and the politically exhausted are welcome … All night happy hour. Burgers, wings, fish & chips & pub favorites.”

Red Derby3718 14th St. NW“Live Streaming RESULTS Watch Party: 1/2 price BURGERS, $4 Natty Boh’s, Blue Wave Shooters.”

Roofers Union2446 18th St. NW“Red or Blue? We’re voting for tacos! … Live election coverage, Taco Tuesday specials & margaritas.”

Highlands Tavern3421 Connecticut Ave. NW“To keep the energy going through the early morning hours, we are pouring $5 pints of local Senate Beer all night long.” 

Pitchers 2317 18th St. NW“Join us at Pitchers for an election watch party and bingo as we watch the results unfold together.”

Busboys and PoetsAll locations“Enjoy live election coverage on TVs throughout the restaurant, games and activities, great food, community conversation, and all-night happy hour beginning at 3 p.m.”

news.text:
In today’s GOP, it would be next to impossible to find a Republican ready to stand behind the statement “Islam is peace,” words uttered by none other than Republican former President George W. Bush just weeks after 9/11. That’s because in the subsequent 25 years, the Republican Party has decided that scapegoating the Muslim community for the country’s problems is a way to galvanize white Christian voters to elect Republicans.

Nowhere is that strategy more evident than in the state of Texas. Politicians there this election cycle have been even more vicious than usual in proudly peddling Islamophobia. What these actions reveal is a deepening desperation within the Texas GOP as they face down once-in-a-lifetime political headwinds that suggest Democrats are on the verge of flipping Texas. But it’s no longer 2001, and American Muslims have been asserting more and more political clout. There’s actually a decent chance that Texas Republicans’ extreme Islamophobia backfires by alienating the one group that was shaping into a growing GOP demographic: Muslims.

“It’s especially bizarre for the Republican Party to do it because it’s supposed to stand for conservative values, religious freedom, all of that. That’s not what they’re doing,” Mohamed Hussein, a self-described conservative Texan and a practicing Muslim, recently told me. While attending a GOP convention in Houston over the summer, he says he was told to convert to Christianity or leave the country.

“It was shocking, because I wasn’t at a religious convention, to be told to convert. It kind of came out of left field,” Hussein said. He attended a Judeo-Christian seminar where attendees were told that non-Christian immigrants will create problems for America and that Muslims were lying to win political power. This was a version of the Republican Party that Hussein did not recognize; “I don’t think that had this convention occurred a year ago, it would have been this nasty toward Islam and Muslims.”

Clearly, a lot has changed since 2025. Americans went from having a Democratic president to a Republican one, suddenly finding themselves at war with Iran, facing record high gas and diesel prices, skyrocketing healthcare costs, and immigration agents knocking down their doors. It has made the 2026 midterms an especially consequential election cycle, and in Texas, Republicans have decided Muslims could be their ticket out of the backlash to the mess created by President Donald Trump. As I am an American Muslim myself, and have plenty of family and friends in Texas, it is a phenomenon I was curious to explore. So I took a trip to Houston, home to one of the country’s largest Muslim populations, to see what it’s like for Muslim Texans, especially those who may have voted GOP in years past but were now looking at a party they didn’t recognize.

Though Muslims only make up about 1 percent of Texas’ total population—roughly 300,000 people—the state is home to the fourth-largest population of Muslims within the U.S. and the largest in the South. And Islam has long been considered one of the fastest-growing religions in the country, with Pew Research estimating that by 2040, Muslims will replace Jews as the nation’s second-largest religious group after Christians. By 2050, Muslims are projected to account for 2 percent of the total U.S. population, compared to the 1 percent they currently represent.

Muslims’ growth is especially pronounced in Texas, where the Muslim voter population grew 35 percent from 2016 to 2020, which translated to an additional 80,000 registered voters, according to the Muslim civics group Emgage. Yet, state Republicans, this cycle at least, seem not to want anything to do with these voters. Since at least last year, they have been aggressively inciting anti-Muslim rhetoric and policies, starting at the top with Gov. Greg Abbott, who is currently locked in a surprisingly tight race for reelection. He went to war with EPIC City, an Islamic development project that sought to build a K–12 school, mosque, retail space, and housing units, and it took over local headlines. Abbott went so far as to sign a law banning EPIC City from moving forward, characterizing the developers as “bad actors” who would subject occupants to “Sharia law,” whatever his definition of that might be. His fellow Republicans were taking notes.

Soon enough, Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for a Texas Senate seat who’s also locked in a tight race against Democrat James Talarico that could determine control of the U.S. Senate, followed up with a lawsuit against EPIC City, while Texas Rep. Keith Self also called on the Justice Department and IRS to investigate the developers. Then Abbott struck again, this time sabotaging plans for a celebration of Eid, one of the holiest Islamic holidays celebrating the end of 30 days of fasting, that was supposed to take place at a local water park—a venue that the community had used for the past two years with no issue. Suddenly, Abbott was threatening to pull over half a million dollars in state funds from the city of Grand Prairie if they allowed the Eid swim party to proceed. It worked, and the city canceled the Eid celebration.

Soon the slogan “Don’t Sharia My Texas” was taking over the state, inspired by an anti-Muslim propaganda film that features conspiracy theorist Alex Jones and right-wing former national security adviser Michael Flynn. Sharia is a set of religious and worldly values for Muslims to follow and is entirely separate from Islamic law, though Republicans have rarely—if ever— attempted to explain what it is they are fearmongering against. “Like racism, Islamophobia can be adapted to align with the political and economic interests of those in power,” Khaled Beydoun, a professor of law at Arizona State University who studies Islamophobia, told the Dallas Morning News.

Islamophobia may have hit its peak in America immediately following 9/11. President Bush declared a “war on terror,” and, again, failed to clearly define terrorism, which made the concept borderless and timeless, as explained by the Bridge Initiative at Georgetown University. This oversimplification created two sides: terrorists versus everyone else, with Muslim Americans becoming targets of both the state and the general population. This period gave way to controversial policies like the National Security Entry-Exit Registration System, the Terrorism Screening Database, and even the establishment of Guantanamo Bay. It would take decades for the public to learn that Bush’s wars were utter failures, and slowly but surely it became normalized to publicly criticize American foreign policy. Eventually, Muslim Americans were empowered to be a part of America’s shifting governance, while also changing the narrative around Islam.

Voters began electing Muslim candidates to Washington, and today, Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani are some of the most recognizable political figures in the country, and are also practicing Muslims. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed is hoping to make history as the first Muslim American to serve in the U.S. Senate (while also facing perhaps the most bigoted campaign in recent memory). Notably, each of these figures are Democrats, as their party has largely embraced a diverse coalition of voters. Meanwhile, Republicans have decidedly gone the opposite direction, reinvigorating an especially pernicious element of the culture wars of the early aughts. In fact, it was Texas Rep. Chip Roy who cofounded Congress’ “Sharia-Free America Caucus.” He’s also running in a competitive race for Texas AG, and in the process “has posted from both his campaign and official accounts about Muslims, Islam, or ‘sharia law’ more than 244 times since January—the most of any member of Congress,” according to a Washington Post analysis.

In the run-up to Texas’ March primary, blatantly anti-Muslim ads were running rampant across the state on behalf of Republican campaigns that baselessly tied Islam with terrorism and crime. All of it was considered “solid gold” by one Republican strategist, who told CNN: “It is playing as well as anything I have ever seen with Texas Republican voters.”

Why would overt bigotry that pits fellow Texans against each other be resonating with voters? Perhaps because Republicans themselves have spent decades perpetuating the very Islamophobia the rest of America has been trying to heal. Equality Labs, a South Asian–focused civil rights group, found that Texas led the country in promoting Islamophobia-related disinformation in 2025, largely driven by online posts suggesting Muslims were invading the U.S. and attempting to impose Sharia law. Consider Bo French, a longtime far-right activist who’s currently running for Texas Railroad Commissioner. In September, he characterized a photo of a group of South Asian University of Texas students celebrating the school’s football team’s win: “Like body-cams exposed criminals, social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners. It’s everywhere and far worse than any of us could imagine.”

French’s comment quickly went viral and ignited a national conversation about blatant bigotry against minorities. Equality Labs also found that nationwide, Republicans are largely responsible for spreading Islamophobic content, as opposed to Democrats and independents. This phenomenon is particularly insidious in states like Texas where Republicans hold a supermajority, because “the primary electorate becomes the decisive contest, and candidates have to appeal only to a very small sliver of their own electorate,” Brandon Rottinghaus, a political scientist at the University of Houston, told the New York Times.

All of this is having a discernible impact nationwide, as Pew Research found U.S. adults’ attitudes toward Islam have worsened since 9/11. In 2002, six months after the al-Qaida attacks, 25 percent of U.S. adults said Islam is more likely than other religions to encourage violence, but when asked the same question in 2026, that figure had more than doubled to 51 percent. Republicans and independents who lean toward the GOP were far more likely than Democrats and Democratic leaners to say Islam encourages violence—76 percent versus 29 percent.

Particularly In Texas, this puts hundreds of thousands of Muslims in an untenable position. People like Hussein are actively being disenfranchised by a political party whose conservative values they typically align with. Khalid Hamideh, spokesman for the Islamic Association of North Texas, told me: “We’re more aligned with the values of the Republican Party when it comes to abortion, same-sex marriage—on all of the social issues, we’re very conservative. We’re very aligned with the people that hate us most.” As they’re left with no other option, Hamideh believes the recent GOP attacks on Texas Muslims have pushed many toward the Democratic Party unwillingly.

Jida Nabulsi also holds conservative values, but doesn’t identify herself as either a Democrat or a Republican. “You could say that I would have aligned more with the Republican Party. But given the current state of things, there’s just no sympathy from the Muslim community,” she told me. Nabulsi is the Texas state director for Emgage, a group that has been supporting Talarico’s candidacy. She believes there are plenty of Muslim conservatives in Texas who share her perspective. “The conversations I’m having with my community and other community members, they are telling me that even though they identify with Republicans, nobody should be voting Republican. Nobody should be aligning with that.”

Because they are obsessed with perpetuating anti-Muslim hate, Nabulsi believes Texas state lawmakers are forgoing talking about the actual issues voters care about. “Their top priority as a group is not affordability, bringing down prices or making life easier for us, but to target one community,” she said. ”It does not make sense.” Democrats aren’t necessarily viewed more positively than Republicans right now, but Nabulsi believes they’re at least signaling an open line of communication with a message she interprets as “We are not here with hate.”

Just a few weeks ago, Talarico’s campaign met with local Muslim officials and community members in Dallas, where he emphasized a bill he filed that would include Muslim imams as legally recognized marriage officiants. One October poll found Talarico leading Paxton by nearly 17 points among Asian American and Pacific Islander voters, though it’s challenging to carve out Muslim voters here as they can fall under the listed “Asian,” “South Asian,” “Middle Eastern,” and “African” ethnic groups, all of which also include other religions. Nonetheless, getting Texas Muslims on board could be the windfall Talarico needs to get him over the line against Paxton.

Given the serious risk Texas Republicans face right now of losing their ruby-red grip over their state, it might make strategic sense for them to widen their tent, particularly to voters who are already inclined to support them.

Muslims are especially primed for the taking, as they’ve increased their voting power over the past 10 years. The Institute for Social Policy and Understanding found that in 2016, 60 percent of eligible American Muslims reported being registered to vote, and by 2025 that figure had jumped up to 85 percent. And since 2024, Muslims have been shifting away from Democrats over their handling of Israel’s war in Gaza, which culminated in tangible action with the “Uncommitted” movement that galvanized voters who were unhappy with the Biden administration’s Israel policy to refrain from voting for either Joe Biden or Kamala Harris.

Plenty of ink has been poured over whether the Biden administration’s Israel policy cost them the 2024 election, but the data suggests there has been a clear shift. Exit polling conducted by the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the largest Muslim civil rights group, found in 2020 that Biden earned 69 percent of the Muslim vote, compared to Trump’s 17 percent. Four years later in 2024, Harris earned only 20 percent, while Trump received 21 percent and third-party candidate Jill Stein notched 53 percent. That is a lot of voters ripe for the taking.

The shift in Muslim voters’ politics is comparable to that of America’s Hispanic electorate, who were considered solidly Democratic until Trump arrived. In 2024, he captured 42 percent of the Latino vote as discourse around immigration doomed the Biden and Harris campaigns. Ironically, Latinos now may swing back to Democrats in 2026, thanks to Trump’s deeply unpopular mass-deportation agenda. The current vitriolic rhetoric being spewed in Texas by Republicans could similarly push Muslims right into Democratic hands.

This doesn’t surprise Hussein, who senses that Texas Republicans’ true loyalty always goes back to White Christian nationalist voters. “I think it probably appeals to a portion of the base. I think it’s also a distraction from other things that matter to Texans,” he told me. “It’s a reliable boogeyman to blame Muslims.”

This time around, they may just be shooting themselves in the foot.
news.summary: American Muslims have been asserting more and more political clout.

news.title: Haley Stevens Did What?
news.text:
When a politician makes a move that changes nothing, the reaction should be a shrug.

A shrug is not what Haley Stevens got.

On Sunday, two days before Election Day, the Democratic congresswoman who lost Michigan's Senate primary walked into Perfecting Church on Detroit's east side, a black congregation, and sat down next to Republican Mike Rogers and his wife, Kristi. Then she posted a video endorsing him.

"Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers."

One congresswoman. One church service. One video.

A few miles away, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed was at another church with Jim Clyburn, Debbie Dingell, Angela Alsobrooks, and Mallory McMorrow, trying to project unity. The Associated Press called the morning a split-screen. It was a split-screen with a gospel soundtrack.

It got there fast. On Friday, Stevens asked El-Sayed to condemn an ad from an outside left-wing group linking American support for Israel to high grocery prices. El-Sayed said he didn't agree with the ad, then accused her of relitigating a primary that ended three months ago. By Sunday, the joint church appearance was off. Dingell said she pulled it because it had become "way too distracting."

Now watch the reaction.

Nancy Pelosi, the former Speaker, went to X to say Stevens "has chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families' healthcare, freedoms, and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers."

Horrific. For a church service and a video.

Chuck Schumer, who backed Stevens in the primary, called it "a despicable betrayal."

Pramila Jayapal, the House's leading progressive, said Stevens "has shown her true colors" and "has no place in our party." She told Politico she supports removing Stevens from the caucus.

Michigan's own Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she'd stayed quiet until now because voters care more about the cost of living than "daily political drama," but that "there is simply too much at stake."

State party chair Curtis Hertel said Stevens "abandoned everything she claims to care about," then announced she "is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future." Her chief of staff of eight years resigned, and more staff are expected to follow. Rep. Jared Huffman of California called her move "pathetic, petty, selfish, unhinged."

Former Speaker. Senate leader. The party's top progressive in the House. Michigan's sitting senator. The state party chair.

That is not how you respond to a move that doesn't matter.

Even the quiet part leaked. A centrist House Democrat told Axios who deserves the blame: El-Sayed "created this mess."

El-Sayed's own answer to reporters? "None of this matters."

His party's reaction suggests otherwise.

Stevens, for her part, didn't apologize. She told reporters she isn't "turning my back on Democrats," called her vote a personal choice made as a "proud Democrat," and said El-Sayed standing with Hasan Piker was "not acceptable." Days earlier she had told CNN she was voting for the nominee while urging his campaign to "shut out the hate and call it out."

You can doubt her motives. But a reason offered in public is still a reason, and the party's answer was a pile-on, not a rebuttal.

The heat comes from August. Stevens beat El-Sayed in Wayne and Oakland counties. She won Detroit with more than 60 percent, and El-Sayed became the first Michigan Democrat since 2018 to win a statewide primary without winning the state's largest city. AP notes her support came from black and Jewish voters, the two pillars of the coalition Democrats need to turn out Tuesday. Last week her fiancé, who is Jewish, told The Detroit News he would vote for Rogers because El-Sayed hasn't done enough to address the Jewish community's concerns.

Then Stevens sat in a black church in Detroit with a Republican, two days out.

El-Sayed has had Barack Obama in Detroit. Kamala Harris joined him on the trail. Clyburn was at church Sunday morning. That is a great deal of establishment firepower for a candidate whose own primary opponent just reminded everyone which voters chose her.

To be fair, the polls favor him. Eleven of twelve October surveys had him ahead, by one to seven points. Every one of them was taken before Sunday. His lead leans on young voters, independents, and anti-establishment energy. Whether the church-going, traditional Democratic voters who carried Stevens in August show up with the same enthusiasm is a question none of those polls could answer.

Does Stevens' endorsement mean Rogers wins? I don't know. Neither does anyone else. Maybe Detroit turns out. Maybe it doesn't.

But I know what a snarl sounds like. When the former Speaker of the House hears about a church service in Detroit and reaches for "horrific," she isn't describing Haley Stevens. She's describing her own party's nerves.

That's panic. After the week this slate has had, it was bound to show up somewhere.

Early voting started October 24, and plenty of ballots are already in. The ones still out belong to voters who just watched which Democrats got angry, and about what.

news.title: In Michigan’s election battle, Canada keeps coming up
news.text: As Americans head to the polls for midterm elections Tuesday, the outcome could have significant consequences for Canada. CTVNews.ca will have live results, breaking updates, real-time election data and on-the-ground reporting from key battleground states. OTTAWA – Nowhere in the U.S. will tariffs be more top of mind for midterm voters than in Michigan. According to a website launched by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation (NTUF), tariffs cost Michigan households more than in any other state. U.S. President Donald Trump’s taxes cost per household in the Wolverine state is more than US$5,600. Twenty-five per cent auto tariffs imposed by Trump in 2025, have contributed to that cost in the state, which is the heart of the American automotive industry. The highly integrated supply chain with Canada is making it even more painful for people who live and work in Michigan. If there is no trade deal with Canada by January 2027, auto tariffs on Canadian-made cars, trucks and auto parts will double to 50 per cent. “It’s two countries, one region,” said Sandy Baruah, president and CEO of the Detroit Regional Chamber speaking about the bilateral relationship between Canada and the U.S. “We also want our companies in the United States that actually build the facilities, that rehab and retool the facilities… to be able to do business in both the United States and Canada, equally well.” Baruah told CTV News that ever since section 232 tariffs were imposed on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos, most businesses are waiting to make any kind of significant investment on either side of the border. “Right now, they’re (companies) still a little frozen because they don’t know what the long-term trajectory is,” said Baruah. “If you’re a CEO of a publicly traded company, you’re saying, ‘well, let’s just see what we can do over the next couple of years, and let’s see where we go.’” Political consensus According to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, Michigan is the third most affected by tariffs of all American states. The recent NTUF report shows importers that bring goods into Michigan have paid more than $23 billion in tariffs in the last 22 months. The unpopularity of those taxes has bled into the hotly contested Senate race with the Republican candidate Mike Rogers even calling for an end to the trade war with Canada. In October the former congressman released a video ad pitching a truce with the U.S.’ northern neighbour. “Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now,” said Rogers in the video, adding that if he’s elected the state’s senator he will “bring both parties together to lower your prices.” It’s one of the rare times both Republican and Democratic candidates are on the same side of an issue with candidate Abdul El-Sayed calling Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods “dumb” in a TV ad. Despite the consensus on tariffs, El-Sayed is consistently polling ahead of Rogers leading up to Tuesday’s vote. With affordability being one of the central campaign issues of the midterms, the Republican record is causing issues for candidates running under the GOP banner, according to CTV News’ U.S. political analyst Eric Ham. “That is clearly one of the drivers that we’re seeing why Republicans are having such a difficult time, because there (Michigan), it’s all about the economy,” said Ham. Trump’s approval rating According to Ham, the problem is further compounded by the so-called “Reagan Democrats.” That type of voter is traditionally registered as a democratic voter who is most commonly a blue-collar worker in the rust belt, like Michigan. They’ve earned the moniker because they’re democrats who would vote for former republican president Ronald Reagan. However, Ham isn’t sure that will happen during Tuesday’s midterms. “What we’re seeing now in this election, even those Reagan Democrats are becoming increasingly problematic for people like Mike Rogers,” said Ham. A number of polls show Trump’s approval rating in the state of Michigan at a record low in the 30 per cent range. A major drop from the 2024 presidential election, where Trump won the state with 49.7 per cent of the vote to Kamala Harris’ 48.3 per cent. It was a narrow victory, but enough for Trump to flip Michigan back into the Republican win column. Keeping the state red could be a tall task, considering the current affordability crisis in Michigan and across the United States. According to the Pew Research Centre survey conducted in August, 60 per cent of Americans say that don’t currently have enough income to lead the kind of life they want. In that same survey, nearly one-in-three respondents said, “they worry every day or nearly every day about the cost of health care and the amount of debt they have.” Twenty-seven per cent of people said they cannot pay some of their monthly bills or can only make partial payments, while more than half say they have not been able to save money for the future.

news.title: Trump Voters Reveal Brutal Regret on Eve of Election
news.text:
Young men who voted for Donald Trump in the last election have revealed why they have now turned their backs on the president.

Speaking to The New York Times, young men who backed Trump in 2024 cited multiple reasons for regretting their votes, including the war in Iran, his handling of the economy and soaring gas prices.

Some of those Trump voters said their anger toward the president was so severe that they would not vote for any Republican candidate in Tuesday’s midterms, a widespread sentiment that could doom the GOP to an electoral wipeout.

Matthew Michels, 26, of Grand Rapids, Michigan, said he was not planning to vote at all on Tuesday because he hadn’t “seen enough pushback against some of the stuff Trump’s been doing from establishment Republicans” on issues such as the deeply unpopular Iran war and gas prices. “If I could go back, I would not cast a vote for him again,” he told the Times.

Malachi Bohlmann, a 25-year-old from Phoenix, Arizona, said he voted for Trump because of his vow to control the border and his foreign policy promises.

However, he now regrets his vote following the hard-line immigration tactics of ICE agents and the war with Iran. “I think the way that ICE has went about things hasn’t been the most humane way,” Bohlmann told the Times.

“When I was in the service, we talked about being able to be ready to strike at any given time to defend our people at any cost,” Bohlmann, an Air Force veteran, added. “I don’t like America attacking first.”

Bohlmann said he still planned to vote in the midterms but had not yet decided whom to support.

One key reason Trump beat Kamala Harris in 2024 was his significant gains among young voters. 

More than half (55 percent) of men between 18 and 29 backed Trump in the 2024 election, a 23-point shift from 2020, according to the Times’ analysis.

However, polls have frequently suggested that the president’s erratic second term and failure to deliver on promises to ease people’s financial hardships have caused the 80-year-old’s support among young people to crater.

Now, seven out of 10 men aged 18 to 29 disapprove of Trump’s job performance, according to an analysis of the final three New York Times/Siena University national polls.

Ranger Irwin, 22, of Las Vegas, Nevada, is one of those who believe Trump “didn’t follow through” on several of his promises.

“He really said he was going to be antiwar, and we’re in war in the Middle East again,” Irwin said. “The price of everything’s gone up; gas is getting ridiculous again.”

However, Irwin said he would still vote for Trump again if he could and planned to back Republican candidates in Nevada on Tuesday. “It’s not their decisions, it’s his decisions,” he said.

Melissa Deckman, a political scientist and chief executive of the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute, said people had read too much into Trump’s gains among young voters in 2024 and wrongly interpreted them as evidence of a historic shift toward conservatism among this demographic.

“I think a lot of people misread the results of 2024, viewing it as young men are suddenly becoming more conservative, that they’re sick of woke politics,” Deckman told the Times. “But a fundamental issue was the economy.”

In response, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told the Daily Beast: “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress. 

“The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”

news.title: Michigan Democrat El-Sayed challenged by 250 rabbis on Israel in nationwide push by liberal Jews
news.text: Shortly before an Oct. 24 rally featuring Michigan US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and former President Barack Obama in Detroit, 250 rabbis from across the country urged them both to take their concerns more seriously about El-Sayed's position on Israel.The rabbis were speaking on behalf of a group called Nonnegotiable Michigan, and they require El-Sayed to commit to their five demands before they will support him. In this case, they wanted him to vocalize support for “Jewish statehood in Israel” and a commitment to safety for “Zionist Jews” - and to do it onstage.To their disappointment, neither headliner mentioned the movement or its demands - and El-Sayed will soon wrap his campaign, likely without having done so at all. Now the nascent movement is facing criticism from Jews to its left that the tactic backfired and made Jews more vulnerable.In the campaign's final days, Nonnegotiable's attempt to find a voice in the race has also been overshadowed by pro-Israel Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens' endorsement of El-Sayed's opponent, Republican former congressman Mike Rogers.Still, the letter was the biggest rabbinical foray into US politics since more than 1,100 clergy signed an open letter last year condemning “rising anti-Zionism and its political normalization” shortly before the election of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The Michigan letter also signaled that even beyond the state, a sizable cohort of Jews are trying to state their principles amid shifting fault lines in the Democratic Party.Nonnegotiable organizers undeterred by silence, seek national platform for liberal JewsThe organizers of Nonnegotiable are undeterred by the party's silence. They are seeking a new national platform for liberal Zionist Jews to assert their priorities in politics. “I do think it's a template for a national model,” Rabbi Aaron Starr, one of Nonnegotiable's co-founders, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. “I'm certainly looking beyond this election. In two years there will be a presidential election, and another slate of candidates for elected office.”Starr, of the Conservative Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield, a Detroit suburb, said Nonnegotiable's biggest goal was to “name the priorities that were most core to mainstream American Jews.” He believes they have accomplished that.As Israel seems sure to remain a hot-button topic for the American electorate in the 2028 presidential race, Starr sees the need for Jews to assert their priorities as urgent. “Everyone recognizes the growing extremism among political parties and politicians these days,” he said. “Everybody, and especially rabbis, recognizes that extremists could pop up in their own districts and their own states. So they want a forum to be able to communicate ways by which we reject extremism.”National spotlightNonnegotiable's organizers told JTA they have gathered 1,900, mostly anonymous, signatures to date within Michigan. That figure would be larger than the combined totals of named Michigan Jews who have signed open letters pledging to vote for El-Sayed (1,000) and Rogers (560).Nationally, the organization says 4,560 people have signed the petition, including the rabbis from out of state who have joined up with the movement in its final days. The other clergy were sourced from rabbinical networks on social media and come from 34 different states and Washington, DC. A good chunk of them serve active congregations. Many are from liberal or swing states, including Rabbi Samuel Stern of Temple Beth Sholom in Topeka, Kansas, where another close Senate race is unfolding. Stern told JTA he signed in order to call out “the anti-Zionist hatred that we see coming out of different political sides and candidates.”For the rabbis on the letter, El-Sayed's rhetoric in Michigan looms large in their states, too - in some cases, larger even than more local antisemitism controversies.At a recent rally in Kansas, US President Donald Trump used the term “Shylock,” widely considered to be an antisemitic slur, when referring to a controversy involving the GOP incumbent senator suing patients with medical debt. Stern, though, said that his Kansas congregation was generally more concerned about El-Sayed's rhetoric on Israel several states away than Trump's remarks closer to home.“It really didn't play that much here,” the rabbi said, of Trump's comment. “I don't know what that means for us, or for any of the other Jewish communities, but it wasn't as prevalent here. We've heard more about what Dr. El-Sayed has said, his anti-Zionism, and been more concerned about that than about the offhand comment by President Trump.”Nonnegotiable has also expanded onto college campuses, with an organizing campaign that has quickly formed at the University of Michigan. Around two dozen Jewish students have publicly added their names to the letter.“I really resonated with what Nonnegotiable stands for,” student organizer Jacob Reich, who is involved in various Democratic Party initiatives on and off campus, told JTA. “I felt torn between both my Jewish identity and my identity as a Democrat.” Among Reich's biggest concerns about El-Sayed, he said, was the candidate's widely criticized “hurt people hurt people” remark made after a March attack on the state's Temple Israel. The attacker's family members were killed in Lebanon in an Israeli strike.El-Sayed has since apologized for those comments, and his campaign has sent mailers to Jewish households in which he pledges to fight antisemitism. Reich said he appreciated the letter, but added, “I don't think it went far enough to address a lot of the missteps that he's taken.”Whose nonnegotiables?Rabbis friendlier with El-Sayed have argued the movement is ineffective at messaging; could boost Republican policies most Jews strongly oppose; and ignores ways in which the candidate has sought to improve his relations with Jews. Some have aired those grievances to the movement's leaders directly.“Nonnegotiable describes itself as an invitation rather than an ultimatum,” Rabbi Alana Alpert, of Detroit-area Congregation T'chiyah, wrote privately to the campaign's organizers in an Oct. 8 letter. “It has had the opposite effect, driving a wedge between the campaign and Jewish interests.”In her previously unpublicized letter, which she recently shared with JTA, Alpert compared Nonnegotiable to Uncommitted, the 2024 activist campaign in Michigan that sought to pressure then-President Joe Biden on Gaza by withholding primary votes for him. The Uncommitted movement later refused to endorse replacement nominee Kamala Harris. Trump went on to win Michigan and the general election.The two campaigns used “similar language,” Alpert wrote. She told her fellow rabbis that they were now “dealing with the choices, coalitions, and consequences of an actual general election with far-reaching implications.”Rabbi Nate DeGroot, who heads the progressive Shalom Center and serves two Michigan synagogues, laid out 10 alternative “nonnegotiables” of his own that he argues “Michigan Jews care just as much about.”In an essay shared with JTA in advance of its publication, DeGroot's own nonnegotiables include “fierce condemnation of Christian nationalism”; support for abortion rights and trans rights; and a “commitment to beating swords into plowshares,” a phrase originating in the bible that DeGroot said should also apply to opposing the US-Israeli war in Iran. Rogers would fail to meet those criteria, DeGroot wrote. Both he and Alpert are supporters of Michigan Jews for Democracy, an ad hoc group organizing for El-Sayed.One argument Nonnegotiable's critics have made is that the movement has had the net effect of benefiting Rogers, who has made an aggressive play for the Jewish vote while employing campaign language about the Muslim Brotherhood that many have argued embraces Islamophobic tropes. Organizers have expressly denied that their cause is partisan, though some of the big names who signed the Nonnegotiable letter have since cast their ballots for Rogers.At a recent Republican Jewish Coalition event staged for Rogers, some speakers directly referenced El-Sayed's refusal to engage with Nonnegotiable as part of the reason not to vote for him.“When rabbis and Jewish leaders within El-Sayed's own party came to him with five basic, nonnegotiable commitments, fundamental principles of Jewish safety, identity, and self-determination, they asked him to affirm these commitments clearly and unequivocally,” Lauren Slutsky, a parent of a Temple Israel preschooler, told the crowd. “Weeks later, we're still waiting.” She argued, “If a candidate cannot clearly say that Jewish safety, including the safety of Zionist Jews, is nonnegotiable, why should our community or anyone in our community give him our vote?”Accusations flyingNonnegotiable's organizers have denied that their group is affiliated with any Jewish cause but their own. Zioness, which bills itself as a progressive Zionist group, is boosting them.Yet some Jews see in the movement an echo of more hardline pro-Israel sentiment. J Street, the national liberal Zionist lobby, seized on a video accidentally posted to Nonnegotiable's Instagram account that showed the account holder texting with David Victor, a former president of AIPAC and a Michigan resident. The pro-Israel lobbying giant has spent millions against El-Sayed in both the primary and the general election.The gaffe, J Street vice president of political and digital strategy Tali DeGroot told JTA, was potential evidence that Nonnegotiable's organizers were coordinating with AIPAC-aligned figures. “Our fear from the start with Nonnegotiable is that it plays directly into the hands of Republicans who are cynically using the issue of antisemitism for their own political gain,” DeGroot, who has no relation to Nate DeGroot, told JTA. The texting, she insisted, “just validates that fear even more.” J Street has not formally endorsed El-Sayed, but the lobby is generally supportive of his campaign and is spending against other AIPAC-aligned candidates this midterm cycle. Neither AIPAC nor Victor responded to JTA requests for comment.Nonnegotiable organizers, however, dispute this account and have expressly denied any involvement from AIPAC in the group. “If I had been aware of any of the establishment forces being involved in this, or if there was a whiff of partisanship, I would not have gotten involved,” Matt Zerwekh, an initial signer of the letter who leads Temple Emanu-El in the Detroit suburb of Oak Park, told JTA. Some have even vocally opposed the powerhouse lobby. One of Nonnegotiable's co-founders, Rabbi Josh Whinston of Ann Arbor's Temple Beth Emeth, published an op-ed in the Detroit Free Press on Friday condemning AIPAC for quoting him in anti-El-Sayed mailers distributed to Jewish households.On Sunday afternoon, hours after Stevens' endorsement of Rogers, Nonnegotiable gathered again on Zoom with guests including Zionist pundit Hen Mazzig and Michigan US Rep. Hillary Scholten. At the exact same moment as the call, pro-Israel congressional candidate Jeremy Moss was joining a cohort of Democrats castigating Stevens for her endorsement. Nonnegotiable leaders saw it differently: Starr praised Stevens for her “bravery.” Others, such as Scholten, didn't raise the subject at all. The congresswoman instead praised the US-Israel relationship and the Iron Dome defensive system. “I'm so proud to stand as a friend and ally of our Jewish community right now,” she told those on the call.The real purpose of the call, though, was for Nonnegotiable to suggest that Jews could write in a candidate instead of voting for either nominee. Their top write-in pick: Emma Lazarus, the 19th-century Jewish poet best known for having her work engraved on the Statue of Liberty.
