news.title: No Need to Worry, Guys! ABC Dismisses Stevens Endorsement, Touts WILD NYT Polls
news.text:
ABC’s Good Morning America did its best to paper over Sunday’s stunning announcement in Michigan, with Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens (D-MI) endorsing Republican senatorial candidate Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul el-Sayed, the man who defeated Stevens by roughly a point in the primary. ABC reassured leftist viewers that “Democrats [are] showing strength despite some last-minute drama in Michigan,” with early votes and some possibly cockamamie polling from The New York Times arguing Democrats will win every single Senate toss-up.

In the teases, co-host and former Clinton official George Stephanopoulos promoted the “surprising” “final twist,” but quickly discounted it by gushing: “Could Democrats flip the House and Senate? What could ultimately decide who wins.”

Stephanopoulos’s build-up to chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce’s report was pure liberal happy talk that even refused to say Stevens’s name: “Democrats showing strength despite some last-minute drama in Michigan, where the Democratic primary loser endorsed the Republican candidate for Senate as President Trump made his final push in red states.”

Bruce said Stevens’s “surprise endorsement...rocking one of the most closely watched Senate races” had left “Democrats fuming after” the “stunning announcement.”

The ABC correspondent downplayed el-Sayed’s ties to radical Islamists: “The breaking point came over this controversial ad from an outside group backing El-Sayed...Stevens called the ad anti-Semitic and urged El-Sayed to denounce it. He has said he disagrees with it. Asked about Stevens’ endorsement of his Republican opponent, the Democratic nominee brushing it off.”

She added Democrats were “outraged,” and promoted the theatre kids in her House office “resigning in protest, saying the team is ‘shocked and heartbroken’ at her decision.”

Bruce also downplayed and oversimplified the fraud in Alaska with the second Dan Sullivan that reportedly was recruited by Democrat Senate candidate Mary Peltola and the national party (click “expand”):

BRUCE: But the President dealt a blow in another critical Senate race: the Alaska contest between Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. The judge saying that since ballots are secret, it would be impossible to determine whether voters who voted for the other Dan Sullivan were confused. The Justice Department says they plan to appeal. Our Trevor Ault is in Alaska, where early voting has surged.TREVOR AULT: Look at this line of people for early voting at the mall in Anchorage. This is snaking all the way through. I’m told every single day it’s been like this for a week. Sometimes, people waiting two hours to get their vote cast early.BRUCE: Even if he loses, Senator Sullivan says he’ll accept the results.

Back in 2024, though, Bruce was giddy over “prominent conservative” Liz Cheney’s endorsement of Kamala Harris for president. On October 4, 2024’s Good Morning America, Bruce swooned at the “astonishing sight” as “a powerful reminder of the difficult choice that many Republicans are facing” because “democracy is on the line.”

Bruce’s fellow virulent Trump-hating correspondent followed with some liberal pom-pom waving of her own.

Rachel Scott trumpeted a set of New York Times/Siena polls released Sunday, which projected a Senate Democrat sweep in all seven swing seats.

Along with it claiming el-Sayed has an 11-point lead over Republican Mike Rogers, it projects a seven-point win in Texas for Democrat James Talarico and a five-point victory for Kansas Democrat Adam Hamilton (click “expand”):

SCOTT: In order for Democrats to take control of the Senate, they need to defend everything they currently have, and then also flip at least four seats. This seemed out of reach just a few months ago because that means Democrats would have to win in red states that the president won by double digits — states like Alaska, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, and also Ohio. But in recent weeks, the final weeks of this campaign, voter frustrations over the economy, over the war in Iran, the cost of living — that has brought these races a lot closer and a lot tighter than what Republicans had hoped to see. In fact, in all of these battleground states, the latest poll from New York Times and Siena shows that Democrats have a nine-point edge over Republicans on that number one issue of the economy. Let’s take a look at that poll because it does show that in states like Texas and Ohio, the Democrats are pulling ahead of Republicans just slightly. But take a look at where this stands in a state like Kansas that has not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century — it is the Democrat, Adam Hamilton, that is pulling ahead just slightly there. It will be voters that will ultimately get the final say tomorrow.STEPHANOPOULOS: Right. Those Times polls showed the Democratic candidate way ahead in Michigan.

Back in reality, thought: The same polls ahead of the 2024 presidential election were cartoonishly wrong:

She vouched for their validity, saying it’s “fueled by voters on the economy, the high cost of living” to give “Democrats...traction” even if they were simply “a snapshot in time.”

“[W]e’ve been all across this country. We have correspondents fanned out all over, and the polls are reflecting what we’re hearing from voters. The economy is the number one issue that is driving voters to the polls,” she added.

news.title: America votes, India waits: what Tuesday's midterms can and cannot change for New Delhi
news.text: Americans vote on Tuesday in elections that will not mention India on any ballot, and could still decide how much of India's trade relationship with Washington is settled by legislation and how much by a president acting alone.The interim trade agreement the two countries have been negotiating for more than a year is still unsigned. Indian negotiators have been in no hurry to close it, and analysts say New Delhi has been waiting for this result to see what shape the American legislative picture takes. What they will learn on Tuesday, however, is narrower than it looks..WHAT IS BEING DECIDEDAll 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 of the 100 Senate seats and 36 governorships are on the ballot. The Senate math is 53 Republicans against 45 Democrats and two independents who caucus with them; 51 seats control the chamber, and a 50-50 split stays Republican because Vice President JD Vance holds the casting vote. Republicans defend 22 of the 35 Senate seats up, Democrats 13. Three races carry the argument: Georgia and Michigan, both Democratic-held and both carried by President Donald Trump in 2024, and Maine, the only Republican-held seat in a state Kamala Harris won.Turnout is already at a record for a midterm. About 54 million ballots had been cast by Sunday evening, against 45.9 million early votes in the whole of 2022. In the states that publish party registration, registered Democrats account for roughly 43 to 45 per cent of early voters and Republicans 31 to 32 per cent. Texas alone has passed seven million early votes. The professor who runs the main academic tracker warns that these numbers cannot predict an outcome..WHERE INDIA'S TARIFF ACTUALLY STANDSIn February, Washington and New Delhi announced a framework that cut the US tariff on Indian goods to 18 per cent from 50 per cent. India was to cut duties on American industrial goods and a range of farm products, and buy $500 billion of US energy, aircraft, precious metals and technology over five years.The legal ground then moved. The US Supreme Court struck down the emergency powers under which the sweeping tariffs had been imposed. A temporary 10 per cent global duty lapsed in July. Indian goods now carry an extra 10 per cent under Section 301 over forced-labour concerns, and India's effective tariff rate is about 13.6 per cent, far below the 35 per cent starting point of February. A separate Section 301 investigation into excess manufacturing capacity, which names India among 16 economies, has a statutory deadline of March 2027 and could reset rates whatever is signed now.The two sides have kept talking past each other on how close they are. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the negotiations were "in the short strokes" but that "I don't think there's something imminent, but we truly have identified the universe of items that are sticking points". Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks had reached a "plateau" beyond which give and take would be very difficult. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in October they were "very, very close". Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on October 29 that the interim deal would fully protect Indian farmers..WHY THE RESULT MOVES LESS THAN EXPECTEDTariff authority in the United States sits with the president, through Section 232 on national security and Section 301 on unfair trade practice, not with Congress. A Democratic House could hold hearings, demand documents, investigate what tariffs cost American consumers and pass bills to repeal them. With Republicans favoured to hold the Senate and the president holding a veto, none of that becomes law. Brokerages put a Democratic sweep at about 63 per cent and a Democratic House alone at 29 per cent, and expect oversight, litigation and uncertainty rather than a dismantled tariff regime either way. The Democratic leader's announced plan to claw back Congress's trade powers would begin in January 2027 and would need a signature it will not get.The lever that can actually hurt India is not in Congress's hands at all. A sanctions law signed in September allows tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, a group led by India and China. It passed with cross-party support, including 58 House Democrats, and the administration waived it on October 16. A Democratic victory would not soften the law; only the White House decides whether to pull that trigger..H-1B AND THE DIASPORAIndians take the large majority of H-1B visas, and the programme is in the courts. A $100,000 fee on certain new petitions for applicants outside the United States, imposed by proclamation in September 2025, has been extended through September 2027, while federal judges have blocked its collection and an appeals court has refused to pause those rulings. Bills in the Senate would tighten the programme further. A Democratic House could block new immigration legislation and hold hearings, but could not end that litigation. Research based on interviews with American officials and congressional staff found support for India in Congress to be broad but shallow, with an intense minority inside the governing coalition whose organising concern is restricting immigration.Indian-American candidates are contesting seats in both chambers this cycle, caught between a party base hostile to the visa programme and a community that has moved sharply away from it..THE DESK POINTPolls close on Tuesday evening in the United States, which is early on Wednesday morning in India. The first calls will reach us between 5 am and 9 am IST. The story for Indian readers will not be who won the House. It is whether a half-finished trade deal gets signed before or after the Section 301 capacity ruling, and whether a tariff instrument that needs no vote in Congress is used.(With inputs from PTI and media reports)

news.title: Haley Stevens Just Did Something Unforgivable. But She’s Not the Only One Responsible for Democrats’ Michigan Mess.
news.text:
The first thing to know about the Democrat-on-Democrat catastrophe engulfing the Michigan Senate election is that it didn’t have to happen. The second thing to know is that there’s a lot of blame to go around.

On Sunday, Rep. Haley Stevens pulled a heel turn for the ages. Stevens, a pro-Israel centrist who narrowly lost the Democratic primary to progressive Abdul El-Sayed, was slated to appear at a “unity rally” on the last weekend before Election Day. Instead, she pulled out—and went to church with El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers. A formal Rogers endorsement followed, completing the betrayal. Now, in a tight race that’s crucial to Democrats’ hopes of retaking the Senate and grinding Donald Trump’s agenda to a halt, a candidate who got almost half of the primary vote is supporting the Republican.

There are a few ways in which this disaster could’ve been avoided. If Democratic Sen. Gary Peters—who in congressional terms is but a 67-year-old whippersnapper—had sought reelection, the messy primary that set up Stevens’ about-face never would’ve happened. The same thing is probably true had either Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer or former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who lives in Traverse City, Michigan, decided to run for Peters’ seat. Once they passed, the state’s Democratic primary voters could have picked a compromise candidate in Mallory McMorrow, a (now-proven) team player who is more centrist than El-Sayed and more progressive than Stevens. After McMorrow dropped out, Stevens and El-Sayed could have pulled their punches instead of sparring nastily over the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza and Stevens’ support from AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group. And once the primary ended, the pair could have buried the hatchet permanently rather than letting the tensions simmer into the general election. In short, everything in the race has broken toward conflict rather than comity.

Michigan wasn’t the only bare-knuckled race in a primary season that served as an extended proxy fight between the Democratic Party’s center-left establishment and its progressive insurgency. The Senate contest in Florida, several House races in New York, and the gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin all got heated. A few other primaries even yielded sore losers; in Texas, Rep. Jasmine Crockett has refused to campaign with fellow Democrat James Talarico after he beat her. Yet even Crockett says she “WOULDN’T, EVER” endorse Talarico’s Republican opponent, so something has clearly gone uniquely sideways in Michigan.

What went wrong? Who’s to blame? And is anyone entirely innocent? Stevens is obviously the headline villain, the architect of a hard-to-find-precedent-for defection that is indefensible on both substance and timing. But the difficult reality is that the blame doesn’t rest with her alone. At the heart of this disaster is a spectacularly poor match of political egos, an issue that promotes intransigence over compromise, and, in El-Sayed, a nominee who failed a critical test.

Let’s start with the person who’s most at fault for Sunday’s explosion: the one who actually pulled the pin out of the grenade. Despite continuing to describe herself as “a very proud Democrat,” Stevens has arguably done more damage to her party’s nominee than Republicans have. It’s certainly possible that El-Sayed will win, and that Democrats could retake the Senate even if he doesn’t. But winning Michigan in what’s shaping up to be a blue-wave election shouldn’t be this hard, and retaking the Senate without it would require Democrats to vastly overperform in much more Republican-friendly states.

But Stevens has betrayed more than just her party: She’d previously argued that a Rogers win would imperil a suite of issues she professed to care about. After losing the primary, she full-throatedly endorsed El-Sayed and argued that Rogers would “keep rubber-stamping Donald Trump’s harmful agenda of higher prices, manufacturing jobs lost nationwide, corruption and abuses of power” while helping “ban abortion, gut health care, and roll back workers’ rights and voting rights.” The only thing that’s changed since then is the candidate Stevens supports.

Then there’s the matter of her rationale. Stevens’ defection followed a war of words over a pro-El-Sayed ad, which argued that groceries have become unaffordable because the U.S. sends weapons to Israel. Stevens criticized the ad as antisemitic and demanded El-Sayed condemn it. (More on that in a moment.) But if bigotry were really her concern, she wouldn’t be throwing in with Rogers, a candidate who built his campaign around Islamophobia. Rogers has accused El-Sayed of adhering to a “radical Islamic agenda” and of backing the Muslim Brotherhood, an extremist group the Democrat has repeatedly denounced. Stevens is also, by her own prior admission, helping a president who mocks El-Sayed’s name (“To me, he’s Mohammed, and he’s a radical jihadist,” Trump said last month) and fearmongers that his victory would “invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.” On Sunday, Stevens characterized her flip-flop as “a personal and private decision” in the middle of a press conference talking about it, which made the whole thing look more petty than principled.

His culpability is more complicated, but it really does take two to tango. Stevens chose to pull her switcheroo, yet El-Sayed has done a bunch of tactically questionable things that seem to have made that outcome more likely—and could make it more politically damaging, too.

One of those questionable choices has been to associate himself with controversial figures. During the primary, El-Sayed campaigned with Hasan Piker, a left-wing streamer who has said that the U.S. “deserved 9/11”. El-Sayed spent months refusing to distance himself from Piker, deriding questions about their joint appearances as “gotcha politics.” And although El-Sayed ultimately did condemn those remarks and others (including Piker’s claim that Jewish Americans, or Jewish American institutions, being too pro-Israel could lead people to “take action” against them), some Democrats already had concerns about El-Sayed’s approach to antisemitism. In March, El-Sayed responded to an attack against a Detroit-area synagogue by saying that “hurt people hurt people,” which sounded to some like a justification for the violence. (El-Sayed later apologized.) “I’m just sick of the people he stands with,” Stevens told Anderson Cooper on CNN on Sunday night.

Self-defeating prickliness also seems to have shaped El-Sayed’s response to the ad Stevens criticized before endorsing Rogers. It’s true that the ad didn’t come from El-Sayed’s campaign; a left-wing commentator named Cenk Uygur, who happens to be Piker’s uncle, posted it online. But even as he distanced himself, El-Sayed also released a statement accusing Stevens of “relitigating” their primary that pointedly noted her millions in AIPAC support and disinvited Stevens from Sunday’s unity appearance, which national Democrats helped broker in a bid to squash their beef.

El-Sayed’s defensiveness, as he runs to be the nation’s first Muslim senator, is understandable. His opponent has put El-Sayed’s religion and ethnicity at the center of his attacks, yet El-Sayed is the one who’s continually asked to disavow bigotry. It must be exhausting. And it’s a challenge for a candidate whose rise was fueled by a combative approach to entrenched power, an approach many of his supporters appreciate. But politics is often unfair and rarely easy, and the job of the candidate is to win. That’s particularly true in an election where Democrats have repeatedly (and accurately) told supporters that their would-be Senate takeover is an essential bulwark against Trump’s authoritarian impulses. In that context, it’s not unfair for Democrats to ask El-Sayed to make sacrifices in the name of winning—and it’s not always clear that he has been willing to.

Before the August primary, El-Sayed predicted a double-digit victory against Stevens, only to end up winning by less than a point. A nominee laser-focused on the general election might have been chastened, hastening to court the 47.6 percent of Democrats who’d backed his opponent. Yet even now, polls suggest El-Sayed is leaving votes on the table. He currently leads Rogers by an average of 5 points, while the Democratic nominee for Michigan governor leads her Republican opponent by almost 9. As my colleague Aymann Ismail has reported, El-Sayed has struggled to convince some core Democratic constituencies, including Black Michiganders, that he will improve their lives.

Of course, it’s possible that nothing could have kept Stevens inside the tent. Some of her criticisms—like going on CNN to accuse El-Sayed of getting “angrier and angrier”—aren’t things politicians say if they’re open to appeasement. Stevens has also refused to explain her apparently spur-of-the-moment decision to switch sides; as of Saturday, she was still telling fellow Democrats that she supported El-Sayed. Maybe getting engaged to a Democratic donor who also recently pledged to vote for Rogers caused a (literal) change of heart. Maybe Stevens snapped after spending another week butting heads with the rival who foiled her Senate dreams. Or maybe she’s been promised a job after she leaves Congress in January in exchange for changing jerseys. (On Sunday, Trump praised Stevens’ “bravery,” and House Speaker Mike Johnson said he’d encouraged her to “keep speaking the truth.”)

The losers of competitive primaries—and their supporters—always face pressure to back their party’s nominee, and lately that pressure has fallen hardest on the left. During the previous three presidential elections, more moderate Democrats urged progressives to shelve their objections and get on board with Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden, and Kamala Harris in the interest of beating Trump. Stevens’ desertion isn’t a great sign that the party’s more centrist losers are willing to return the favor. Still, many moderate Democrats—including erstwhile Stevens supporters, congressional staffers, and House colleagues—have condemned the Rogers endorsement, meaning Stevens’ exit may not bring many voters along. So far, El-Sayed has chosen to downplay it. “This race was never about me. It was never even about Mike Rogers. It’s certainly not about Haley Stevens,” he said on MS NOW on Sunday night. “This race is about the people in the state of Michigan, the people that I’ve gotten to get to know in their churches and synagogues, in their basements, in their living rooms, talking about what they need and deserve.”

Yet if there’s any race in which the “vote blue no matter who” calculus could flop, it’s this one. The tension at the heart of the primary—and the feud between El-Sayed and Stevens—is less a policy disagreement than a moral one. Debates over healthcare have a moral valence, but there’s room to compromise between, say, expanding Obamacare and passing “Medicare for All.” By contrast, there isn’t much of a middle ground between thinking Israel is committing genocide in Gaza (as El-Sayed does) and believing that it isn’t (per Stevens). It’s certainly Stevens’ right to decide that her support for Israel outweighs her desire to see a Democrat win her state’s Senate race, just as it’s El-Sayed’s right to say good riddance to a Democrat who feels that way. But part of the job of being a party’s nominee is uniting as many of that party’s supporters behind you as possible. The reasons for El-Sayed’s failure to do that may be a matter of debate, but he will bear the consequences all the same. On Tuesday, it could cost his entire party.
news.summary: Is it fair to blame Abdul El-Sayed for this mess as well?

news.title: Five dimensional chess: inside James Talarico’s extraordinary bid to break Texas Democrats’ losing streak
news.text:
When a young, untested former school teacher stood up to address a modest gathering of local donors in Austin, the state capital of Texas, Wendy Davis felt sorry for him. “Poor kid,” she remembers thinking.

Then James Talarico began speaking. “He was like five or six sentences in and I knew that something was different about him,” recalls Davis, a former Democratic state senator. “He was as articulate and unique then as he is now. From that day, I started calling him ‘Baby Obama’.”

Eight years after that first fundraising event, “Baby Obama” is no longer a precocious candidate for the state house with paper slogans that read “A future as bright as Texas”. Now 37, Talarico will aim to redraw the political map next week by becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the Lone Star state since 1988.

The threat that he poses to Republicans’ grip on power has become clear in the final stretch of a fraught campaign. Over the past month Donald Trump rallied in Texas and branded him “James Talafreako”; JD Vance implied that Talarico is gay; and rightwing influencers spread a baseless lie that he checked into a mental health clinic in Ohio (in fact, he was ill with flu).

Despite the desperate attacks, most opinion polls give Talarico a narrow edge. On Tuesday the voters will have their say on whether the four-term state representative, a Presbyterian seminarian preaching a gospel of hope, can overcome Republican Ken Paxton, a scandal-haunted state attorney general and Trump ally who has financial backing from tech billionaire Elon Musk.

Facing a barrage of culture war attack ads funded the world’s wealthiest man, Talarico has responded with an unorthodox blend of economic populism, progressive politics and an unapologetically Christian message that challenges the religious right on its own turf. His campaign raised a record $64m in the third quarter, including donations from a vast number of small-dollar contributors.

Last week Talarico told a crowd of young voters and local activists gathered at his alma mater, the University of Texas at Austin, that Republicans’ billionaire donors were starting to fret.“They are terrified because they see what we see: we are about to win this election,” he said.

An eighth-generation Texan, he was born James Dell Causey in Round Rock, a small town north of Austin, in 1989. His mother, Tamara Causey, was a preacher’s daughter who left home at 19 and met his biological father, whom she has described as an alcoholic prone to violence.

One night the abuse became too much. Tamara drove James and all her belongings in a small Ford Escort to the hotel where she worked as a sales assistant. They lived in an empty room at the hotel until they found an apartment in Austin. Tamara subsequently married a sales manager named Mark Talarico, who adopted James and gave him his surname.

At school, Talarico was a keen debater and actor, with roles including Danny Zuko in the musical Grease. Allegra Hobbs, author of a profile in Texas Monthly magazine, reported: “His high school theater director, Aaron Johnson, joked to me that the young Talarico did not so much inhabit the character as play a version of himself. When the theater department handed out superlatives, ‘Jimmy’ was voted most likely to be president – a running joke among his friends that he would laugh off.”

Talarico studied at the University of Texas at Austin, where Mike Garcia, a 38-year-old lawyer and former legislative staffer, first encountered his political ambitions. In 2009, Garcia presided over the College Republicans while Talarico led the University Democrats. Despite their ideological differences, the pair initially found common ground in nonpartisan voter drives and a campaign for tuition relief.

Speaking from Fort Worth, Garcia recalls: “It was a little strange but I was glad that we were putting our differences aside and doing something that would help everybody.”

The goodwill did not last. During student government elections, Talarico’s organisation endorsed establishment candidates who opposed tuition re-regulation, according to Garcia. The move provoked outrage among Democrats who had supported the campaign, some of whom turned up at a College Republicans meeting to protest.

Garcia suspected Talarico had calculated that the endorsement would win him favour with university administrators ahead of a possible run for student body president. “That sounds like exactly something Jimmy would do,” he says.

Years later, when the two crossed paths again at the Texas capitol – Garcia working for Republican legislators and Talarico now an elected representative – Garcia felt he saw a similar gap between political rhetoric and personal charm. Talarico would “routinely just rail against all these people I work for, calling us the worst names ever”, he recalls, before greeting him warmly in the corridor minutes later.

Garcia remains unconvinced by Talarico’s current presentation as a moderate. “He is probably one of the types that is willing to tell you exactly what you want to hear, especially if it helps him politically. Right now he’s running as a moderate and he’s doing a very good job of it,” Garcia says.

But others dispute Garcia’s account. In a statement provided by Talarico’s campaign, Muneezeh Kabir, who was at the University of Texas with him and involved in student government, said: “James has always raised his hand to serve others. Throughout his time in student government at UT, James worked with everyone, even those he disagreed with, to make life on campus better for all of us. He delivered for his classmates at UT, then his community in Austin, and now, he’s ready to step up and serve Texans from every corner of the state.”

After college, and before the state house, Talarico went into education. His first job was teaching sixth-grade language arts at the Rhodes middle school on the west side of San Antonio, a predominantly Latino neighbourhood.

Edward Garcia, 56, who was principal of Rhodes at the time, remembers hiring Talarico during the summer of 2011. In a high-poverty school district where teacher turnover was relentless, Garcia was struck by the young applicant’s poise and purpose. “He knew what his mission statement was in terms of working with students that are in high poverty and high need. He was ready to start the next day,” he says.

Even before the academic year began, Talarico turned up at the school accompanied by his sister, hauling enlarged prints of Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr and Gandhi to create a classroom display devoted to human freedom.

“Teachers are supposed to be universal,” Garcia explains. “There wasn’t an approach in terms of partisan politics. It was just the concept of freedom and what it means for students to truly acquire freedom and leadership in their lives.”

Talarico’s connection with his middle schoolers was immediate. In a profession where novice teachers frequently struggle with classroom management and rely on administrative referrals, Talarico never wrote up a single student or sent one to the principal’s office. “He was an exemplary teacher. Kids were enthralled with his presentation and took a shine to him,” Garcia says. “What you see is what you get: smart, articulate and guided by his heart.”

When Garcia walked into Talarico’s room during his second-year formal observation, he discovered that the young teacher had physically removed his official administrative desk from the room.

“I went in to do his evaluation,” Garcia recalls with a laugh. “I looked around and said, ‘Where’s your desk?’ He goes, ‘Oh, I took it out and turned it into a reading space.’ He put a carpet down right where his desk should be.”

After two years in San Antonio, Talarico returned to the Austin area to lead an education non-profit before making his leap into elective politics in 2018. Winning a state house of representatives seat in a suburban swing district, he quickly established a reputation in the Texas capitol as an authority on public school finance and an exceptionally persuasive orator.

His Republican colleagues in the house began calling him “Baby Gov”, recognising that his ambitions might extend well beyond the state legislature. Talarico focused heavily on public education, prescription drug pricing and property tax relief.

During bitter legislative battles over voting rights and school vouchers – proposals to restrict access to the ballot and use public funds to help families pay for private education – Talarico emerged as a prominent opponent of Republican priorities.

In 2021, he joined fellow Democrats in leaving Texas to block a vote on Republican-backed voting restrictions by denying the state house the minimum number of members needed to conduct business. He later returned to the chamber before the standoff had ended, drawing criticism from some of his own party.

He also repeatedly clashed with conservative committee chairs over LGBTQ+ rights. Talarico used the phrase “God is non-binary” while opposing a bill concerning transgender children in school sports. Republicans have sought to weaponise it against him. Talarico has defended the underlying theological argument while acknowledging that he was being provocative.

While serving in the state legislature, Talarico enrolled at the Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary, which has a picturesque downtown campus of neat lawns, light-filled buildings and functional classrooms with blackboards and rows of desks. He pursued a master of arts in theological studies, diving into church history, ethics, systematic theology and ancient biblical languages.

The seminary’s president, José Irizarry, says: “We are not an assembly line for dogma. We are a place of faith formation which requires people to think deeply and thoughtfully about their faith practices. What does it mean to take your belief system and actually do the work of justice in the world?”

Irizarry recalls working in his office across from the classroom building during Talarico’s first year. “I had no door when I arrived here – an actual open-door policy. He was studying Hebrew across the hall. I could hear the whole Hebrew class because it was with a rabbi and he started the class singing in Hebrew. I would go out during the breaks and see him interacting with all the students. He was a student like everybody else around here, engaged in ministry.”

When Talarico called Wendy Davis in late 2023 to disclose his intention to surrender his safe house seat and launch a long-shot bid for the US Senate, she tried to stop him. Davis, now executive director of the the Blueprint Texas political action committee, admits: “I tried hard to talk him out of it. I told him that my fear was he’d been so impactful in the legislature and I thought it would be a big loss for him. I told him he was probably going to lose and he was going to regret leaving his office. And now look at him.”

Talarico went on to defeat Jasmine Crockett, another rising star of the party, in a bruising Senate primary election. He has since been working hard to unify the Democratic coalition, including Black voters who supported Crockett.

His theological training has proven not merely a personal spiritual exercise but the construction of a political armour. In a state where conservative evangelicals have long dominated public discourse on religion, Talarico’s fluid command of scripture has allowed him to carry out a counteroffensive.

He attacks Christian nationalism, opposes state-mandated displays of the Ten Commandments in public schools and argues that Jesus’s core commandment – to love one’s neighbour – demands support for healthcare, public education and marginalised communities.

Cal Jillson, a professor of political science at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, says by phone: “Usually the vote that takes religion seriously in Texas is an evangelical conservative Republican vote. There’s a possibility that he has a little more purchase beyond the Democratic base into moderates and independent voters in the middle. With Talarico, there’s more of a Sermon on the Mount vibe as opposed to this ‘I’m an angry God’.”

Talarico demonstrated that approach during a legislative committee hearing on a bill requiring the Ten Commandments to be displayed in Texas classrooms. Rather than offering a standard secular objection, Talarico quizzed the author on the text of the Commandments themselves – showing on camera that the politician could not recite them.

For Democrats, there have been plenty of false dawns in Texas. In 2018 Beto O’Rourke’s charismatic campaign for Senate against Republican Ted Cruz attracted national attention and record-breaking fundraising, but he ultimately lost by 2.6 percentage points.

Bill Minutaglio, a prominent Texas author and political historian whose books include A Single Star and Bloody Knuckles, argues that Talarico’s campaign represents a far more calculated and controlled evolution of Texas Democratic strategy.

“Beto was deemed to be the chosen one who would break the spell and obviously it didn’t happen,” Minutaglio observes. “He was a victim of inflated expectations. He seemed too ambitious and too coated with endorsements that didn’t resonate well outside the borders of Texas. People here don’t take kindly to the sense that a candidate is being shaped and endorsed by places like California or New York.”

Talarico, Minutaglio contends, studied O’Rourke’s missteps to avoid repeating them. “O’Rourke appeared on the cover of Vanity Fair magazine. Talarico has learned his lessons. I don’t mistake his quietude and his seminarian step for him not being a truly shrewd politician. He is that and then some. The ability to walk that fine line is rather amazing to me. I find it almost Obama-like. There’s a calmness about him and a thoughtfulness in public. He’s playing right now five-dimensional chess in Texas,” he says.

Part of that strategy involved building a political identity of his personal narrative and Christian faith. “It’s become that sense of armour – holding up the Bible – and people can’t get around it,” Minutaglio says. “Paxton, of course, is the greatest foil that anybody could pray to have. Talarico has found the cheat code in Texas.”

The contrast between the two candidates could hardly be starker. In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House voted overwhelmingly to impeach Paxton on 20 articles alleging misconduct, including bribery, abuse of office and obstruction of justice. The state senate later acquitted him.

A long-running state securities fraud case ended in 2024 with an agreement requiring Paxton to perform community service, pay restitution and complete legal ethics courses in exchange for prosecutors dropping the charges. Paxton has remained bogged down by public revelations regarding his personal life, including an alleged extramarital affair and a high-profile divorce.

Paxton, 63, has also been lethargic on the campaign trail with even Trump poking fun at his dress sense and speaking style. Jon Taylor, a professor of political science at the University of Texas at San Antonio, says: “Paxton is afraid to meet people. He tries to stay in this shell and avoid voters.

“Everywhere Talarico goes, he attracts a substantial crowd. He’s got rock star status. Talarico is charismatic, personable and tells stories that resonate. Meanwhile, his opponent is basically screaming that Talarico believes God is non-binary and that he’s ‘far left’. The message is viewed by voters as shrill and ineffective.”

As the race entered its final lap, national Republicans realised that Paxton’s vulnerability risked forfeiting a seat crucial to maintaining their narrow Senate majority. In response, conservative Super Pacs launched an unprecedented financial bombardment.

Musk, who moved Tesla, SpaceX and his personal residence to Texas, gave $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund in September. The Republican Super Pac subsequently transferred the money to the Texas Pac, which has blanketed the state’s 22 media markets with anti-Talarico advertising. The blitz focused almost entirely on trans culture-war themes, falsely claiming Talarico supported taxpayer-funded gender reassignment surgeries for minors.

At the same time, cracks have emerged in the conservative coalition along the Texas-Mexico border. While Trump made significant inroads among Latino voters in 2024, recent aggressive immigration raids and agricultural disruptions appear to have produced widespread buyer’s remorse.

Cristina Tzintzún Ramirez, a political consultant and former Democratic US Senate candidate, says: “I always say that the portion of Latino voters up for grabs are neither Republicans nor Democrats – they’re poor, and they need candidates who speak to their poverty, their pain and their power.

“Talarico leans more on a moral calling than a political persuasion, and that vision connects to people across a much larger swath of political persuasions than Democrats historically have reached. People are sick of the brazen political corruption and the system not working for ordinary working people.”

Democrats are taking nothing for granted in a state that Trump won by 14 percentage points against Kamala Harris in 2024. Talarico is still careful to characterise himself and his movement as the people-powered underdog against the oligarchy, the David taking on a Goliath that includes the world’s most powerful man and the world’s richest man. For supporters who have spent decades enduring Democratic defeats in Texas, the prospect of a Talarico victory feels less like an ordinary midterm result than a profound turning point.

Minutaglio comments: “If Talarico wins, it will be huge – a sea change in modern Texas history. The reverberation will rocket from the Fortune 500 companies in Dallas to the oil barons in Houston and the high-tech moguls around Austin. For decades, Texas has been addicted to deregulation and unfettered capitalism. Here’s a quiet seminarian who says, ‘Pump the brakes. Let’s think about oversight.’ It will challenge every perception of what Texas is.”
news.summary:

news.title: 10 House Races That Will Decide the Midterms
news.text: With Election Day just hours away, Newsweek has identified 10 House races featuring vulnerable incumbents, returning challengers and contrasting electorates that could reveal both who controls the chamber and how large the winning majority becomes. Democrats need a net gain of three seats to overturn the Republicans’ 220-215 majority. Inside Elections now projects Democratic gains of 20 to 30 seats; this suggests the late question may be less whether the House changes hands than how far the battlefield expands. Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, told Newsweek it would be "an utter shock if Republicans held the House at this point." "A lot of these districts were really close in 2024," Kondik said after reviewing the races featured on Newsweek’s list. He added that a more Democratic national environment should allow the party to capture some narrowly lost seats and threaten Republican incumbents elsewhere. Some of these races could help Democrats secure the 218 seats needed for control. Others would probably change hands only if the party is having an exceptionally strong night. Costas Panagopoulos, a distinguished professor of political science at Northeastern University, told Newsweek that such a wave would involve "a significant number of competitive races moving in a similar direction across a diversity of states and districts." Why It Matters Midterm elections have historically created difficulties for the president’s party, but House control is determined across 435 separate districts. Candidate strength, local political geography and redrawn boundaries can therefore interrupt a national trend. Key Points Pennsylvania’s 10th District Former television anchor Janelle Stelson is again challenging Republican Scott Perry, the former House Freedom Caucus chair who defeated her by approximately 5,100 votes in 2024. It is widely considered one of the most critical battlegrounds of the midterms. The Harrisburg-area district has a Cook Partisan Voting Index of R+3, yet Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate it Lean Democratic. A New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena Research Institute poll of 404 likely voters, conducted October 16 to 22 with a 5.7-point margin of error, found both candidates at 48 percent. Pennsylvania’s 7th District Republican Ryan Mackenzie, who captured this Lehigh Valley seat from Democrat Susan Wild by roughly 4,000 votes in 2024, faces retired Bethlehem firefighter and state union leader Bob Brooks. Both Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball lean Democratic. The same Pennsylvania survey, but with a sample size of 401 likely voters for this district, placed Brooks ahead by 49 percent to 44 percent, although the five-point advantage was within its 5.7-point margin of error. Arizona’s 6th District Republican Juan Ciscomani is defending a closely divided Tucson-area district against Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, a retired Marine and veterans’ advocate who served for 20 years in the military. Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball place AZ-06 in the Lean Democratic column, while Inside Elections rates it Tilt Democratic. Colorado’s 8th District Republican Gabe Evans, an Army veteran and former police officer, faces Democratic attorney and former state representative Manny Rutinel. Kamala Harris carried the district in 2024, but Evans won its House race by less than one percentage point, making CO-08 a notable example of ticket splitting. All three forecasters give Democrats an advantage, making this a test of whether the party can recover ground in a diverse suburban and exurban seat. Virginia’s 2nd District Two former Navy officers meet again in Hampton Roads: Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans, a former helicopter pilot and geriatric nurse practitioner, and former Democratic representative Elaine Luria, a retired commander. Kondik described VA-02 as relatively "low-hanging fruit" for Democrats and a useful early indicator because Virginia closes its polls before many other battleground states. Iowa’s 3rd District Republican Zach Nunn, an Air Force Reserve colonel, is seeking a third term against Democratic state senator and Lutheran minister Sarah Trone Garriott. The Des Moines-area district backed Trump by 4.5 points in 2024, when Nunn won by 3.9. Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the contest Lean Democratic, while Inside Elections calls it Tilt Democratic. North Carolina’s 1st District Democratic incumbent Don Davis, a former Air Force officer and state senator, faces retired Army colonel Laurie Buckhout for the second consecutive election. Republican lawmakers redrew the district for 2026, making territory that Davis narrowly retained two years ago substantially more favorable to the GOP. Kondik said NC-01 would test whether a district Republicans made more favorable to their party can still deliver a GOP gain in a difficult national environment. New York’s 17th District Republican Mike Lawler is defending a Hudson Valley seat narrowly carried by Kamala Harris against Cait Conley, an Army combat veteran and former national security official. Kondik identified Lawler as one of the few Republicans attempting to survive in a district won by the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee. Cook Political Report, Sabato’s Crystal Ball and Inside Elections all call NY-17 a toss-up. Wisconsin’s 3rd District Republican Derrick Van Orden, a retired Navy SEAL, defeated small-business owner Rebecca Cooke by 2.7 points in 2024. Their western Wisconsin rematch will test whether Democratic gains extend into more rural and small-city territory. Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball lean Democratic, with Inside Elections rating it Tilt Democratic. California’s 22nd District Republican former dairy farmer David Valadao, a repeated survivor of difficult Central Valley elections, faces Democratic college professor Randy Villegas under boundaries redrawn after voters approved Proposition 50. Kondik said the heavily Latino constituency would test whether movement back toward Democrats among Latino voters can overcome Valadao’s history of outperforming his party. Cook Political Report and Inside Elections rate CA-22 a toss-up, while Sabato’s Crystal Ball leans Democratic. How Large Could a Democratic Majority Become? Kondik said Democrats should move beyond the narrow House majorities of recent Congresses. "At this point, Democrats should be able to get into the 230s," he said. A narrow majority would consequently be a disappointing result for Democrats, even though it would transfer control. Inside Elections’ projection of a 20-to-30-seat gain broadly supports that assessment. Virginia may offer the quickest indication of scale. Kondik said VA-01 would suggest a firmer Democratic majority if it flipped, while an upset in VA-05 could point to a result exceeding the party’s 2018 performance. What Happens Next Virginia and Pennsylvania should provide early clues, while Arizona and California may take longer to resolve. Democratic gains in the 10 districts would establish the likely majority; victories in more Republican territory would indicate a wider wave. GOP survival across several regions would show that incumbency and local campaigns limited the national movement. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Sam Stevenson and James Debens Register for our November 10 discussion, 'Newsweek Webinar: How the Politics of AI Could Shape Midterms,' which will examine how AI policy played in key races, data centers, lobbying and the political lines that emerged.

news.title: Map Shows Senate Races Most Likely to Determine Control
news.text: The battle for a Senate majority is seen as competitive ahead of the midterm elections, and the balance of power is likely to come down to seven toss-up races in which both major parties have invested significant funds and energy. Tuesday's Senate races in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas are seen as the most competitive, all rated toss-ups, where neither Republicans nor Democrats have a clear edge heading into Election Day on Tuesday. With the exception of Michigan, all of those seats are currently held by Republicans. Seven States Could Determine Balance of Power: Map The GOP’s Senate majority has been seen as increasingly vulnerable in the final weeks ahead of the elections. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, compared to 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them. That means Democrats must flip four seats to win a majority—a task that was seen as an uphill battle at the beginning of election season due to the limited number of clear pickup opportunities. Maine and North Carolina represented the only GOP-held seats up for grabs in states that President Donald Trump either won by single digits or lost in 2024. But polling suggests Democrats have been able to expand the battleground to compete in more conservative states that Trump carried by double digits in his most recent elections, giving them a chance at winning control of Congress' upper chamber. Democrats are favored in every seat they currently hold, except for Michigan, and are seen as having an advantage to flip the North Carolina seat held by retiring Republican Thom Tillis, according to the Cook Political Report. They also hope to make a play for more conservative states like Mississippi and South Carolina, but Republicans still have an edge there. That leaves those seven core races as those that could determine control of the Senate in the next Congress. Bernadette Breslin, the National Republican Senatorial Committee's national press secretary, expressed confidence in Republicans' chances in a statement to Newsweek. "Senate Democrats’ socialist surge has reached a fever pitch, and their desperate conspiracies to defraud voters appear criminal. Common-sense voters across red-leaning battlegrounds are prepared to reject the dangerously unaffordable agendas of Abdul El-Sayed, Troy Jackson, and Mary Peltola—along with the Democrat Party’s dying brand," she said. Newsweek reached out to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) for comment via email. Why Senate Is Competitive for Democrats Despite Difficult Map The Senate has become more competitive as Trump’s approval rating fell to record lows in new polls. Historically, the party in the White House suffers losses in the midterms when the president is unpopular, so Trump’s declining approval has been seen as a red flag for Republicans in competitive races. The drop in Trump’s popularity has been attributed to increasing economic anxiety among voters amid a high cost of living. Soaring gas prices amid the Iran war, which has caused disruptions to the global oil supply, are also seen as a contributing factor. Stephen Farnsworth, political science professor at the University of Mary Washington, told Newsweek that Democrats appear likely to gain a seat in North Carolina and keep the seats they currently hold. They have been effective in recruiting “strong candidates” in those more conservative states that have emerged as battlegrounds, he said. “The main advantage Democratic candidates have is the unpopularity of the president, who seems to be campaigning largely in what are usually Republican-dominant states,” Farnsworth said. The latest poll from YouGov and The Economist showed Trump’s net approval rating at -19 points, with 39 percent approving and 58 percent disapproving of his job performance. It surveyed 1,440 registered voters October 23-26 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. It found that only 33 percent of Americans are satisfied, compared to 60 percent who are dissatisfied, with the direction of the country. Democrats are also more motivated, polling suggested. Fifty-three percent of Democratic respondents said they are “more enthusiastic” to vote this year compared to other elections, to only 40 percent of Republicans. Closest Senate Races in 2026 Polling has been close in the seven battleground races for U.S. Senate. The Cook Political Report classifies all seven as toss-ups, but Sabato’s Crystal Ball considered Alaska and Michigan to be Leans Democratic. Alaska The Alaska race between Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and Democratic former Representative Mary Peltola has become one of the most closely watched of the midterms, despite Trump winning the state by 14 points in 2024. Democrats view Peltola as one of their top recruits of the cycle in a state that has shifted a bit in recent years. A leftward shift in cities like Anchorage and Fairbanks has narrowed the GOP’s margins, and the state has an independent streak. The vast, rural state is difficult to poll, but recent surveys point to a close election. The latest Data for Progress poll gave Peltola a 2-point lead on the final round of ranked-choice voting, 51 percent to 49 percent, among 675 likely voters October 8-16. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Peltola also led by 2 points in an InsiderAdvantage poll, 50 percent to 48 percent. It surveyed 1,200 likely voters October 9-10 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. The Department of Justice (DOJ) sued the state of Alaska in October over the presence of another candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan. The DOJ said the “sole purpose” of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy is to “benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan," the DOJ wrote in its lawsuit. The lawsuit seeks to block the certification of the results if the incumbent does not win the election and if he would have won the election "had all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's ranked-choice process played out accordingly." Iowa In Iowa, a former battleground that has shifted toward Republicans over the past decade, Republican Representative Ashley Hinson is facing a competitive challenge from Democratic state Representative Josh Turek. Trump carried Iowa by 13 points in 2024, but the Senate race has become more competitive as the state faces the impact of tariffs and high diesel prices. Iowa was previously more competitive, backing former President Barack Obama twice before supporting Trump in all three of his runs. Hinson led by fewer than 2 points in an InsiderAdvantage poll, 47 percent to 45.5 percent, among 1,200 likely voters October 21-22, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Turek, however, had a single-point lead in a YouGov poll, 47 percent to 46 percent, conducted from 2,245 likely voters October 6-12, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. Hinson and Turek have aimed to strike more of a centrist tone in the final stretch of the campaign. Hinson has called for an “immediate end” to the Iran war, saying that the state has been “squeezed” economically because of it. Turek, meanwhile, has embraced a more moderate position on social issues like transgender athletes. Kansas The Kansas race emerged as a late battleground as polls showed a closer-than-expected race between GOP Senator Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton. Kansas has become more competitive as a farm state that could be particularly vulnerable to impacts of soaring diesel prices amid the Iran war. Democrats also view Hamilton, a pastor, as a particularly strong candidate in the historically conservative state against Marshall, a physician who has faced criticism after The New York Times reported that he allegedly sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills. Marshall led by a point in an InsiderAdvantage poll, 48 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 1,200 likely voters October 13-14 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. A YouGov poll was more favorable to Hamilton, showing him up 3 points, 48 percent to 45 percent, among 2,253 likely voters September 24-October 4. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points. Maine Maine is expected to be one of the closest races of the midterms as longtime GOP Senator Susan Collins faces a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. Collins has defied the partisan lean of the state, which backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 7 points in 2024, in the past due to her personal popularity and moderate image. But Democrats believe she may be more vulnerable in the difficult national environment that 2026 presents for Republicans. Democrats have faced a tumultuous season in Maine, despite hopes of flipping the seat. Jackson emerged as the nominee after Graham Platner, who won the primary in June, withdrew from the race following sexual assault allegations he has denied. Jackson emerged victorious from a Democratic convention over the summer. Jackson held a 2-point lead over Collins, 49 percent to 47 percent, among likely voters in a new Marist University poll. It was conducted October 22-25 among 1,449 registered voters and had a margin of error of plus or minus 6.6 percentage points. A Suffolk University poll gave Jackson a 2-point lead, 49 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 500 Maine voters October 8-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Michigan Michigan is the only toss-up seat held by a Democrat, retiring Senator Gary Peters. Progressive Abdul El-Sayed and GOP former Representative Mike Rogers are vying to succeed him in a swing state that narrowly went to Trump in 2024 after backing former President Joe Biden in 2020. Republicans believe that El-Sayed’s progressive record could alienate moderate voters who are key in the state that has backed Trump in two of his three White House bids. It’s a concern that some Democrats raised in the primaries, when El-Sayed defeated centrist Representative Haley Stevens, but the party hopes that the national environment will carry him across the finish line. Rogers has been courting moderate Democrats in hopes of pulling off a win in what appears to be a tougher year for the GOP. El-Sayed was up a single point, 47 percent to 46 percent, over Rogers in the latest InsiderAdvantage poll, which surveyed 1,200 likely voters October 21-22, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. The Democratic candidate had a 2-point lead, 50 percent to 48 percent, in a Marist University poll of 1,185 likely voters October 15-18. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.3 percentage points. Ohio Ohio is another Midwest former battleground state where Democrats hope to make a comeback this year. Ohio backed Obama in 2008 and 2012 before shifting rightward in 2016 and voting for Trump in all three of his runs. But former Senator Sherrod Brown is a rare Democrat who has found success in the Trump-era Ohio, winning in 2018 before losing in 2024. He is running against GOP Senator Jon Husted, the former lieutenant governor who was appointed to fill the vacancy left by Vice President JD Vance. The race has centered on economic issues like affordability, as well as the development of data centers. Polling has been close, but Brown has generally held a narrow lead. A new Suffolk University poll showed Brown with a 3-point lead over Husted, 47 percent to 44 percent, among 500 likely voters October 21-26. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Brown was up 2.3 points in the latest InsiderAdvantage poll of 1,200 likely voters October 21-22. Some 46.7 percent said they would vote for Brown to 44.4 percent for Husted. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Texas Democrats are hoping 2026 is the year they can flip Texas, which for decades has been one of the most conservative states in the nation. Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton unseated Senator John Cornyn in the GOP primary and is set to face Democratic state Representative James Talarico. Paxton, who has faced a series of scandals, is viewed as particularly vulnerable despite millions of dollars of outside spending by Republican groups to boost his campaign. Democrats have been let down in Texas before. They were increasingly optimistic about the state in the late 2010s due to growth in cities like Austin, Dallas and Houston, as well as their blue-trending suburbs. But the state shifted back rightward in 2024, backing Trump by 14 points, in part due to the stronger national environment for Republicans and his inroads with Latino voters. Polls have given Talarico an edge, but the race is still expected to be tight. Talarico led by 5 points, 50 percent to 45 percent, in a YouGov/Univision poll of 1,000 registered voters October 13-21. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. A Fox News poll, conducted among 1,398 likely voters October 15-19 by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, pointed to a tied race, with each candidate receiving support from 49 percent of respondents. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Seven U.S. Senate races could determine the balance of power in Congress' upper chamber after the November 3 midterm elections.

news.title: A Look at the South as Midterms Shift
news.text:
As polls shift almost uniformly in favor of Democrats in the final days of the 2026 midterm elections, some boosts for the opposition party are coming from the American South, a region that has been reliably Republican for decades.

Democrats currently lead in contested Senate, gubernatorial, and House races across the Southeast.

Republicans hold narrow leads or are falling behind in deep red areas such as South Carolina, Mississippi, and Texas. The party has all but given up on key Senate races in North Carolina and Georgia. In recent days, new warning signs are emerging for the GOP even in the reddest bastions, with polls showing closer races in Alabama and Louisiana.

It’s a situation that would have been unthinkable just a year ago, when the American South voted to return President Donald Trump to the White House by double-digit margins in most states.

Here’s where things stand south of the Mason-Dixon line as Election Day looms.

In the final days of the cycle, national attention is laser-focused on Mississippi’s Senate race.

In that race, District Attorney Scott Colom is giving incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith a solid fight. Cook Political Report recently downgraded the race from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican.”

The latest poll, sponsored by Democrats, found Hyde-Smith leading by just 3 percentage points.

Asked about the shift toward Democrats in Mississippi and elsewhere, Debbie Fancher told The Epoch Times that it was driven by “the promises broken” by Trump and Republicans.

“People have woken up to—the promises were not real,” Fancher said. “They were made as a campaign, not as something that was going to happen.”

Fancher is part of a group of Democrats who protest different causes every Friday in downtown Columbus, Mississippi.

Bridget Pieschel, a Mississippi voter who’s also part of the group, told The Epoch Times that people switching their votes were being driven by kitchen-table issues.

“I think people … who are seriously considering switching the party vote, their concern is they can’t afford gas. Our hospitals in the rural parts of the state are closing,” she said.

A voter attending a Trump rally in Mississippi gave a different appraisal.

“Every election is important. This one more so than most, I think, because we’re in the middle of a war and need a strong president,” John Brown of Huntsville, Alabama, who attended the Mississippi rally, told The Epoch Times. “President Trump is our leader, and he needs Republicans in Congress to finish the job.”

South Carolina has long been seen as a reliably conservative bastion.

In 2024, the Palmetto State voted for Trump by around 18 percentage points. South Carolinians last sent a Democrat to the Senate in 1998.

Despite that, Dr. Annie Andrews is closing the gap with incumbent Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who was appointed to the seat after her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), passed away.

In a recent poll by the South Carolina Policy Council, Graham was leading by just one percentage point.

The governor’s race looks more solid for Republicans, with state Attorney General Alan Wilson leading state Rep. Jermaine Johnson by about 10 percentage points.

Also of interest is the race for South Carolina’s First Congressional District. The Republican-favoring district is currently held by Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) (who is not seeking reelection after unsuccessfully pursuing a bid for governor) but sent a Democrat to Congress—Rep. Joe Cunningham (D-S.C.)—as recently as 2018.

Margaret Weir is one of the ticket-splitting South Carolinians who will drive Tuesday’s result.

Weir, a registered Republican, told The Epoch Times that she voted against her party because she wants a change in Washington.

“There needs to be some control in our federal government that is completely out of control right now, and there needs to be some disciplinary action for what’s going on,” she said. “It’s embarrassing.”

Weir said the shift in the South toward Democrats signals a broader realignment.

Bob Morrow said he voted for the Republicans on the ballot because he’s “tired of the Democrats.”

He approves of Trump’s presidency, saying: “He’s closed the borders. He’s getting rid of the trafficking of narcotics and fentanyl. Everything he said he’s done.”

Morrow echoed a defense of increasing prices that Trump and his defenders have given: that prices will decrease when the war with Iran is over.

Daniel Suggs, a Republican, split his ballot by voting for Wilson for governor and Andrews for Senate because he’s “very unhappy with the politics right now” as “there’s no stop on the presidency or no checks and balances.”

A poll in Louisiana shows that Democrats are closing the gap in the state’s Senate race.

Released Nov. 1 by Lincoln Park Strategies, it shows Democratic nominee Jamie Davis and Republican nominee Julia Letlow as tied, with each candidate sitting at 47 percent support.

Earlier this year, Letlow bested incumbent Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), a longtime Trump critic, for the Republican nomination.

After the Supreme Court struck down the Pelican State’s 2024 congressional map—which created a second majority-black congressional district in the Sixth Congressional District—the Republican-led Legislature redrew the state congressional map, leaving no competitive House races in the state this year.

One of the most-watched races of the entire cycle is in Texas, where Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has maintained a strong lead over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton across the election cycle.

Talarico has led in most polls conducted since July.

David Block of Rockwall told The Epoch Times that Paxton better reflects his Christian values.

“I think this is going to be another Beto O’Rourke scenario,” he said, citing the Texas state lawmaker who came within 2.5 percentage points of unseating incumbent Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) in 2018.

​Robin Shipman told The Epoch Times that a Paxton campaign event felt “almost like a prayer meeting.”

“He backs what I back: faith, freedom, the American way, Texas, and family,” she said.

Democrats also hope to use their advantages in this political environment to oust incumbent Republicans such as Gov. Greg Abbott and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick.

Abbott has faced criticism for his early support of data centers. His Democratic opponent, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has embraced public opposition to data centers in her campaign.

Two years ago, North Carolina was a top political battlefield that ultimately preferred Trump to Vice President Kamala Harris by 3.3 percentage points.

Now, North Carolinians are seemingly on track to send former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper to the Senate by margins that could end former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley’s political career.

In an average of recent polls, Cooper leads by about 11.7 percentage points.

In a sign that Republicans are abandoning the state’s Senate race this year, the Senate Leadership Fund has withdrawn funding from North Carolina entirely and instead sent it to other embattled states such as Kansas.

A key House race in the state’s First Congressional District is also closely contested.

Republicans have selected retired Army Col. Laurie Buckhout to face incumbent Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.). Though the district was altered to favor Republicans, most analysts consider the seat a pure toss-up.

Though the Senate race is close in South Carolina, the same isn’t true in the Peach State.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is overwhelmingly favored by observers and polling to hold onto his seat in the blue-shifting state, leading Republican nominee Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) by 9.8 percentage points in an average of four recent polls.

The governor’s race is closer, with Republican Rick Jackson leading Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms by 1.2 percentage points in an average of five recent polls.

As the Atlanta metropolitan area has grown, the state as a whole has trended increasingly toward Democrats in recent years, beginning with President Joe Biden’s victory over Trump in 2020.

In 2024, amid a favorable national environment, Trump reclaimed Georgia by about 2.2 percentage points; Republicans’ lowest margin of victory in the Peach State since 1996.

Several races are close in Florida, though Republicans have better signals in the GOP-dominated Sunshine State.

In the Senate race, Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) leads state Rep. Angie Nixon—a member of the Democratic Socialists of America—by 5.7 percentage points in recent polling averages.

The two are vying for the remainder of the term in the seat vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

A fight for the governor’s mansion is also on, with Gov. Ron DeSantis ineligible to seek a third term.

In polling of the gubernatorial race, Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) leads former Rep. David Jolly, who left the GOP in 2018 and joined the Democratic Party last year.

Unlike some of their regional neighbors, Alabama Republicans are well positioned in the gubernatorial and Senate races, according to polls.

Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) leads the gubernatorial race by 10 percentage points in an average of recent polls, though one poll showed challenger Doug Jones within 3 percent.

Rep. Barry Moore leads Senate polls by more than 15 percentage points.

In one congressional race in Alabama, Rep. Shomari Figures (D-Ala.) faces an uphill battle to hold onto his seat in a newly redrawn district.

He faces a challenge from Republican state Rep. Rhett Marques after the state redrew its congressional maps in line with the Supreme Court’s ruling on the Voting Rights Act.

Figures’s southern Alabama district was drawn earlier to include more black voters, helping him win by about nine percentage points in 2024.

Though the district is less favorable to Democrats this year, Cook Political Report rates the seat as leaning Republican, and the latest poll found the race tied.

Bob Morrow said he voted for the Republicans on the ballot because he’s “tired of the Democrats.”

He approves of Trump’s presidency, saying: “He’s closed the borders. He’s getting rid of the trafficking of narcotics and fentanyl. Everything he said he’s done.”

Morrow echoed a defense of increasing prices that Trump and his defenders have given: that prices will decrease when the war with Iran is over.

Daniel Suggs, a Republican, split his ballot by voting for Wilson for governor and Andrews for Senate because he’s “very unhappy with the politics right now” as “there’s no stop on the presidency or no checks and balances.”

A poll in Louisiana shows that Democrats are closing the gap in the state’s Senate race.

Released Nov. 1 by Lincoln Park Strategies, it shows Democratic nominee Jamie Davis and Republican nominee Julia Letlow as tied, with each candidate sitting at 47 percent support.

Earlier this year, Letlow bested incumbent Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), a longtime Trump critic, for the Republican nomination.

After the Supreme Court struck down the Pelican State’s 2024 congressional map—which created a second majority-black congressional district in the Sixth Congressional District—the Republican-led Legislature redrew the state congressional map, leaving no competitive House races in the state this year.

One of the most-watched races of the entire cycle is in Texas, where Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has maintained a strong lead over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton across the election cycle.

Talarico has led in most polls conducted since July.

David Block of Rockwall told The Epoch Times that Paxton better reflects his Christian values.

“I think this is going to be another Beto O’Rourke scenario,” he said, citing the Texas state lawmaker who came within 2.5 percentage points of unseating incumbent Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) in 2018.

​Robin Shipman told The Epoch Times that a Paxton campaign event felt “almost like a prayer meeting.”

“He backs what I back: faith, freedom, the American way, Texas, and family,” she said.

Democrats also hope to use their advantages in this political environment to oust incumbent Republicans such as Gov. Greg Abbott and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick.

Abbott has faced criticism for his early support of data centers. His Democratic opponent, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has embraced public opposition to data centers in her campaign.

Two years ago, North Carolina was a top political battlefield that ultimately preferred Trump to Vice President Kamala Harris by 3.3 percentage points.

Now, North Carolinians are seemingly on track to send former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper to the Senate by margins that could end former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley’s political career.

In an average of recent polls, Cooper leads by about 11.7 percentage points.

In a sign that Republicans are abandoning the state’s Senate race this year, the Senate Leadership Fund has withdrawn funding from North Carolina entirely and instead sent it to other embattled states such as Kansas.

A key House race in the state’s First Congressional District is also closely contested.

Republicans have selected retired Army Col. Laurie Buckhout to face incumbent Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.). Though the district was altered to favor Republicans, most analysts consider the seat a pure toss-up.

Though the Senate race is close in South Carolina, the same isn’t true in the Peach State.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is overwhelmingly favored by observers and polling to hold onto his seat in the blue-shifting state, leading Republican nominee Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) by 9.8 percentage points in an average of four recent polls.

The governor’s race is closer, with Republican Rick Jackson leading Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms by 1.2 percentage points in an average of five recent polls.

As the Atlanta metropolitan area has grown, the state as a whole has trended increasingly toward Democrats in recent years, beginning with President Joe Biden’s victory over Trump in 2020.

In 2024, amid a favorable national environment, Trump reclaimed Georgia by about 2.2 percentage points; Republicans’ lowest margin of victory in the Peach State since 1996.

Several races are close in Florida, though Republicans have better signals in the GOP-dominated Sunshine State.

In the Senate race, Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) leads state Rep. Angie Nixon—a member of the Democratic Socialists of America—by 5.7 percentage points in recent polling averages.

The two are vying for the remainder of the term in the seat vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

A fight for the governor’s mansion is also on, with Gov. Ron DeSantis ineligible to seek a third term.

In polling of the gubernatorial race, Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) leads former Rep. David Jolly, who left the GOP in 2018 and joined the Democratic Party last year.

Unlike some of their regional neighbors, Alabama Republicans are well positioned in the gubernatorial and Senate races, according to polls.

Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) leads the gubernatorial race by 10 percentage points in an average of recent polls, though one poll showed challenger Doug Jones within 3 percent.

Rep. Barry Moore leads Senate polls by more than 15 percentage points.

In one congressional race in Alabama, Rep. Shomari Figures (D-Ala.) faces an uphill battle to hold onto his seat in a newly redrawn district.

He faces a challenge from Republican state Rep. Rhett Marques after the state redrew its congressional maps in line with the Supreme Court’s ruling on the Voting Rights Act.

Figures’s southern Alabama district was drawn earlier to include more black voters, helping him win by about nine percentage points in 2024.

Though the district is less favorable to Democrats this year, Cook Political Report rates the seat as leaning Republican, and the latest poll found the race tied.
